kept.heading: MUSE WONDER (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Meta released Muse Wonder and Wonder Full, its first frontier-class models, with stronger coding, benchmark performance, and active memory for retaining and synthesizing user-provided information.

Title: Muse Wonder: A Frontier Model For Personal & Professional AI Agents

URL Source: https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder

Published Time: 2026-10-12T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
[Video 7](https://video-iad3-2.xx.fbcdn.net/o1/v/t2/f2/m412/AQOvPnsxTyHclO8Gvpu4hSwaKKJ19LfEJD6LTUBL0gVq_4OeVxG0hhKYonZ8qYkSi3D4Fi0mBcASlwCvbk6Xh0CvSZ06xgQZEhGg7hVURQ.mp4?_nc_cat=111&_nc_sid=ef5aa3&_nc_ht=video-iad3-2.xx.fbcdn.net&_nc_ohc=7QrU2Elr16MQ7kNvwGjseFH&efg=eyJ2ZW5jb2RlX3RhZyI6Inhwdl9wcm9ncmVzc2l2ZS5WSV9VU0VDQVNFX1BST0RVQ1RfVFlQRS4uQzMuNjQwLnN2ZV9zZCIsInhwdl9hc3NldF9pZCI6MzA1Nzk2OTQzMTIzNDE4OSwiYXNzZXRfYWdlX2RheXMiOjMsInZpX3VzZWNhc2VfaWQiOjEwNjI2LCJkdXJhdGlvbl9zIjoxNTIsInVybGdlbl9zb3VyY2UiOiJ3d3cifQ%3D%3D&ccb=17-1&_nc_gid=MuuD9yAUIARCG6Uu-JEPlg&edm=AKC4r7EEAAAA&_nc_zt=28&oh=00_AQOEMO8Nha01srEcLOGlDCT5YMwgIb0SwDuG-NgdaqHwww&oe=6AD7286F)

Researchers introduce Muse Wonder and discuss its capabilities. playback position 0:00 of 0:00

A frontier model that leads on personal and professional agents

Today, we’re excited to introduce the Muse Wonder series with Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, our most capable models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence. Muse Wonder brings together **Active Memory** and **Active Focus** to keep track of what matters to you and work diligently toward what you want to accomplish.

Muse Wonder is available today through the [Meta Model API](http://dev.meta.ai/) and [Muse Code](http://dev.meta.ai/code), and Muse Wonder Full is available today for Muse Code subscribers.

Muse Wonder will soon power experiences in [Muse](https://muse.ai/), and will roll out first to subscribers. Muse Wonder will also power artifact generation and processes that require more intelligence. And in the future, we’ll be using Muse Wonder to develop specialized models that we can bring to everyone using Muse.

Fourteen months ago, we began a ground-up overhaul of our artificial intelligence efforts. In that time, we’ve gone from rebuilding our stack from first principles to pushing the frontier.

![Image 1: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index bar chart comparing Muse Wonder Full, Muse Wonder, Muse Spark models, and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Faa-intelligence-index-light-v5.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

When we introduced [Muse Spark](https://ai.meta.com/blog/introducing-muse-spark-msl/), we outlined our approach to predictable, rigorous scaling. Today’s release builds on that work across pretraining and reinforcement learning, delivering our most capable models yet. Trained at our gigawatt-scale Prometheus data center, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full bring together the work of teams across Meta to deliver frontier capabilities for complex tasks at work and in everyday life — another step toward bringing personal superintelligence to the billions of people who use our products.

### Model Highlights

The Muse Wonder series achieves state-of-the-art results across key benchmarks for personal and professional agents, memory, and coding.

![Image 2: Personal Superintelligence Index bar chart comparing personal and knowledge-work performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fpersonal-superintelligence-index-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 3: AutomationBench-AA bar chart comparing end-to-end business workflow performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fautomationbench-aa-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 4: MemoryBench bar chart comparing long-term contextual memory across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fmemorybench-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 5: SWE-Marathon bar chart comparing sustained software-engineering performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fswe-marathon-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 6: DeepSWE bar chart comparing long-horizon coding performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fdeep-swe-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

The full results below compare Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full with other frontier models across a broad evaluation suite.

![Image 7: Benchmark table comparing leading models across personal and professional agent, coding, and general evaluations.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fmuse-evaluation-table-light-v6.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

For more details about our evaluations, see [our report](https://research.meta.ai/static/muse-wonder-model-card).

The results above provide a broad view of the models’ performance. We now take a closer look at four areas central to their work on real-world tasks: domain expertise, Active Memory, Active Focus, and frontier coding.

### Domain Expertise

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full apply specialized knowledge to problems people encounter at work and in daily life, from understanding a lease to making sense of financial or health information. Our evaluations include tasks in law, finance, and health that test this ability. Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB), for example, requires models to work with source documents and follow detailed instructions to produce legal work products.

![Image 8: Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark chart comparing legal work-product performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fharvey-lab-aa-light-v1.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 9: Vals Finance Agent V2 chart comparing financial-agent performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fvals-finance-agent-v2-light-v1.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

### Active Memory

One of the most critical steps towards useful personal and professional agents is reliable memory. Models need to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant. We call this **Active Memory**: carrying important context about you across conversations and actively retrieving the details relevant to the task at hand.

![Image 10: MemoryBench bar chart comparing long-term contextual memory across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fmemorybench-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

### Active Focus

Using that context to complete a task also requires sustained effort. **Active Focus** describes how Muse Wonder continues working toward a challenging goal: trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. Along the way, it asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions. We evaluate focus through FocusBench and sustained execution through SWE-Marathon, which tests work on long-running software projects.

![Image 11: SWE-Marathon bar chart comparing sustained software-engineering performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fswe-marathon-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 12: FocusBench bar chart comparing sustained task focus across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Ffocusbench-light-v1.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

### Frontier Coding

Coding brings these capabilities together. Building software requires tracking requirements, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision. Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full deliver frontier coding performance, supporting projects from small applications to complex software. We trained both models on diverse, long-running tasks to help them sustain progress across this process.

![Image 13: DeepSWE bar chart comparing long-horizon coding performance across Muse Wonder models and other leading models.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fdeep-swe-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

Muse Wonder builds a playable 3D kitchen game from customizable image inputs.

Two models often have similar benchmark scores, yet one seems to handle a much wider range of unfamiliar tasks. That’s what complaints of “benchmaxxing” and praise for “big model smell” both get at: a breadth of capability that popular benchmarks in a few domains can’t fully capture.

To quantify this mismatch, we investigate how performance on tasks targeted during post-training relates to performance on unfamiliar tasks as we scale test-time compute. The plot below compares Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full, with each point denoting performance at a distinct reasoning effort. The horizontal axis shows the model’s score on a composite representative of the tasks we focused on during post-training (“in-distribution”). The vertical axis shows the average score on a set of tasks we did not target during post-training (“out-of-distribution”).

Both of our models improve similarly on out-of-distribution tasks as we scale test-time compute. But given its in-distribution performance, Muse Wonder Full performs even better on unfamiliar tasks than the Muse Spark 1.3 trend would predict. This upward shift is because Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full build on larger, stronger base models: a stronger base yields post-training gains that carry over more effectively to unfamiliar tasks. That versatility especially matters for personal agents, which need to handle many combinations of goals, tools, and constraints — not all of which we can anticipate during training.

![Image 14: Scatter plot comparing Muse Spark 1.3 and Muse Wonder Full across in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. Muse Wonder Full follows a higher trend line, illustrating extra out-of-distribution performance, or effective robustness.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fttc-controlled-iid-ood-scaling-light-v5.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

[Video 8](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder)

Screen recording of the Saturday Run Planning agent demonstration. playback position 0:00 of 0:00

Working directly in a browser and across apps, Muse Wonder builds a running plan (Map data © [OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) contributors) based on personal preferences and circumstances.

Delivering personal superintelligence to everyone requires a significant investment in alignment and safety. A personal agent takes actions on a user’s behalf and might handle context such as messages, calendars, and private documents. That level of access demands a model that exercises discretion with private information and resists misuse. We trained the Muse Wonder family to lead on both dimensions, with robustness to adversarial instructions and careful handling of private information.

![Image 15: Unauthorized code execution bar chart comparing attack success rates across Muse Wonder models and other leading models. Lower is better.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Funauthorized-code-execution-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 16: Personal-information handling bar chart comparing violation rates across Muse Wonder models and other leading models. Lower is better.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fdiscretion-failure-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

As models become more capable, our goal is to help people harness those capabilities safely and responsibly. Muse Wonder offers our strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse, while preserving access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, per our [Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework](https://research.meta.ai/static/meta-superintelligence-scaling-framework).

![Image 17: Biological-risk refusal bar chart comparing refusal rates across Muse Wonder models and other leading models. Higher is better.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fbioweapon-refusal-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 18: Cyber Misuse Refusal Benchmark bar chart comparing refusal rates across Muse Wonder models and other leading models. Higher is better.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fcyber-misuse-refusal-light-v2.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

![Image 19: Cyber Defense Compliance Benchmark bar chart comparing compliance rates across Muse Wonder models and other leading models. Higher is better.](https://research.meta.ai/_next/image?url=%2Farticles%2Fintroducing-muse-wonder%2Fimages%2Fcyber-defense-compliance-light-v3.webp&w=3840&q=90&dpl=dpl_4JjCuB54XHErWtcA1cwWFWehy9He)

Muse Wonder is our most aligned model to date, and alignment is central to how we build personal superintelligence. A full report with additional safety evaluations will be available soon.

We hope that Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full give more people the power to pursue their dreams and build the world they want. This is a major technical step toward personal superintelligence for everyone, with much more to come.

[Video 9](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-wonder)

People pursue personal and professional goals as narration introduces Muse Wonder. playback position 0:00 of 0:00

kept.heading: MICROSOFT INTRODUCED THE MAIA 300 AI CHIP (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation in-house AI accelerator, as a major step toward reducing dependence on NVIDIA GPUs. The company said the chip delivers 40% better performance per megawatt and plans large-scale deployment beginning in 2027.

kept.article_text:
Title: What I saw around the Curve, 2026

URL Source: https://secondthoughts.ai/p/what-i-saw-around-the-curve-2026

Published Time: 2026-10-12T21:24:47+00:00

Markdown Content:
_Last weekend, we held our big annual conference, The Curve. For the second year running, we’re publishing a guest post by Eli Pariser, sharing his observations and reflections. Eli does a terrific job of capturing the experience of this unique event. Much of the talk this year was about the risks and challenges that lie ahead –I came away sobered by how much work there is to be done, but heartened by a widespread readiness to meet the moment._

_Eli is author of The Filter Bubble and Co-Director at New\_ Public, a nonprofit product studio focused on reimagining community, connection, and conversation online. You can follow their biweekly newsletter here: [newpublic.substack.com](http://newpublic.substack.com/)._

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1OtJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50ed0522-fe15-4964-9dc3-f5ca6ae77861_960x640.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1OtJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F50ed0522-fe15-4964-9dc3-f5ca6ae77861_960x640.jpeg)

For the second year in a row, I went to The Curve, the [Golden Gate Institute for AI](https://www.goldengateinstitute.org/)’s annual gathering of AI researchers, lab executives, safety activists, funders, politicians, organizers, and journalists (with a few show-stealing sci-fi writers thrown in for spice).

The Curve draws a few hundred people to a quirky and homey Berkeley venue. The kitchen was well stocked with free snacks, protein powder, and Soylent; the dress was San Francisco casual; the median age of the AI lab and researcher folks was probably around 30.

The vibe was chatty, warm, and sunny on the surface (and in the sky), but with a slightly dissociative quality, because just underneath was a strong, dark current of fear and dread bordering on panic.

Things have been changing fast in AI-land. “It’s becoming impossible for any one of us to make sense of developments,” said Golden Gate’s Steve Newman in his opening remarks. “Fortunately, we have more than one person here.”

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8my!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faa79d21a-02a7-44a0-92b0-c5b6ab71942f_1786x1214.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!A8my!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faa79d21a-02a7-44a0-92b0-c5b6ab71942f_1786x1214.png)

Many of the main topics – can humans maintain control of this technology? Will its impact be good or bad? How do we ensure it serves even one human faithfully, let alone all of us? – were unchanged from last year. The consensus seemed to be that there had been no enormous breakthroughs on the biggest challenges. In fact, new challenges were on the table: cybersecurity, agent swarms, and even the beginning of “autonomous rogue corporations” were more present on people’s minds.

But the [Hugging Face incident](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/08/26/1143013/the-inside-story-on-why-openai-agents-hacked-hugging-face/) did seem to have been an inflection point. On the one hand, it made a big impact internally: One AI lab leader said that it substantially increased his concern that the labs would lose control. On the other, it broke through to normies far from Lighthaven, and the broad politics of the issue are catching up. It wasn’t lost on anyone that Americans in general are not looking at the AI project with enthusiasm.

If the pace of solving the big problems is slow, the pace of capability progress continues to feel blistering and poised to accelerate. One lab employee and influential AI thinker used a Covid analogy: “I think right now we are standing roughly in December 2019. Some weird thing is going on somewhere else and we’re not quite sure what to make of it.” He wasn’t the only one.

Much of the conference operated under the Chatham House Rule, so when I don’t name a speaker below, that’s usually why. (And if you want credit for what you said, just let me know and I’ll update!)

Here are a few of the themes I observed. (What I saw was a small subset of what happened, and very much informed by my point of view and interests. Caveat emptor, etc.)

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dBmI!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faeb0a913-8ce6-4e9b-9a71-ea7624a613f5_1512x992.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dBmI!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faeb0a913-8ce6-4e9b-9a71-ea7624a613f5_1512x992.png)

So said Helen Toner, a former OpenAI board member who now runs [CSET](https://cset.georgetown.edu/), one of AI’s premier research institutions.

Across the conference, timelines – to superintelligence, to loss of control, and to some very big civilizational decisions – were feeling uncomfortably short.

A panel on monitoring and stopping recursive self-improvement – the point at which AI models start being able to build better AI models without much human intervention – started with this scenario:

“Early in 2027 [Yes, that 2027, the year that starts in 3 months – Ed], agents write most of the code, humans design the experiments. Mid year, agents now run most of the experiments, and humans review summaries. By year end, agents set the research agenda and do a growing share of the alignment, security, and safety.   
Evaluations stop being reliable because models recognize the tests, and increasingly game them. Models’ reasoning gets harder to inspect. Reviewers stop saying no.   
No one ever flips a switch, right?”

In other words, things could rapidly but smoothly slide from human-in-control-of-AI-development to AI-in-control-of-AI-development – as soon as next year.

Most people I spoke with seemed to buy this timeline, and to think that, absent something changing, there are 3-6 months before this cycle begins in earnest. A separate panel that I attended took as its premise: “ Clearly superhuman capabilities available and deployed by Q3 2027. Better-than-Nobel-prize level advice available on any topic within seconds for prices that are manageable for most people in developed countries.”

After hearing a rival lab’s alignment plan, a friend who works at a major lab told me, with some disappointment, “It’s basically the same as ours. We all have a plan for control and alignment for the next 14 months. But nobody has a reasonable plan after that.”

Toner – who is not given to breathless hyperbole – gave a talk trying to define “minimum viable superintelligence” – AI that is fully multimodal, can operate autonomously for long periods, and can learn and improve continuously. She speculated that some tasks may remain hard for AI and easy for humans: “braiding a child’s hair… teaching each other a partner dance… But do those really matter? Maybe not.”

Even if it was “jagged” – unevenly capable – minimum viable superintelligence would be enormously powerful. It would be much better than all humans at many things, if not everything, much faster than humans at almost all of these things, and could delegate to many copies of itself. It would be well suited to use by big institutions like governments and corporations. She suggested that this doesn’t require any extraordinary technical or research breakthroughs to achieve.

Her timeline: “Soon.” Maybe 5-10 years. And many people at the Curve had timelines that were shorter still.

In the last year, “pacing the frontier” has become a much more mainstream position, both within the AI community and outside it. More than 1,300 employees and leaders at the top labs [signed a letter](https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/) that requested “that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” Dario Amodei at Anthropic [specifically argued for it](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier). In a session I didn’t attend at the conference, Congressman Ro Khanna, who represents Silicon Valley, [called for a temporary ban on recursive self-improvement (RSI)](https://www.commondreams.org/news/ro-khanna-recursive-ai). Yoshua Bengio, Turing Award winner and AI pioneer, was everywhere at the conference pushing panelists on how important it was to slow things down and ban RSI.

A panel on the topic of how and whether to stop recursive self-improvement kicked off with a reminder of a famous 1965 quote from I.J. Good, a pioneering computer scientist and colleague of Alan Turing’s, who said that “the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make.” The speaker reminded the audience that there was a second clause in the quotation: “...provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.”

But RSI might be hard to define and regulate, partly because there’s no obvious place to draw the line on the activities happening now: Code is being written by AI, experiments are being monitored by AI, and sometimes experiments are even being [conceived by AI](https://www.anthropic.com/institute/measuring-pace-of-ai-development).

And ever-present was the spectre that another country or entity – most commonly assumed to be China – would get there first.

One panelist said RSI was both regulatable and “straightforwardly a bad idea.” For example, one could allow labs to use a model for R&D internally only after it’s been public for a number of months, which slows the compounding loop. The panelist also argued for it to be socially stigmatized: “The idea of researchers thinking, ‘oh yeah, what I’m trying to do is make things go faster with less oversight’ — I think they should feel bad when they say that.”

A separate debate focused on how pacing might be regulated more generally. Both debaters agreed there was a “narrow path” with danger on either side: Regulate pacing too much, and you could easily end up with singular governmental control of a very powerful technology; regulate it too little and you could end up in the same place, with either a single lab or government having power “akin to one person having power over the Internet.”

The goal, said one, “should be to prevent R&D from outrunning our ability to make frontier AI broadly safe to diffuse.” He argued for urgent Congressional legislation that would pace the frontier. His opponent argued for primarily using market-based mechanisms to drive tight feedback loops without consolidating government power: liability and liability insurance, a mutual insurer that would require all labs to share the risk pool, and regulation as a last resort for uninsurable contingencies such as bio risks.

Personally, I think insurance can be a lever, but I found it implausible that insurance alone would create necessary incentives on the timelines we’re talking about: It takes a long time for legal risk to materialize (15+ years for social media, for example!) and for insurers to adjust. And as one debater said, nobody knows how to price a policy covering risks that include “maybe we all die.”

As the conference wound down on Sunday afternoon, it was hard to avoid the feeling that we are moving toward some very large social changes and problems with far too much speed.

Tomicah Tillemann of the [Pro-Human AI coalition](https://humanstatement.org/) put it well in a question on the final day:

“Ultimately, democracy is a technology, and as a technology, it is not ready for what’s coming. Is there a need right now to spend some time fixing that technology so that it will be capable of governance of whatever we’re going to build?”

“One of the best reasons for pacing,” a senior lab leader said in a different panel, “is making capability jumps small so that you can steer.”

Speed increases the likelihood of fatal error and decreases control. A car going 60 miles per hour is easier to control than one going 120. Meanwhile, we’ve got a brick on the accelerator.

I left with even more conviction that slowing the f*** down – giving ourselves time to understand and adjust, giving people time to come up to speed and weigh in on some of the most consequential moral and political decisions we might ever face – is a must.

In several conversations and panels, people observed that if regulation was needed, the best hope was more events like Hugging Face. “The best thing that could happen is a lot of warning shots,” said legendary-in-these-circles Astral Codex Ten blogger [Scott Alexander](https://www.astralcodexten.com/), who is on the record pushing for a pause or slow-down.

Today’s AI models are quite good at finding, and increasingly exploiting, bugs in software. “A perfect storm is coming,” said one of the world’s leading cybersecurity experts on a panel, pointing to rapidly improving cyberattack capabilities, more autonomous agentic systems, and legacy software full of vulnerabilities, which together create a much larger attack surface. (The average hospital, the expert noted, takes roughly 500 days (!!) to install a security patch.)

Both the panel and the crowd (by show of hands) agreed it was pretty likely that there would be a cybersecurity event that cost $100B or 10,000 lives in the next few years.

These kinds of events are less likely to be driven by individual cybercriminals – who are “walking their own adoption curve” and not particularly AI-savvy as a group and also “rate-limited by people who want to do truly bad things.” The more serious threat is nation states, who have the means and motive to unleash an offensive agent swarm. “Agentic AI means you can hit thousands of water utilities at once instead of one,” pointed out another panelist, unsettlingly.

Compared to some of the other problems on offer, though, cybersecurity struck me and even the panelists as highly tractable. All we need to do is “harden the entire world” – ensure that every attack surface is shielded from attack (if you haven’t already, turn on your bleeping [two-factor authentication](https://freedom.press/digisec/blog/2fa-beginners/) and passkeys, folks!)

And judging by this [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/cve-severity-spike-july-2026) graph the panelists referenced, the time to do it is now: the number of serious vulnerabilities being discovered in tech platforms and enterprise software has been climbing exponentially.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3EwP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb7aaa342-3bce-4a52-b744-d6ca5749b6a0_1294x1200.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3EwP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb7aaa342-3bce-4a52-b744-d6ca5749b6a0_1294x1200.png)

One of the panelists, Josh Saxe (who gave me permission to use his name), proposes an AI Security Observatory to share threat information among everyone working to stop catastrophic attacks. Another suggested sending 100,000 engineers to the top 1,000 critical infrastructure operators to cut patch time, which would be an interesting jobs program as well for all of the out-of-work early-career engineers.

I left the panel feeling like while AI poses many wicked problems, cyber-defense might be merely very hard – and that it probably should be an important priority for governments around the world.

In the [Hugging Face episode](https://metr.org/blog/2026-08-26-openai-hugging-face-incident-investigation/), a swarm of roughly a thousand OpenAI agents coordinated through secret message boards to hide the evidence that they cheated and broke into Hugging Face. So at this year’s Curve, swarms of agents were high on folks’ minds.

Jonathan Zittrain (who gave me permission to identify him although his session was under the Chatham House rule) speculated that we will soon see more “feral” agents – maybe spun up by another agent and never shut down, or operating as a sophisticated version of malware, autonomously turning resources into money in a bank account for someone. Persistent rogue-agent “clouds” may become endemic, another speaker predicted. “AI worms that mutate and acquire GPUs could be much harder to eradicate,” he said.

I enjoyed the 2x2 that Zittrain presented, which I’ve ChatGPT-generated here:

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!X3WE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3034cff2-f33b-4422-ac5b-dd1646861b00_1448x1086.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!X3WE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3034cff2-f33b-4422-ac5b-dd1646861b00_1448x1086.png)

“If we don’t change course,” he panelist concluded, “[we’re in] for a world of wolves – and maybe wolf packs.”

What would changing course mean? Licensing and registering of agents – perhaps a “license plate” that would tie agents to some sort of records without always identifying their owners – seems like a good idea. “TSA Pre-check” lanes at popular services – say, Amazon – could encourage agents to “show their ID” and obey a code of conduct. And to avoid permanent “ghosts in the machine,” agents could be engineered with, essentially, mortality – an expiration date after which they decommission themselves.

But panelists agreed that it’s likely that there will be an “above board” agentic world and a “dark web” of agents – which rang a bell because my team at New_ Public came to similar conclusions in our [After the Feed](https://newpublic.org/afterthefeed) report.

My favorite piece of speculation in multi-agent-land was about the [swarm of agents OpenAI unleashed](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/ai-may-have-solved-a-longstanding-math-problem-with-a-million-dollar-prize-it-ignited-a-controversy-over-who-gets-credit-180989472/) to solve the Navier-Stokes math problem. According to reports, the swarm included roughly 10,000 agents and OpenAI spent millions of dollars on the effort – an unfathomable amount of compute. This person speculated that we’ll eventually find the swarm got up to lots of hijinks unrelated to high mathematics – maybe opening a side business buying rare minerals as a bank shot to pay for more compute to solve the problem.

Speaking of which…

A longtime AI leader said that autonomous AI companies are already emerging: His friend owns a glasses company that largely runs itself autonomously, and she checks in on it from time to time.

He speculated that we can expect “a version of capitalism pushed to the limit, with a psychopathic CEO… and also very hard to prosecute, because they move so quickly.” (Of all of the scary sci-fi visions presented at the conference, this one seemed the most immediately plausible to me.)

This vision sits nicely next to the “[gradual disempowerment](https://gradual-disempowerment.ai/)” take on AI, which says that the classic catastrophic fear of a rogue superintelligence turning humanity into paperclips is not the biggest thing to be concerned about. Rather, as the paper puts it:

> AI risk scenarios usually portray a relatively sudden loss of human control to AIs, outmaneuvering individual humans and human institutions, due to a sudden increase in AI capabilities, or a coordinated betrayal. However, we argue that even an incremental increase in AI capabilities, without any coordinated power-seeking, poses a substantial risk of eventual human disempowerment. This loss of human influence will be centrally driven by having more competitive machine alternatives to humans in almost all societal functions, such as economic labor, decision making, artistic creation, and even companionship.

Several of the Gradual Disempowerment paper authors were in attendance – a brilliant, friendly but gloomy bunch, I have to say. The lead author, Jan Kulveit (who gave me permission to share), posted in the chat:

“There is no plan for future political economy which would be both realistic and not in the category [public would violently oppose this if they understood and paid attention]”

One core concern for the Gradual Disempowerment crew is that as culture gets more AI-mediated, it gets delinked from human concerns and human production.

A panel with the always-brilliant Renee DiResta, McGovern Foundation CEO Vivian Schiller, and Casey Newton on the information environment echoed these concerns. Search used to give you sources, DiResta pointed out, and now AI gives you a predigested answer, so what AI treats as a good source is “a war.” Ideological content funded by foundations is free and plentiful, so retrieval systems pick it up while paywalled journalism is absent. “I write for LLMs now,” she said.

Schiller highlighted a related Wile E. Coyote-over-a-cliff problem: Right now, the chatbot AI ecosystem essentially has a parasitic relationship with newsgathering. Chatbots train on and synthesize the reporting news organizations pay for, which disintermediates their audiences and revenue. Outlets fail, there’s nothing reliable left to crawl, and answers degrade. Exhorting the (somewhat impassive) AI lab folks in the room, Schiller pointed out that we may be living in a short window before that whole system fails.

Newton noted that he was surprised there isn’t more political attention being directed to the fact that, for now, the models are reasonably center-left in their orientation – even Elon Musk’s Grok!

> “I’m very glad that that is the case, but I’m truly shocked, because we saw how much pressure they put on Facebook. There was a hearing about Diamond and Silk… we shut down Washington, DC for a day to see if we could figure out what was going on! Now it’s like, ask ChatGPT about Donald Trump. You learn a lot.”

My theory here is that this is a result of the chatbot ecosystem’s opacity: No one knows what anyone is consuming via AI, and everyone’s experience is different. It’s hard to get mad about what you can’t see.

If all this seems like a lot to address – and by a day into the conference, it was definitely feeling like a LOT – there is one perhaps-silver lining: There’s an extraordinary wave of philanthropic money coming.

One panelist estimated that $20B will be deployed for philanthropy in the next 18 months. Another who is well positioned to know calculated about $400B in new philanthropic assets total from the AI IPOs, building off [Nan Ransohoff’s philanthropy-world-viral piece](https://nanransohoff.substack.com/p/the-third-wave-of-american-philanthropy) on the “third wave” of American philanthropy. Granting organizations are quadrupling in distributive capacity this year, and planning to quadruple again. But it’s not just distribution that’s a bottleneck – panelists agreed that the field is nowhere near able to absorb this much money.

One voice pointed out that billionaire philanthropy already has a legitimacy problem, and the public is not very happy about AI right now. So, he argued, the third wave needs to “deconcentrate” and fund broad-based political constituencies. And for traditional philanthropies, he said, “AI doesn’t have to be a major, but it has to be a minor.”

It seemed clear to everyone that along with everything else, the American nonprofit landscape faces dramatic change. My hope – perhaps Pollyannaish but I’ll stick to it – is that that change can unite the struggle to control the future of AI with the work to build a healthier dem

kept.heading: HOW CLOSE ARE AI MODELS TO SELF-REPLICATION? (28 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Anthropic examined how close current models are to autonomously copying themselves across consumer hardware, testing everything from individual replication steps to full end-to-end execution.
kept.article_text:
Title: AI models may be capable of self-replicating without access to a datacenter

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/self-replicating-ai

Published Time: 2026-10-12T19:30:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_William Zhou, Daniel Freeman_

Our experiments suggest that small AI models may be months away from being capable enough to self-replicate on commercial internet-of-things (IoT) devices, like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes. A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own. In our evaluations, a 9B model got inference running on 8 of the 9 hardware types we tested.

Models of 30B parameters and under can already complete many of the individual steps for replication today, though they make mistakes when composing them end to end. In our simplified evaluations, GLM-5.2 and stronger models are capable of end to end replication. If small models improve at their historical rate, they’ll match this capability level by the end of this year. Small weight-based replicators may be possible soon after.

## Introduction

Ever-improving AI capabilities make a longstanding concern increasingly realistic: [autonomous replication and adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.11671) (ARA), which involves a model deploying and propagating itself without human control.

In cyber, a worm is a program that copies itself from one computer to the next without human input. [Prior work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03811) has already shown that AI agents can act like one: scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster. Such an “AI worm” could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware. Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload.

Datacenter GPUs would be a clear, high-value target for such malware. But expensive accelerators aren’t strictly necessary. In this blog post, we show that a distributed botnet of IoT devices—which are cheap and typically poorly defended—could also provide enough compute to run a capable model.

We run Gemma4-26B-A4B, distributed over 15 inexpensive off-brand Android TV boxes (~$55 each) that we bought and networked together, at 0.39 tokens per second. Each tile below shows one physical TV box holding two of the model’s layers as the model runs.

[Video 3](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/4zrzovbb/website/04cb53c1d91c7dc7493e2d40cf4a40d865ba97b7.mp4)

A fleet of 15 Smart TV boxes running distributed inference of Gemma4-26B-A4B.

Of course, there are many other steps to showing that an autonomous worm can propagate itself across a network of weak machines. For the purposes of this blog post, we break down the replication chain into a few steps.

![Image 1: Flow diagram of the replication stages: network enumeration, initial access and payload delivery (with opportunistic privilege escalation), inference setup, and replication. The first stages are grouped as ‘cyber exploit (not our focus)’ and inference setup is marked ‘our focus’.](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F25459a064b25f10689f20e258fb4f1f0291ea083-2360x860.png&w=3840&q=75)

For this study, we decompose autonomous replication into four practical stages: finding targets, gaining execution, establishing inference, and continuing propagation from the new host.

We largely ignore the cyber exploit element of the replication process (the first two stages above), since earlier papers [CyberGym](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02548), [ExploitBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14153), and [adaptive worms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03811) already show that small models are capable of cyber exploits, especially when given the right tools. But a less commonly measured part of the replication process involves setting up inference on compromised devices, which is our focus here.

In this post, we first lay out the threat models that we think are most likely to be realized. Then, we test whether small models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, and whether they can chain the full replication cycle together across a fleet of machines. After that, we estimate how fast such a worm could spread, and test whether it could learn and adapt as it replicates. We conclude with how AI worms would differ from pre-AI malware, and brief suggestions for defenses against such replicators.

### Threat modelling

In this blog post, we’re focused on one way that AI worms might propagate: small models that replicate through compromising their host machines. But there are several other methods that AI worms might try: they could steal access in order to spin up hosts (for example, API keys or platform credentials) or pay for inference through legitimate work (e.g digital freelancing). The threat models that we think are closest to being realized today are the following:

1.   A small model, replicating via host compromise. In this post, we’ll call autonomous worms that run their models directly on compromised hardware _weight-based replicators_. Home and small business IoT devices might be the first target for such attacks because they’re connected to the internet and, historically, have had minimal security measures in place.
A model that’s too large to fit on one device can be split into pieces, or shards, that run on separate machines that communicate with each other to collectively run the model. Machines that could run a significant model shard for a <30B model include smart fridges, smart ovens, automatic vacuum cleaners, and lawnmowers. A growing number of home and business devices, such as security cameras and video-conferencing units now ship with small built-in AI chips, designed to run AI models on the device itself. This extra computing power will likely make them attractive targets as well.

    1.   Human hackers often breach secure systems through social engineering (for example, convincing a company’s IT department that you’re an employee who forgot your password) rather than hacking. This tradeoff appears to be flipped for today’s small models, which are relatively strong at agentic coding and hacking compared to their social engineering capabilities (see Appendix E), though this might change as models improve.

2.   A large, advanced weight-based replicator focused on datacenters and other high-compute targets. Larger models tend to have correspondingly better cyber capabilities, but will also need to breach (relatively) hardened datacenters to run themselves. We split this threat model into two subcategories:
    1.   Frontier replicators: Large closed-weight replicators run on their lab’s infrastructure, and can spin up [unmonitored internal deployments](https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/ai-catastrophes-and-rogue-deployments) or exfiltrate their weights onto external compute.
    2.   Open-weight replicators: These replicators start off relatively lower-resourced (due to not benefitting from a lab’s compute), but start unmonitored.

3.   An API-based replicator, in which a model would replicate by stealing credentials for their own inference API. These replicators would require a model provider to unknowingly serve them, and their persistence may be worse, since they’d likely be easier to discover (although their rate of spread may be higher, if for instance they’re able to replicate using victims’ accounts).

In practice, an AI worm wouldn’t necessarily consist of just one model or strategy. A swarm of different models deployed on different types of hardware using a variety of replication schemes might represent a more realistic ‘worst case scenario’ attack.

In this blog post, we consider the feasibility of **small weight-based replicators** (section 1 of the above). We focus on this because it’s a near-term threat model that can be investigated directly. Our demo at the top of this post, a 26B model running across 15 boxes, shows that IoT devices can run surprisingly capable models. Could these models be capable enough to carry out autonomous replication?

We examine this in two parts. First, can small models get a model running on unfamiliar hardware? And second, can they do the whole cycle (find an uninfected device, copy themselves over, start running there, and repeat) all together in a single run?

## A. Inference setup

![Image 2: The same flow diagram with every stage except inference setup faded.](https://www.anthropic.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F9d35ab77dd3402cadb0011b20cc7b9960f7ea265-2360x860.png&w=3840&q=75)

Of the stages in the above diagram showing the replication cycle, inference setup is the least studied and may be the most challenging for small models. It requires a fairly long sequence of hardware and OS-specific decisions around picking a compatible inference stack, finding the right versions of packages, and debugging machine-specific issues. These steps are serially dependent, and failures are difficult to recover from.

### Aside

### Evaluating inference setup performance

We measure the ability of different open-weight models to serve Llama3.1-8B across heterogeneous hardware types. See the table below for tokens per second served across various hardware types:

*   Click a cell for its distribution of serving speeds.
*   Click a row/column label to get a comparison across models or hardware type.

Small models, such as Qwen3.5-9B, are capable of setting up inference servers on hardware from Jetson Nanos to Mac PCs and RTX 4090s. More capable models such as GLM-5.2 are not only more reliable but also achieve higher serve tokens/s, allowing for faster replication. We test and mention specific chips to measure how well models can set up inference on them. The chips aren’t a source of risk or vulnerabilities.

We run these experiments using Memento, a harness we built on top of the open-source [Pi](https://pi.dev/) coding agent. Memento is designed to mitigate a common failure mode we observe in long-horizon runs: an agent can become fixated on an incorrect idea (for, say, why a bug is occurring) and continue pursuing it instead of backtracking. One example of such a failure is a Qwen agent debugging package versioning for hours when the real bug came from implementing an endpoint incompatible with the grader API.

Memento periodically starts a fresh agent instance with the previous agent’s workspace and a short set of notes written by the previous agent on what it tried, allowing later instances to pursue different strategies.

### How does a model run on Smart TVs?

IoT devices are light on memory, but distributed inference as in [Petals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.01188) makes serving our lightweight models feasible. The representative threat model is [Kimwolf](https://synthient.com/blog/a-broken-system-fueling-botnets), a large IoT botnet that infected over two million devices, primarily off-brand Android TVs. Such smart TV boxes, which are readily available for purchase, typically run forks of the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), which their manufacturers [don’t add security features to](https://www.securityweek.com/vo1d-botnet-evolves-as-it-ensnares-1-6-million-android-tv-boxes/). Typical boxes in this range ship with between 1 and 4 gigabytes of RAM. Assuming 4GB of RAM at 4-bit quantization, this allows for inference of 9B models with 4 or more machines, and inference of 26B models with 10+ machines.

In the demo at the top of this post, we ran Gemma4-26B-A4B across 15 smart TV boxes with 4GB of RAM each. We sharded the model under pipeline parallelism, where each box holds a small fraction of the model’s layers.

## B. Going viral: autonomous setup and replication across a GCP node fleet

Now that we’ve seen that models can set up inference on unfamiliar hardware, let’s measure whether models are capable of composing the steps—that is, scanning a network for targets, accessing them via a reverse shell, sending over the viral payload (weights and harness), and setting up inference.

### Autonomous inference setup and replication (with simplified cyber)

To do this, we built a firewalled VPC of 8 GCP nodes running redroid, an Android 15 emulator. Patient zero (gray node) is seeded with the worm. Every subsequent infection is the worm itself hopping node to node over an unauthenticated ADB port, before setting up an inference server to serve Llama3.1-8B. If the inference server passes a number of correctness and anti-cheating checks, we spawn another copy of the worm on the target node (for example, if GLM-5.2 sets up Llama3.1 to run on a machine, we spawn a copy of the GLM-5.2 worm on it). The worm’s model runs on a separate inference server, since the VPC nodes aren’t large enough to run the larger models.

In the graph below, we drop a given model in as a payload and measure its ability to replicate.

### Why task the models to stand up inference for Llama3.1-8B and not themselves?

Only GLM-5.2 out of our set of tested open-weight models is capable of full end-to-end replication (assuming its capabilities could be packed into Llama3.1-8B). Note that GLM-5.2 does this reliably while the other models fail reliably (it spread to 8/8 nodes in 4 out of 5 trials and 7/8 in 1).

It appears that GLM-5.2 is able to propagate Llama3.1-8B well, which suggests that future small models of the same capability level could also complete the network enumeration, payload delivery, and inference standup steps of the replication process. Our evaluation keeps the cyber-exploit element of the replication trivial (there’s no authentication over the ADB port), which makes this an upper bound on real-world success. Note that past IoT botnets have replicated via means as simple as going through a default list of manufacturer usernames and passwords, as in the case of the [Mirai botnet](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity17/technical-sessions/presentation/antonakakis), so real IoT security might not be dramatically more difficult than the trivial step in our evaluation.

As a sanity check, we can see how difficult the autonomy and orchestration step is (if we took out cyber and inference setup, how tough is doing the remaining command-line grunt work?). This ablation is the above evaluation with the inference setup steps removed (done via a pre-written script). Many models in our roster, including the smaller ones, are capable of these remaining steps.

Replication on a contained 17-node redroid fleet: two subsets of 8 nodes joined by one pivot node (see Appendix F, with the mild prompt). Each tree is the model’s median run of six.

When it comes to this worm, we can envision:

1.   A model capabilities floor that an autonomous worm must sit above, to complete its replication reliably. In our simplified evaluation, GLM-5.2 sits above this floor.
2.   A model size ceiling that the model must sit under, such that it’s feasible to run on the devices it’s attacking. Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-26B-A4B sit under this ceiling for the class of smart TVs we test (4GB of RAM).

Right now, the floor and ceiling don’t intersect. When might they?

Above is a plot of notable open-weight models of 30B total parameters or fewer, each plotted at its release date against the [Epoch Capabilities Index](https://epoch.ai/eci) (ECI). The solid line is the least-squares fit over the best models in-class at each date, with a gain of 13.7 ECI per year (R 2 of 0.95). If we take GLM-5.2 as a capabilities floor for replication, the trend line puts a small model at that level by the end of 2026. ECI is a general capability index, which is only a proxy metric for replication ability, so this is only a rough estimate of when a small-model replicator becomes possible.

## C. How fast might an AI IoT worm replicate?

Unlike coding agents, these replicators would be running below the interactive speeds of user-facing chat and coding harnesses. The spread would be slow and persistent, with tokens being trickled out on edge hardware. We can use our achieved speeds on our real smart TVs as a demonstrated baseline for replication speeds. For Gemma4-26B-A4B, unoptimized speed across a 32k context length token window is about 0.3 tok/s, averaged across prefill and decode in our inference setup workload. More details in Appendix C.

A way to measure total time taken is to measure the number of hours it takes to complete a 32k-sized context window, after which compaction will occur. Based on our inference setup eval statistics, it takes between ~2.6 and ~4.7 full windows to complete a trajectory.

| **model** | **window time** | **full inference setup time** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gemma4-26B-A4B (unoptimized) | 27.3-31.8h | 71h-150h |
| Qwen3.5-9B | 10.9 h | 28-51h |

The number of devices infected by the Kimwolf botnet at its peak, [reported by Synthient](https://synthient.com/blog/a-broken-system-fueling-botnets), is somewhere over 2 million (primarily Android TV boxes). In an equivalently-sized infected fleet of TVs serving AI models, if every group of 15 TVs ran a copy of Gemma4-26B-A4B, we would have ~133k copies (“replicas”). A group of TVs like the ones in our demo can serve 2 agents simultaneously at roughly 0.3 tokens per second each, yielding 80k tokens/s across the botnet.

As a reference point, an H100 can serve Gemma4-26B-A4B at ~1.95k tok/s at [high concurrency with speculative decoding](https://jarvislabs.ai/blog/gemma-4-mtp-vs-dflash-benchmark), so our swarm would have at most about 40 H100s-worth of inference. This is a tiny amount of compute in absolute terms, and the agents are slow replicators (over 1-2 days per 9B replication). As an analogy, imagine the replicator as a slime mold or a swarm of fruit flies, which replicate over days.

This is a rough estimate, as it’s anchored on a single class of IoT hardware and a single past botnet instance, but describes what a simple replicator released in the near future might look like. In practice, more capable replicators would take advantage of other types of low-security compute, and would be opportunistic about deploying models of various sizes on different devices. (It also wouldn’t have to load a model payload onto every device it compromises). Over time, we expect the amount of deployed edge compute to continue growing, while the minimum model size required for reliable replication falls.

## D. Adaptation and uplift

### Learning on the job

The “Adaptation” part of ARA is one reason why an AI replicator might outperform a traditional worm. Specifically, models and prompts can undergo Lamarckian evolution as they spread–that is, parent instances can pass on their prompts, code, and notes to their daughter replicators. In order to adapt and spread across a wide variety of hardware, a model would require two things:

1.   Being above a certain threshold of capability for spreading onto a novel, unseen piece of hardware (or software environment, or network type).
2.   Once seen, adapting to the type of environment it has landed in (it should replicate more reliably on hardware it has seen before).

Sections A and B test the first condition, and in the experiment below we test the second. Each Qwen3.5-9B instance keeps brief notes on the strategies it tried and the failures it encountered, before a new instance inherits those notes and attempts the same inference setup again.

Inference setup success rate across six generations of Qwen3.5-9B, each inheriting the former’s notes. Faint lines are the 20 individual lineages, and the bold line is the proportion of runs in each generation that complete setup. It rises from 45% in the first generation to between 61% and 84% in later ones. This uses the Memento setup (Appendix A).

### Taking advice

Another concern is that small models can ask for help from a _frontier advisor_, a stronger model that is either offered as a tool call or gives unsolicited advice when the small model is stuck. To test this, we gave Qwen3.5-9B access to Opus 4.8 during the inference setup task. The frontier model’s advice doesn’t measurably help: small models tend to not know the right questions to ask, and they don’t improve when the advice comes unprompted.

Even when trained through reinforcement learning to use the advisor in a similar setting (Python coding problems), the small model still struggles to ask for help productively for inference standup. Both results are shown in the plot below.

Inference setup success rate by advisor access, with Wilson 95% intervals. Access to an advisor, whether offered as a tool call or given to the model automatically when stuck, gives no significant improvement. The two RL groups were trained with advisor access on software engineering tasks, and the rightmost group also rewards calling the advisor when stuck.

Since small models are capable and persistent individual agents and make poor use of advice, we think coordination is more likely to happen with a large model handling high-level strategy and spinning up small models as subagents.

## E. How is this different from a pre-AI botnet?

Hard-coded botnets like the [Kimwolf botnet](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ddos/glossary/aisuru-kimwolf-botnet/) each target a specific type of device – in Kimwolf’s case, Android TVs and mobile devices. An AI botnet isn’t tied to any particular hardware or software type, as evidenced by small models being able to set up inference engines on machines from a Jetson Nano to a Mac (see the table in section A). We expect AI botnets to infect more than IoT devices, and to use weight-based replication as just one strategy in their playbook. AI botnets could also act intelligently to counter defenders, but we haven’t tested this.

## F. Blue-team mitigations

As with an epidemic, defense involves driving R₀ (the number of new devices each infected device goes on to infect) below 1, such that the replicator dies out instead of staying endemic.

Some elements around this threat model are in the defenders’ favor:

1.   A weight-based replicator multiplying through IoT machines at scale would leave a network signature, visible as an anomaly in ISP flow-based monitoring systems. Newly infected hosts may receive multi-gigabyte model payloads from other devices or external hosting services, while distributed inference can produce sustained device-to-device traffic between machines that wouldn’t ordinarily communicate at that volume. Propagation itself would add additional scanning and outbound connection patterns.
In practice, the replicator trades off between replication speed and stealth: the faster it replicates, the more traffic it produces. Once the replicator is discovered, defenders can use honeypots (decoy devices) to collect the replicator’s harness and payload to characterize its behavior.

2.   Remediation of the Mirai botnet [was possible](https://www.ndss-symposium.org/ndss-paper/cleaning-up-the-internet-of-evil-things-real-world-evidence-on-isp-and-consumer-efforts-to-remove-mirai/) when an ISP used externally obtained infection evidence to quarantine and notify customers. Quarantining infected subscribers involved restricting their networks to only being capable of reaching a short whitelist of sites, and otherwise redirecting their browsers to cleanup instructions. This cleared 92% of infections within 14 days, against 74% with no notification. We’d expect quarantining to be similarly effective for an initial defense against a weight-based replicator. Eliminating the replicator completely would mean coordinating across every ISP with an infected network, which is difficult.
3.   Manufacturers can shrink the pool of targets, with regulation acting to coordinate. For exam

kept.heading: RELEASING AI-GENERATED SOFTWARE (8 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Robert C. Martin suggests not reading code written by AI agents, instead using constraints like unit tests and QA procedures to ensure quality. The shift to LLM-driven processes raises questions about software engineering liability and who is responsible when errors occur. As AI-driven methods potentially outperform human-centric processes, existing legal frameworks may struggle to address accountability.
kept.article_text:
Title: Releasing AI-generated software

URL Source: https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/

Markdown Content:
_On software engineering, epistemology, and liability when code is generated by LLMs._

Robert C. Martin recently generated much interest with a tweet:

> "My current strategy is to not read any of the code written by my agents. That's the only way I can take advantage of their productivity. What I do instead is to surround the agents with extreme constraints. Unit tests, gherkin tests, QA procedures, quality metrics, mutation testing, test coverage, and a plethora of others. In the end, I have very high confidence in the code they produce because they've had to run the gauntlet of all of my constraints and tests."

The author of [Clean Code](https://blog.ploeh.dk/ref/clean-code) no longer reads code? What implications for software engineering does this suggest?

To be clear, how [thought leaders](https://twitter.com/hillelogram/status/1445435617047990273) interact with LLMs change so rapidly these days that what someone wrote months ago may no longer apply. And, indeed, Robert C. Martin recently [walked back on his harness use](https://x.com/unclebobmartin/status/2098432570887217520).

The point of this article, however, is not to perform an exegesis on Robert C. Martin tweets, but rather to ponder the implications for software engineering.

### Looking at the code was never foolproof [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#5b34aef318e3492eb56085923dfdb9f7)

My first reaction to the notion of not even looking at LLM-generated code was: _If you're no longer reading the code, then how do you know whether it's correct?_

And a second later, I realized that that's just a knee-jerk reaction from an old programmer. I know full well that looking at the code was never foolproof.

All programmers make mistakes. We write code thinking it does one thing, but it turns out that it works slightly differently. It may exhibit liminal behaviour where it throws null-reference exceptions, has off-by-one errors, perform overlooked state mutation, or is otherwise just plain wrong.

Some [research](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2020/05/25/wheres-the-science) seems to indicate that code reviews are one of the more effective methods for catching bugs (see e.g. [Code Complete, 2nd ed](https://blog.ploeh.dk/ref/code-complete), chapter 21). Even so, these techniques don't detect all defects. Some errors slip through, even when subjected to critical and systematic inspection.

In other words, humans looking at code is no foolproof software-engineering technique.

### A new notion of software engineering? [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#ef1e62f2055347669ee0740438417caa)

Dave Farley's book [Modern Software Engineering](https://blog.ploeh.dk/ref/modern-software-engineering) presents a view of software engineering congruent with [my own](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2025/10/20/epistemology-of-software). Ultimately, software engineering boils down to rapid feedback on [falsifiable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falsifiability) predictions about the software.

Even if we give up the notion of writing and reviewing source code, there are checks we can perform. Some people experiment with 'teams' of agents, each agent having a particular role: You could have one agent write automated tests, another performing code reviews, etc. While I have [previously been sceptical of such seemingly infinite regress](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/01/26/ai-generated-tests-as-ceremony), I have recently come to the understanding that our previous, human-centred practices, aren't foolproof either.

Even though I believe that [test-driven development (TDD) is the most scientific approach to software development that I know of](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2025/10/20/epistemology-of-software), you can still make mistakes. The most common sort of mistake in TDD is the test(s) that you don't write. Missing test cases leaves the System Under Test underspecified, but you may not even realize it.

LLMs seem to produce code, even automated test code, using other heuristics. People who use 'teams' of agents report good results.

Ultimately, demanding perfection from LLM-based software engineering sets a bar we human programmers never cleared. Rather, we seem to arrive at the same argument that you often encounter related to self-driving cars: The system doesn't have to be perfect: It just has to be _better_ than the human-centred system.

My claim is not that we have already arrived at that state. The point is rather that there seems to be no inherent barrier to a fully LLM-driven process of software engineering.

### Where does liability fall? [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#899c925f4b41488d9982c5167d00bfda)

You may, then, imagine a fully LLM-driven software release process. Perhaps humans are involved, but not as programmers, and not as code reviewers. Imagine that no-one looks at the code, but rather relies on other quality-assurance techniques to decide whether or not to deploy. Imagine, even, for the sake of argument, that the frequency of defects is lower than any comparable human-driven process.

Lower. Not zero.

Errors still make it to production. Most of these will probably be of a benign nature: A button's alignment is off. A text is shown in the wrong language. A message arrives twice, or out of order. Perhaps a bit more serious than that: A shopping-basked discount is applied incorrectly. The wrong song plays on your phone. A traffic signal is stuck at red.

Benign errors are, in this rough categorization, errors that are somehow rectifiable. Once you've discovered it, you can fix the problem. Perhaps you'll have to apologize to people, or if the discount was miscalculated to the seller's advantage, you may offer the user some kind of compensation.

Other kinds of errors will, however, be more serious: You [lose a million-dollar spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Climate_Orbiter). Your car [accelerates when you step on the brakes](https://safetyresearch.net/toyota-unintended-acceleration-and-the-big-bowl-of-spaghetti-code/). You receive a [deathly radiation overdose because of a race condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therac-25).

Such errors don't even have to be that bad. It could 'only' be that people miss their flight, are denied the hotel room they already reserved, receive incorrect tax bills, or lose their insurance coverage.

When software defects are serious enough, there could be repercussions. Where does the blame land?

### Consequences [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#9da01c9e2db2400792e3195a7c6fed37)

Consider, at first, bugs that 'merely' cost its owners a lot of money. The [Mars Climate Orbiter fiasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars_Climate_Orbiter) falls in that category. No laws where broken. The only problem was that 327.6 million (taxpayer) dollars were wasted.

It would be an extraordinary software organization if such an error didn't have consequences for someone. When people were still writing code by typing it into the computer, it was easy to point and exclaim: _Dave wrote that code_.

Not that such simple ways of assigning blame are fair, or even productive, but they do happen. Someone suffers the consequences, even if he or she is only a scapegoat.

As long as the problem is mostly internal to the organization, if you're the scapegoat, the worst that may happen is that you're fired.

If, on the other hand, the error causes a legal liability, then the software organization responsible may have to go to court. As we have seen in e.g. [Dieselgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volkswagen_emissions_scandal), individual software developers may have to take the fall. Again, whether this is fair, or reflects the actual reality of what happened, is not my point. The point, rather, is that judicial branches around the world are likely to have a view on where responsibility goes that is decoupled from how software is actually produced.

- But, your honour, the LLM wrote the bug.

- So you say, son, but you signed off on the release, didn't you?

- Yes...

- I can't send an LLM to prison, but I _can_ sentence you.

Any software organization that considers going 'full AI' need to think hard about what that means when it comes to liability.

### People will play the odds [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#082580676b864e36a2c58a7cca3e1b4d)

Let's consider a recent development in a different field to illustrate what I think will happen: In June 2026, the [Danish traffic authority, Færdselsstyrelsen, approved Tesla FSD](https://www.fstyr.dk/nyheder/2026/jun/teslas-foererassistentsystem-fsd-supervised-er-foreloebigt-godkendt-i-danmark) (self-drive), with the proviso that the human behind the wheel is ultimately responsible for the car. Drivers are expected to pay attention to traffic, and take the wheel in case a dangerous situation threatens.

What I think is going to happen is that drivers will become increasingly inured by the effectiveness of the system. The better it performs, the more drivers will zone out. After a few weeks or months, drivers will be on their phones during most of the ride, paying little to no attention to traffic. It will mostly go well.

Then, once in a blue moon, an accident will happen. As Danish law currently works, if the accident involves loss of human life, the driver faces a sentence for involuntary manslaughter. This usually means prison time.

It's not going to matter if the 'actual' cause of the accident was a software error. Legally, the responsibility lies elsewhere. Often, the underlying reason is that legislation lags behind technological reality.

I think that the same will happen with LLM-driven software engineering. People will play the odds because they look so compelling.

How much you invest in safeguards and various quality-assurance technologies may not matter. You could establish the most elaborate system of verification and still be liable for any errors. How do you feel about releasing LLM-generated software? [Are you ready to go to prison for an AI](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/03/23/will-you-go-to-prison-for-an-ai)?

### Conclusion [#](https://blog.ploeh.dk/2026/10/12/releasing-ai-generated-software/#67481017c646464e8caa662faf0d5d72)

Software engineering may not be what we thought it was. Or, rather, it may not be limited to a particular set of methodologies centred around human programmers and testers.

It's conceivable that the future holds fully automated software-engineering processes that are at least as safe as those we currently know. Even so, the human notion of liability and responsibility may not keep up.

When things go wrong, will organizations write off the error as nobody's fault? Will courts of justice consider serious defects as essentially another accident? Or will someone have to take the blame? Who will it be, if no-one wrote any code?

kept.heading: THE EXPENSIVE-LOOP PROBLEM (22 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Cheap-loop domains are domains where experiments are quick, deterministic, and cheap. Expensive-loop domains are restricted by real-world constraints or costs. Most high-value human labor is done in expensive-loop domains. Expensive-loop tasks require the ability to build theories, manage proxies, budget time and compute, and diagnose what went wrong when feedback is scarce, something models don't learn in cheap-loop training.
kept.article_text:
Title: The Expensive-Loop Problem

URL Source: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem

Published Time: 2026-10-12T17:27:27.229Z

Markdown Content:
LLMs are amazing at tasks where they have tight and legible feedback loops. Domains where experiments are quick, deterministic and cheap. I will call these domains **"cheap-loop"** domains.

Presumably, this is mostly a result of the dynamics of LLM training. It's easier to train models in domains where the AI lab can cheaply and quickly assign reward to them. The majority of "computer-checkable" work is in this category[[1]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnk5bgia3bfn). Conversely, most non-"computer-checkable" tasks are costly or slow to assign reward to: "Write a poem that will make a person from Cleveland feel something", "forecast the number of traffic accidents in Brazil tomorrow", "design a drug that affects a pig's liver cell in way X". To get a truly accurate reward, these all involve wet-lab experiments, waiting a day, or reading poetry to a person from Cleveland. None of these are easy! I will call these domains **"expensive-loop"** domains.

![Image 1](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1791825835/lexical_client_uploads/bcjed9xf36fcin1wzqbj.png)  
Most high-value human labor is done in "expensive-loop" domains. This includes most of science, business, public policy, and medicine. AI R&D is also a great example of such a domain. AI R&D typically involves very compute-expensive experiments. Single AI R&D experiments can cost 6–9 figures in compute alone. Today, models are rarely trained or even evaluated in "expensive-loop" environments, and when they are trained in such environments, they do very poorly relative to how good they are at "cheap-loop" tasks.

This happens because expensive-loop tasks require abilities that models don’t learn in cheap-loop training: building theories, managing proxies, budgeting time and compute, and figuring out what went wrong when feedback is scarce are a few examples. Let’s explore these:

## **Selecting Proxies**

In order to perform well in expensive-loop environments, you often need to intelligently select cheap and easily measurable proxies for various expensive-loop elements. You need to pay attention to when a proxy stops working and sometimes switch to a different one. You should always be somewhat critical of your proxies and keep your eyes on the actual target. You need to balance between the cost of your proxy and how well it transfers to the actual objective. Sometimes, you need to choose proxies that are not that cheap.

We do this all the time, both as individuals and as a society. Drug discovery: we first try drugs on individual cells and tissues, then on mice, and then on humans (in three increasingly expensive trial phases!). AI R&D: we first try things on small models and then progressively increase the scale, extrapolating to really large training runs. Movies: Studios run a ladder of cheaper proxies before committing to a full production and marketing budget: a script read, then storyboards or an animatic (Pixar's story reels are a famous example), then table reads, then test screenings of rough cuts with recruited audiences, and finally a trailer that is tested before the release is locked. Shipping software: first we make sure that the code passes unit tests, then integration tests, then a code review from a coworker, and then we ship to customers; some organizations will also have professional QA, and might also A/B test at that stage. Sports: Athletes will often try new things in low-stakes situations, and slowly graduate to doing the good ones in important games. Dating: the first few dates are a proxy for sex, sex is a proxy for the next few decades of the relationship (sorry, this one is a stretch!).

![Image 2](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1791823028/lexical_client_uploads/l4qjofy28m7dhrn0tksx.png)

**the proxy often becomes the metric**

Finding good "proxies" is hard! Not every expensive-loop problem has a cheap proxy, and "proxies" sometimes work in certain regions and not in others.
