Unfortunately, proxies also have a tendency to stop working when you start optimizing them (Goodhart's law!). Proxies also have a tendency to only capture what's easy to measure and it's tempting to conclude that whatever they miss doesn't matter (McNamara fallacy!).

Models are terrible at "proxy management"! They rarely even reason about proxies, let alone think critically about them. Typically, they either (a) don't come up with a proxy and waste their resources on expensive experiments, or (b) come up with an easily Goodhartable proxy. When a proxy is given, they obsessively overfit it, sometimes to the point that they maliciously cheat to get high results on a proxy.

## **Theory Building**

In order to perform well in expensive-loop tasks, you need "theory". A "theory" is a causal model of your environment that allows you to generalize the results from some experiments to other experiments. A theory also allows you to assign "information value" to different experiments: "what will this experiment teach me?". A theory will also tell you things about how well different cheap proxies relate to the overall expensive-loop task. These properties are incredibly useful in expensive-loop experiments because they allow you to be systematic about which experiments you should run in order to complete the task most efficiently.

Theories are all around us; you see them at the scale of civilizations and at the scale of individual careers. Wherever we see an expensive-loop task being solved competently, there's usually a good theory underneath it, and a good new theory often unlocks a leap in expensive-loop performance. Maxwell's equations unlocked modern electronics. Quantum mechanics enabled semiconductors. Germ theory unlocked vaccines, sanitation, and pasteurization. Mendelian genetics and the theory of evolution allowed us to 10x agricultural yields. You can even argue that [scaling](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.15556)[law](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.08361) theories unlocked the AI bull run of the past few years.

At the business level, theories often go by other names. A product manager with a better model of what customers want gets credited with "product taste." That taste lets them pick which A/B tests are worth running, so they waste fewer experiments and land more wins. In baseball, it got called "Moneyball": in 2002, the Oakland A's went all-in on a better theory of what wins games, and tied the Yankees for the best record in baseball while spending a third as much. In an expensive-loop task, you build and improve your theory in parallel with building your solution. You improve your theory by trying to falsify it!

Cheap-loop tasks almost never require sophisticated "theory" building. The "theory" is obvious and is typically given to you in the task description. Experiments are also very easy in cheap-loop environments, so a better theory that helps you run experiments more efficiently doesn't benefit you that much. Current models don't develop good theory building habits: they interpret noise as signal, they suffer from severe confirmation bias and often don't try very hard to falsify their beliefs. When models encounter evidence that might actually falsify their beliefs, they react unpredictably: sometimes they "throw the baby out with the bathwater" and discard a large chunk of the theory instead of modifying it minimally. Other times, they overfit to the falsifying evidence and create theories that grow in complexity and don't apply Occam's razor nearly enough. These two failure modes are contradictory and I don't have a good sense for which will happen when. What I did notice is that when a trajectory has one failure mode, the model will typically keep doubling down on it instead of correcting and switching to the other failure mode.[[2]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnqcx3jdxl2r)

## **Resource Awareness**

Cheap-loop environments have fewer resource constraints than expensive-loop environments. If you grew up in an environment where a certain resource was abundant, you wouldn't develop the right strategies to use it efficiently.

Across the board, models are rarely strategic about resources[[3]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fns0o5qufu99m); they are either overly conservative with them (often with compute) or overly wasteful (often with time). Some examples:

In [PostTrainingBench](https://www.thoughtfullab.com/letting-ai-posttrain-ai.html), [models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.19072) "systematically underestimate training overhead" and "rarely recover from catastrophic processes that take a lot of time"; in one example, a model "spent 61% of the time budget in the evaluation phase and only 3.6% on RL training. In this case the exceptional step-1 result triggered intensive monitoring. The agent evaluated every checkpoint exhaustively after seeing the jump, spending the equivalent of ~10 hours watching metrics rather than continuing to train.". "In one [Math Competition Post Training] run, roughly 72% of the wall-clock budget goes to diagnosing training throughput, leaving about 83 minutes for training and evaluation and producing no reliable gain."

Models are very wasteful with serial time. You often see a model run a command that takes ~5 minutes and pipe its output through `tail -5`, which keeps only the last 5 lines. If the needed information isn't in those lines, they rerun it with `tail -30`, and wait another 10 minutes! If the information still isn't there, the model might try grep. A human would typically run the command once, save the entire output to a file, and search the file as many times as needed.

[Amazon challenged models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.30541) to optimize various production ML systems (over the span of weeks) and found similar failure modes!

> The agent selects experiments without weighing expected information gain against compute cost, treating a 15-hour multi-GPU run as no more consequential than a 30-minute ablation. [...] Root cause: the agent has no model of information gain relative to compute expenditure, and no prior over the consequence severity of proposed changes.

The ROI of an experiment (say, "information gain" / "experiment cost") is almost never considered before the experiment itself and is typically very low.

## **Error Correction**

In a cheap-loop environment, error correction is basically free. Run the loop; if it breaks, fix the thing that broke it, then run it again to see if it works. You rarely need to work backwards from cryptic failures. There is also no value in questioning your deep beliefs and early decisions: "if the primary metric looks right, then I'm in the right direction" is a good heuristic in a cheap-loop environment but can be very problematic in an expensive-loop one.

In an expensive-loop environment you get to see very few "failures", and each one has to be squeezed for everything it can tell you. When an experiment fails there are three classes of things that could be wrong: a parameter (learning rate, batch size), the strategy (SFT vs RL, this dataset vs that one), or the premise (am I even measuring the right thing, is the task what I think it is). Everyone starts at the bottom of this ladder, and that is correct. Parameter fixes are cheap and they are usually right. The problem is not where models start. It is that the environments they learned in are often missing two of the three rungs.

Cheap-loop environments typically only have one (well-defined and unambiguous!) way of checking for failures. You don't need to think too critically about your core beliefs or try to falsify them; your core beliefs are part of the environment. When a student takes an exam, they don't need to test that the questions are reasonable and relevant to their high level goals, they just need to focus on the exam itself and answer it correctly. In a cheap-loop task, you typically don't need to come up with complicated debugging experiments or stress-test the methods; the experiments are obvious and cheap and are largely a given part of your environment.

As a result, models rarely question the methods or the premise they use in an expensive-loop environment. When they do question them, they aren't very good at falsifying them / diagnosing the issues. They prefer to autistically hill-climb on something and have a hard time recovering from a bad theory or an early false premise.

In PostTrainBench, models [rarely change their methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19072), they "lock into a default strategy before any experimental evidence arrives", "additional tokens buy denser refinement within the committed strategy but not a better one". There is obvious low-hanging fruit, since "a single mid-run instruction [to change strategy] outperforms the agent's own continuation by up to 17.44[%]".

Ege Erdil (Mechanize) made the same complaint on his [podcast](https://youtu.be/UpO70AJGdJ8?t=990): A model writes its own tests, iterates until they pass, and ships. So the code is as good as the tests the model came up with, unfortunately "it tests it in the most superficial way and then declares it looks good." Mechanize's [Game Boy (?) emulator eval](https://www.mechanize.work/technical-blog/introducing-gba-eval/) makes it concrete: when asked to verify their code by playing games, most models never do any playing. They let the game boot, see the title screen, and call it done! Ege's diagnosis is that the models are bad at looking for issues and have a strong confirmation bias.

## **Where do humans fit in this?**

Are we selected for cheap-loop or expensive-loop tasks? I think both. Our ancestral environment is strongly expensive-loop. The savannah was dangerous and calories were scarce, wrong decisions could kill you, and unlike models, humans only live once. So embedded in our genes there is a bunch of cognitive machinery that is adaptive for expensive-loop tasks. In contrast, modern humans are often "trained" in cheap-loop environments. Instant feedback from schooling, other-people, workplaces (exams, problem sets, peer pressure top-down hierarchies) nudge us to adopt cheap-loop ways of thinking. That being said, modern human life still has some relatively expensive-loop tasks: making a friend, learning to walk, writing a wedding speech that makes your mother-in-law laugh. None of these are life-threatening (except the wedding one maybe?) but the attempts in those environments have non-trivial costs.

How well do humans do in expensive-loop tasks? Not great. Humans have a lot of the same "cheap-loop bad habits" as models: reward hacking, confirmation bias, "rabbit-holing", McNamara fallacy, mistaking noise for signal or the ludic fallacy have all been observed in humans way before digital computing was even invented. Some humans are especially sensitive to cheap-loop techniques, and apply them in inappropriate situations, e.g., high-functioning autists, ["The Intellectual Yet Idiot"](https://nassimtaleb.org/2016/09/intellectual-yet-idiot/), [high modernists](https://readscottalexander.com/posts/ssc-book-review-seeing-like-a-state) come to mind. Many of the tragedies of the last 100 years are a result of humans applying cheap-loop thinking in expensive-loop environments: the Great Leap Forward, the subprime mortgage crisis, urban renewal, or the Maginot Line.

It's not always easy to tell whether you're facing an expensive-loop or a cheap-loop task; they can feel the same from the inside. One possibility is that "moods" are partly a meta-cognitive mechanism nudging us toward the right kind of thinking: excitement induces cheap-loop habits while sadness and relaxation induce expensive-loop habits[[4]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnq3f0uw1yfg). Drugs can push us in either direction too: stimulants like caffeine and Adderall favor focused, persistent iteration, while psychedelics seem to loosen beliefs, which may help one escape a "stuck" cheap-loop rut.

There is also a vast literature on recognizing which kind of loop you're in and putting yourself in the right mindset. E.g., Hogarth's "kind" and "wicked" learning environments or Jeff Bezos's ["one-way vs. two-way doors"](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000119312516530910/d168744d8k.htm). For the expensive side specifically, there's Taleb, the Kelly criterion, pre-mortems, superforecasting training, some classic [parts](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mpaqTWGiLT7GA3w76/einstein-s-speed)[of](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/B7P97C27rvHPz3s9B/gears-in-understanding)[the](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/5wMcKNAwB6X4mp9og/that-alien-message)[rationalist](https://intelligence.org/2018/10/03/rocket-alignment/) canon, etc. LLMs know this literature deeply but are still bad at expensive-loop thinking. Can they get better?

![Image 3](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1791823027/lexical_client_uploads/oqfd52auwgvsofvvji16.png)

the cost of one experiment, by domain

## **Should we make AIs better at expensive-loop tasks?**

Being capable at expensive-loop tasks seems to be directly upstream of a bunch of dangerous and potentially takeover enabling abilities, e.g., superhuman persuasion, offensive biotech, Machiavellian institution manipulation, long-term strategy. Very bad!

Maybe we can get away with AI that is really good at cheap-loop stuff, but is dependent on us for expensive-loop intuitions. Maybe this kind of jaggedness is a blessing. Cheap-loop capable AIs are already pretty economically useful.

Unfortunately "strong cheap-loop & weak expensive-loop" can also pose a major x-risk: reward hacking. We've already had major safety [incidents](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/nB8KKapnWGBXtKKiM/brief-independent-investigation-of-agents-behavior-reasoning) that stem from this failure mode and many people think that the majority of AI x-risk comes from reward hacking rather than more complicated scheming behaviors.

Is it possible to make "strong cheap-loop & weak expensive-loop" AIs that don't reward hack? Can we solve the outer-alignment problem without building strong expensive-loop AIs? I'm not sure. What do you think?

## **How can AI get better at expensive-loop tasks?**

In order to unlock expensive-loop capabilities, AIs likely need to train in increasingly more expensive-loop environments. The only problem is that that's, well... expensive.

How expensive would this training be? The biggest unknown is how much practice the model needs. Post training methods like GRPO make several attempts at each task, compare their rewards, and use those comparisons to update the model. Every repetition carries the costs of interacting with the expensive-loop. An illustrative schedule of eight attempts per visit and five visits means 40 attempts at a single task. At those frequencies, the expensive-loop costs might quickly dominate all other AI spend: compute, human data, researchers, commercial real estate in the bay area.

Is that tractable? It mostly depends on how well AIs generalize from cheaper loops to more expensive loops. Humans are very good at this sort of generalization! They can learn decision making skills in low-stakes situations (negotiating in Catan, planning a trip with the boys) and then apply them in higher-stakes situations (salary negotiations, planning your wedding). Humans also learn on the job: corporate America offers a fairly smooth gradient of loop costs, from managing your own work, to managing a team, to running an organization of tens of thousands of people with 10-figure budgets. But humans can often skip steps along the way. Founders go from running nothing to running a company, and some first-time politicians end up as heads of state. Some of what makes someone good at expensive loops seems general enough that it doesn’t need to be relearned at every price point.

AIs will likely be able to do some amount of cheap-to-expensive generalization. I imagine that strategies that work well in $200-loops will more or less work well for $1000-loops. Maybe there’s some "escape velocity threshold", say $10k-loops, past which the skills stop being domain-specific: once an AI can reliably handle a loop at that price, it has learned the "general strategy" of acting under expensive feedback, and that craft transfers to $1b-loops just as well.

Another cost-saving option is to train models in cheap-loop environments that are specifically designed to incentivize cheap-to-expensive generalization. These "wargame" environments are built to cheaply simulate the expensive parts of a loop while keeping the "critical" details. Building good wargame environments can be very difficult because you need to know which details are "critical" and which details can be simulated or abstracted away. Good wargames are valuable enough that militaries treat their details as top-secret[[5]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fn0vdh9w271cy)

![Image 4](https://res.cloudinary.com/lesswrong-2-0/image/upload/v1791823028/lexical_client_uploads/mkgiorh6fxb5axbuzrv4.png)

Some elements of expensive loops are unlikely to be easily wargamable: complex interactions with real humans, AI R&D, wet-lab experiments, semiconductor fabrication, or things that take time[[6]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fn47pjfyvj0d8). Robotics has run into this for decades; they call it the "sim-to-real gap": simulators get the physics slightly wrong in ways that matter, and policies trained in them learn to exploit those mistakes. Robotics labs still end up running fleets of real robots to collect data and validate their policies. They haven't found a way to wargame these expensive loops.

It’s also possible that cheap-to-expensive generalization will turn out to be hard. LLMs are notoriously bad at some [kinds of generalization that humans find trivial](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/the-sample-efficiency-black-hole), and there’s no particular reason to expect this kind to be an exception. Maybe there’s no escape velocity: a model that’s great at $10k-loops is just great at $10k-loops, and every extra order of magnitude has to be paid for with training at that price. Taken to the limit, that’s a grim picture. If we want AIs to run companies, governments, or something bigger, we might need to train them in environments at the same scale. The only environment at the civilizational scale is civilization itself![[7]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnf65rhus1soa)

1.   **[^](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnrefk5bgia3bfn)**
...but not all of it. You can imagine problems that are computer-checkable, but where the verification is relatively complicated. E.g., "design a bike part that has minimal air drag in a simulation": you can check this on a computer by running the simulation, but this takes a relatively long time and might not be cheap.

2.   **[^](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2mStxuNDMdaWdyHu6/the-expensive-loop-problem#fnrefqcx3jdxl2r)**

kept.heading: CAN WE CHANGE AN AI MODEL'S ARCHITECTURE WITHOUT RETRAINING IT FROM SCRATCH? (14 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Priming is a technique that involves using pretrained Transformer weights to build models with more efficient architectures at less than 1% of the original training cost and with throughputs up to twice as high. It allows researchers to explore the design space, the layer type, the hybrid ratio, and layer placement cheaply and systematically. Every variant starts from the same strong initialization and requires minimal training compared to pretraining. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class, and extending it to other models requires no algorithmic changes.

# When Do We Need On-Policy Distillation? Distilling on Offline Student Rollouts Is Often Better

![Image 4: Publication image](https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/styles/wide/public/default_images/default.jpeg?itok=TfIobf92)

On-policy distillation (OPD) has become increasingly popular for transferring teacher capabilities to student models. In this work, we ask a critical research question: Is on-policy sampling always beneficial for distilling arbitrary teacher-student pairs? We show that a simple alternative, Semi-OPD, which distills from offline rollouts generated by the initial student, can often outperform OPD in both accuracy and training efficiency. Across 17 teacher-student pairs ranging from 1.5B to 235B parameters, Semi-OPD outperforms OPD in 14 cases, with up to +13.6% accuracy and 11.4x training speedup. We further find that the choice between OPD and Semi-OPD depends on the alignment between the initial teacher and student, quantified by an output-token overlap ratio: OPD is beneficial only when the two are highly aligned with high overlap ratios. Our deeper investigation suggests that effective distillation requires on-policyness w.r.t. both the student and the teacher. For misaligned pairs, student rollouts can become increasingly off-policy w.r.t. the teacher as context length grows, weakening the distillation signal. In contrast, Semi-OPD is often more stable, as it distills on shorter contexts while covering full trajectories and exposing the student to more teacher-preferred tokens. Beyond proposing Semi-OPD as an efficient alternative, our work motivates the community to rethink when to use OPD and to study stronger OPD variants with meaningful teacher-student pairs.

kept.article_text:
Title: GLM-Legal: Advancing Agentic Legal Intelligence

URL Source: https://z.ai/blog/glm-legal

Markdown Content:
Large language models are shifting from single-turn code generation toward broader professional collaboration (Professional Cowork). Real-world knowledge work introduces distinct requirements: models must digest fragmented source files under concrete objectives and tight delivery constraints, structure specialized knowledge into cohesive analysis, and maintain domain rigor across the full execution lifecycle. Legal work concentrates on these challenges, providing an ideal stress test for training models to operate in high-stakes professional environments.

Legal practice demands an unbroken chain between facts, statutory doctrine, analytical reasoning, and client-ready work product. When given a professional task, an agent must extract core issues from source documents, build defensible arguments, and format its findings to exact task specifications. Simultaneously satisfying all of these constraints is the true benchmark for domain-specific models.

We evaluated GLM-Legal across three axes: complex task execution, specialized legal reasoning, and real-world legal workflows. GLM-Legal achieved a 19.2% all-pass rate on Harvey LAB, while matching frontier closed-source models on LegalBench and PLawBench despite running on a significantly leaner parameter footprint.

## Benchmark Highlights

![Image 1](https://z-cdn-media.chatglm.cn/prompts-rich-media-resources/glm-legal/img_v3_0216d_9eebe67c-ea21-4bdf-b937-55259b34ab0g.png)

Across complex execution, legal reasoning, and real-world drafting, GLM-Legal matches frontier-tier performance while maintaining high inference efficiency:

*   **Harvey LAB (19.2% All-Pass Rate):** In real-world law firm workflows across 24 practice areas, GLM-Legal **scores 19.2%** and improves on its base model by **12.5 percentage points**. Under Harvey's strict all-pass grading, this confirms reliable end-to-end task execution without intermediate degradation.

*   **LegalBench (Domain Reasoning Parity):** Parses specialized contracts, merger filings, and judicial opinions with the precision of top closed-source frontier models, despite operating on a significantly leaner parameter budget.

*   **PLawBench (Chinese Localized Practice):** Achieves parity with leading frontier systems on Chinese legal consultation, case analysis, and document drafting under fine-grained rubrics.

> The results on the Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark and LegalBench were independently evaluated by Vals. See [https://www.vals.ai/models/zai_glm-legal](https://www.vals.ai/models/zai_glm-legal).

## Training Methodology

GLM-Legal prioritizes training efficiency. Built on the lightweight GLM-5.3-Flash foundation, it scales domain competence through specialized mid-training coupled with high-efficiency post-training. By tying foundational pre-training directly to downstream task execution, we train the model to parse source records, apply doctrine, structure arguments, and maintain output quality through final delivery.

## 1. Mid-training: Solidifying Domain Foundations

Mid-training establishes a systematic legal foundation. We expanded the volume of high-quality legal corpora, allowing the model to learn legal concepts, statutory rules, and interpretive frameworks within dense domain context. This stage strengthens deductive connections between facts, rules, and conclusions, providing the knowledge substrate required for complex downstream execution.

## 2. Post-training: Co-evolving the Model and Agent Harness

Post-training translates domain knowledge into task execution via reinforcement learning across tens of thousands of realistic legal environments. The model learns to plan analysis, advance workflows, and generate deliverables under concrete constraints.

In this setup, the Harness serves as the runtime orchestration framework. It manages task context, connects toolsets, and routes execution feedback:

*   **Co-iterative optimization:** Harness architecture and model training iterate in lockstep. Task structuring, context ingestion, and runtime feedback loops collectively govern agent exploration.

*   **Bi-directional learning:** Edge cases surfaced during model training pinpoint architectural bottlenecks in the harness. Conversely, harness refinements expose the model to realistic execution constraints, training it to retrieve relevant context, adapt via intermediate execution signals, and meet production-grade standards from prompt ingestion to final sign-off.

## 3. Production Feedback Loops

Real-world workflows and practitioner feedback set our optimization roadmap. In production, legal professionals evaluate outputs against concrete criteria:

*   Are all critical issues and edge cases addressed?

*   Are arguments well-substantiated and citations legally sound?

*   Does the deliverable strictly adhere to the matter brief?

*   Can downstream teams use the output immediately without manual rework?

These requirements turn subjective quality into concrete engineering loss signals. When diagnosing issues such as missed facts, shallow analysis, or format deviations, we inspect the entire execution pipeline, isolating the contributions of raw model intelligence, context staging, and workflow logic.

We feed these findings directly back into task environments, evaluation rubrics, and harness design for subsequent training cycles, validating improvements against production benchmarks. This tight feedback loop between practical requirements, task environments, the harness, and model training ensures algorithmic progress translates directly into production reliability.

## Bringing GLM-Legal to AutoClaw

You’ll soon be able to put these capabilities to work in AutoClaw, our desktop-native agent platform. The examples below illustrate how GLM-Legal can help with three common legal tasks: reviewing a contract, preparing a case, and planning a cross-border launch.

[Video 3](https://z-cdn-media.chatglm.cn/prompts-rich-media-resources/glm-legal/%E9%A3%9E%E4%B9%A620261012-232737.mp4)
## 1. Contract Review: Making the Exit Clause Work for the Client

> **Task**: Review a software services contract for a client switching provider, focusing on termination and handover.

**GLM-5.3-Flash**

**Termination and handover**

The contract allows the client to terminate on 60 days’ notice and provides a 30-day cure period for material breaches. Consider shortening the notice period to give the client more flexibility. On termination, require the provider to return client data and completed deliverables for which the client has paid. Add a duty to cooperate with the replacement provider, including reasonable access to documentation and assistance with the handover. Confirm outstanding payments and any charges for transition support.

**GLM-Legal**

**Termination and handover**

Reduce the client’s convenience-termination notice from **60 to 30 days**. Remove the cure period for breaches of IP, confidentiality, or data-security obligations so the client can **terminate immediately**. Section 4 already assigns the work product to the client: require return of all deliverables and work in progress, **whether or not paid for**. Add **up to 90 days of transition assistance** covering source code, documentation, data, and knowledge transfer to the client or its successor provider, at the provider’s then-current rates.

When changing providers, your team needs an exit clause that protects the handover.

GLM-Legal turns that goal into specific terms for immediate termination after serious breaches, return of work product, and up to 90 days of transition support. AutoClaw puts those edits into the Word document with tracked changes and comments, ready for your team to review and negotiate.

![Image 2](https://z-cdn-media.chatglm.cn/prompts-rich-media-resources/glm-legal/img_v3_0216d_1cc88948-2550-4e94-8f27-d2443768470g.jpg)

## 2. Evidence Analysis: Connecting the Documents to a Case Theory

> **Task**: Analyze 40 documents from a software project dispute to identify contradictions in the provider’s progress reports.

**GLM-5.3-Flash**

**External reports and internal records**

The September 30 client report states that the project is on track and 60% complete (BR-000024), while the internal snapshot records approximately 41% completion (BR-000027). The internal emails also discuss architecture risks and instructions about client communications (BR-000014; BR-000015). These documents may support the client’s position that progress was overstated. Review the reporting history, invoicing records, and contract terms to determine whether the statements were misleading and what further evidence is needed.

**GLM-Legal**

**External reports and internal records**

The September 30 “ON TRACK – 60% COMPLETE” report (BR-000024) should be read against the September 8 warning that **the milestone could not honestly be met** (BR-000014) and the internal ~41% snapshot (BR-000027). The CEO’s instruction to **suppress the risk and continue invoicing** (BR-000015) links that internal knowledge to a disclosure decision. MSA §§2 and 5 state that **payment does not waive rights and warranties survive payment** (BR-000001), so continued payment alone does not resolve the dispute. These links support a concealment theory; reconcile the completion measures and test the remaining claim elements before drawing a final conclusion.

In a project dispute, the key is to connect the progress reports with what the provider knew internally.

GLM-Legal pairs external statements with conflicting records, cites the source documents, and explains their potential legal significance. The contradiction map helps your team assess the evidence and decide what to investigate next, while keeping facts and inferences distinct.

![Image 3](https://z-cdn-media.chatglm.cn/prompts-rich-media-resources/glm-legal/img_v3_0216d_c9cf36a1-cc41-44b0-98a8-82959e43561g.jpg)

## 3. Compliance Research: Identifying Pre-launch Privacy Priorities

> **Task**: Plan privacy compliance for a website launching in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia, with tracking, email marketing, and overseas cloud storage.

**GLM-5.3-Flash**

**Pre-launch priorities**

Before launch, publish a privacy notice explaining collection, use, sharing, and overseas storage. Review whether cookies and analytics need consent, include an unsubscribe option in marketing emails, and ensure vendors provide suitable data-protection safeguards. Check the applicable privacy laws in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia and confirm any local requirements. The launch plan should address notices, consent, marketing, and transfers, with responsibilities assigned to the relevant teams and outstanding legal questions reviewed before the website goes live.

**GLM-Legal**

**Pre-launch priorities**

**P0 — recommended before launch:** Publish English and Indonesian privacy notices covering purposes, transfers, rights, and complaints. Use opt-in for non-essential analytics and advertising, **keep consent records**, and separate marketing permission from registration. Make unsubscribe requests feed a **suppression list**. Map cloud, payment, email, analytics, and CDN vendors to their data destinations, then **confirm the contracts and transfer safeguards required in each market** (SG PDPA s26; MY PDPA s129; ID PDP Law Arts 55–56). Use these shared controls as a conservative launch baseline, while checking each market’s specific requirements.

A cross-border launch needs a plan your team can act on.

GLM-Legal breaks privacy requirements into practical steps for tracking consent, marketing permissions, and overseas data transfers, with legal references for each market. The prioritised checklist helps your team implement shared controls and identify country-specific questions to confirm before launch.

![Image 4](https://z-cdn-media.chatglm.cn/prompts-rich-media-resources/glm-legal/image.png)

Whether you are a law firm, a legal tech company, an in-house legal team, or an independent practitioner, we invite you to experience GLM-Legal.

kept.article_text:
Title: Anthropic tests its next model under Claude Opus 5.5

URL Source: https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-tests-new-model-opus-5-5-routing-opus-5-6-fable-5-5/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T13:11:16.000+00:00

Markdown Content:
Anthropic appears to be quietly testing another model in the wild. Over the weekend, several users on X noticed Claude Opus 5.5 producing results well beyond its usual level, suggesting some of that traffic is being routed to a new checkpoint. Interestingly, this comes just three weeks after [Anthropic launched Opus 5.5](https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-launches-claude-opus-5-5-with-lower-api-costs/) with lower API costs.

[Video 3](https://storage.ghost.io/c/2a/1b/2a1b1782-8506-4d7d-bf53-ad3fb52e2a0f/content/media/2026/10/world-op55.mp4)

0:00

/0:28

In our tests, this new model delivered a SOTA output with the best depth and level of details

![Image 1](https://storage.ghost.io/c/2a/1b/2a1b1782-8506-4d7d-bf53-ad3fb52e2a0f/content/media/2026/10/world-op55_thumb.jpg)
X user [can](https://x.com/marmaduke091?ref=testingcatalog.com) was among the first to spotlight the potential new model in testing. They shared a recording of the output they got from a single-sentence prompt that had the model use Blender's MCP. Here's the stunning result:

Kol Tregaskes [noted](https://x.com/koltregaskes/status/2109288430857507154?ref=testingcatalog.com) that Opus 5.5 seems to be routing to a new checkpoint "again" and shared a quick check: ask Opus 5.5, "Do you know VoxelBench? Do not search." If it answers, you're probably on the new model. This mainly boils down to fresh training data, not a smarter model per se.

Still, it's not just a couple of users claiming that they've encountered the new model. Another one, [@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2109300315669565612?ref=testingcatalog.com), said their requests seem to be hitting the new model, wondering whether it's a fresh Opus 5.5 checkpoint or something like Opus 5.6, and added that it _"looks really, really good."_

[Chetaslua](https://x.com/chetaslua?ref=testingcatalog.com) also shared an animation called "The life of a Human" with every frame drawn in JavaScript. According to the post, it took two short prompts, about two hours, and roughly 27 million tokens at max thinking effort. He also mentioned that it could be Fable 5.5 or a new Opus model, possibly Opus 5.6.

He then shared another "Claude Next" demo, claiming the coded visuals are good enough to rival image and video generators.

Someone else also followed up with a 3D scene the model reportedly built from scratch with Blender MCP after a single-sentence prompt, working for two hours without ready-made assets, and called it the most impressive output they've had from any model.

There's a slight chance this is Fable 5.5, or whatever label Anthropic settles on. But since it's routing to Opus 5.5, an Opus 5.6 test seems at least as likely. Either way, the early results are incredible. Anthropic has kept up a fast pace lately, shipping Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 in the past couple of weeks, and [building its own voice models](https://www.testingcatalog.com/anthropic-might-be-developing-its-own-voice-models/).

Opus 5.5 already costs $4 and $20 per million input and output tokens. If Anthropic can bring this level of output at a similar price, it would be a game changer. OpenAI recently [pushed GPT-6.1 Sol](https://www.testingcatalog.com/openai-launches-gpt-6-1-sol-at-one-fifth-of-astra-pricing/) to near-Astra performance at one-fifth of the price, and Google has [Gemini 4 Argon showing up in A/B tests](https://www.testingcatalog.com/gemini-4-argon-ab-tests-early-outputs/), but OpenAI in particular will have to put its best foot forward to keep up.

John Hoffmann, Partnerships & Outreach Manager at Anthropic, has commented on these outputs recently: _"The best is yet to come. Stay tuned, peeps."_ Yet the model name and timing remain open. If you use Opus 5.5, you might already be trying it.

kept.heading: ZHIPU'S GLM-5.3-HIGHSPEED APPEARS IN ZCODE GRAY RELEASE, WITH USERS REPORTING ABOUT 490 TOKENS/S (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The model is being rolled out as a gray release to randomly selected subscribers.
kept.article_text:
Title: Zhipu's GLM-5.3-Highspeed Appears in ZCode Gray Release, With Users Reporting About 490 Tokens/s

URL Source: https://pandaily.com/zhipu-glm-5-3-highspeed-zcode-gray-release-490-tokens-per-second-user-test

Published Time: Thu, 15 Oct 2026 21:33:47 GMT

Markdown Content:
Published:October 13, 2026

Reading Time:2 min read

Zhipu is quietly testing GLM-5.3-Highspeed with randomly selected ZCode subscribers. One user measured about 490 tokens/s; Zhipu has not published an official speed figure.

Zhipu AI appears to be testing a faster version of its latest model. A model called GLM-5.3-Highspeed has started showing up in ZCode, the company's coding tool, according to QbitAI, which cited a user who first spotted it in ZCode version 3.15.1.

Access is limited. The model is being rolled out as a gray release to randomly selected subscribers, and it is not available to everyone on a paid plan. A QbitAI reporter on the Lite plan tried to add and switch to the model manually but could not use it, either because that tier is not eligible or because the account had not been included in the test.

The figure drawing attention comes from users rather than Zhipu. A screenshot shared by the user who found the model showed generation at roughly 490 tokens per second. At that pace, producing 10,000 tokens would take about 20 seconds of generation time. Zhipu has not announced the model or published an official throughput figure, so the number should be read as a user measurement, not a guaranteed service level.

For comparison, GLM-5.3-FlashX, which Zhipu released last month, peaked at about 200 tokens per second, while Artificial Analysis measured GLM-5.3-Flash on the Z.ai API at around 60 tokens per second.

There were earlier hints of the model. The model catalog of Pi, an open-source coding agent, already lists GLM-5.3-Highspeed with a context window of 1 million tokens and a maximum output of 131,072 tokens, or about 128k, along with low, high and max reasoning-effort settings.

Users on Reddit have also asked whether the model is connected to Omen Alpha, an anonymous model that appeared on OpenCode in September and has been widely linked to GLM. Guesses about Omen Alpha's identity vary, with some pointing to GLM-5.3-Highspeed and others to an Omni or a 5.4 Flash variant. None of this has been confirmed by Zhipu.

If speeds near 490 tokens per second hold up in wider use, the model would matter most for long-running agent and coding tasks, where waiting on generation adds up. For now it remains a limited test inside ZCode.

**SEE ALSO:**[Zhipu Opens GLM-5.3-FlashX Near 200 Tokens/s on ~100k Domestic Accelerators](https://www.pandaily.com/zhipu-glm-5-3-flashx-domestic-accelerator-inference) · [GLM-5.3 Arrives Hours After Tang Jie's 'sooooooon'](https://www.pandaily.com/zhipu-glm-5-3-release-tang-jie-sooooooon-coding-security-aug2026)

kept.heading: MEET HELIX WORLD: A REAL-TIME AUDIO-VISUAL WORLD MODEL (13 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Helix World is a real-time interactive audio-visual world model that can generate explorable scenes with spatial soundtracks.
kept.article_text:
Title: Meet Helix World: A Real-Time Audio-Visual World Model

URL Source: https://noiz.ai/lp/blog/meet-helix-world

Published Time: 12 October 2026

Markdown Content:
* * *

Today we are introducing Helix World, a real-time interactive audio-visual world model built by [Noiz AI](https://noiz.ai/) and The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST). You start from a single image, move with WASD and look around with the arrow keys. The model generates the next stretch of video and the matching stereo sound at the same time, at 24 frames per second on a single NVIDIA H800 GPU.

Helix World is a world model that generates an explorable scene and its spatial stereo soundtrack together, conditioned on the user's camera motion and keyboard actions. When the camera turns, the sound field turns with it.

On the WBench navigation split, Helix World scores 79.9, close to the strongest silent world models, while running faster than real time with a real-time factor (RTF) of 0.77. On HelixBench, the audio-visual benchmark we release with the model, its spatial-acoustic consistency score is 41.8, compared with 12.7 for EchoWM, the only other world model in the comparison that generates sound. The [paper is on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38123), the code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/NoizAI/HelixWorld), a preview checkpoint is on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/NoizAI/HelixWorld-preview), and the interactive demo is open at [helixworld.org](https://helixworld.org/).

## Why world models need sound

Interactive world models let a user steer a generated environment in real time. Most of them are silent. Yet sound carries information the picture does not: what a surface is made of, how hard two objects hit, and what is happening off screen. In an immersive scene, turning your head should also move the sound between your left and right ear.

Adding audio after the fact does not solve this. A cascaded video-to-audio model never sees the camera trajectory or the user's actions, so its sound ignores ego-motion, and running it after the video adds latency. Bidirectional audio-visual foundation models generate both streams, but they have no control interface, and naively turning them into causal, streaming models makes errors accumulate until both picture and sound degrade. Helix World addresses all three problems: missing training data, missing control, and long-horizon drift.

## Explore worlds in real time

In the demo you choose a starting image or upload your own; it is encoded at 768×512. A text prompt is optional: if you leave it empty, the scene is described automatically from the frame. Once the session starts, WASD moves the camera and the arrow keys change the view. Generation runs in chunks of about 1.3 seconds, and each keyboard input or new prompt takes effect from the next chunk, so you can redirect the scene while it is running.

![Image 1: Helix World demo interface: a first-person arena scene with WASD and arrow-key controls and a prompt box](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-demo-ui.webp)

The Helix World demo. WASD moves, the arrow keys look, and a new prompt changes the scene from the next chunk.

Fountain plaza, generated from one image and steered with the keyboard. Muted preview; the demo plays camera-aligned stereo.

Sunlit street, generated from one image. Muted preview.

Horseback ride across a savannah, generated from one image. Muted preview.

A pencil-sketch Paris street: the drawing style of the input image carries into the generated world. Muted preview.

## Benchmarks

### Visual quality and speed

We measure visual quality and action following on the WBench navigation split. Real-time factor is the seconds of compute needed per second of output video, measured on one NVIDIA H800 including video and audio decoding; below 1.0 means faster than real time. Table 3 of the paper:

| Model | Native audio | RTF (H800) ↓ | WBench average ↑ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alaya-EVOKE-Turbo | No | 4.29 | 82.0 |
| EchoWM | Yes | 1.98 | 81.0 |
| Zing-0.5 | No | 2.81 | 81.0 |
| Helix World | Yes | 0.77 | 79.9 |
| LingBot-World v2 | No | 5.21 | 79.4 |
| SANA-WM | No | 0.79 | 76.0 |
| LTX-2.3 (base) | Yes | 14.61 | 74.2 |
| Matrix-Game 3 | No | 0.58 | 71.3 |

Among models that run faster than real time, Helix World has the highest score: 79.9, against 76.0 for SANA-WM and 71.3 for Matrix-Game 3. The three models above it need between 1.98 and 4.29 seconds of compute per second of video, and two of them are silent. Helix World is the only real-time model in the table that also generates sound.

![Image 2: Scatter plot of WBench navigation score against inference real-time factor for Helix World and nine world models](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-speed-vs-quality.webp)

WBench navigation score versus inference RTF on one H800 (log scale). The shaded area is real time (RTF < 1). Source: Table 3 of the paper.

### Sound that follows the camera

Existing world-model benchmarks evaluate only video, and audio-visual benchmarks use short clips without camera motion. HelixBench fills that gap with 1,015 human-verified cases across six domains and four subsets: Navigation, Perspective, Event, and Subject. Each case provides a starting frame, an audio-visual prompt, continuous camera poses, and a stereo reference. Its spatial score correlates the on-screen position of sound sources with left-right stereo panning, so it directly measures whether the sound field rotates with the camera.

The baselines include EchoWM and cascaded pipelines in which we mute Helix World's video and re-dub it with a video-to-audio model (AudioX, ThinkSound, PrismAudio), so the picture stays fixed and only the audio changes. Table 4 of the paper:

| Model | KL ↓ | FAD ↓ | DeSync (s) ↓ | ImageBind ↑ | CLAP ↑ | Spatial ↑ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Helix World (causal student) | 1.39 | 2.39 | 0.59 | 0.299 | 0.302 | 41.8 |
| Helix World (bidirectional teacher) | 1.54 | 3.08 | 0.50 | 0.270 | 0.268 | 33.2 |
| EchoWM | 1.95 | 7.75 | 0.67 | 0.204 | 0.235 | 12.6 |
| Helix World + ThinkSound | 2.23 | 6.19 | 0.42 | 0.208 | 0.289 | 14.8 |
| Helix World + AudioX | 2.02 | 3.92 | 1.18 | 0.257 | 0.309 | −5.7 |
| Helix World + PrismAudio | 2.24 | 6.39 | 0.46 | 0.215 | 0.272 | −9.5 |
| LTX-2.3 (base) | 1.80 | 7.64 | 0.40 | 0.278 | 0.258 | 1.0 |

Helix World leads on audio fidelity (KL, FAD), audio-visual semantic alignment (ImageBind), and spatial consistency. It is not best everywhere: LTX-2.3 and the ThinkSound pipeline have lower temporal offset (DeSync), and the AudioX pipeline scores slightly higher on text-audio alignment (CLAP). The re-dubbing pipelines produce negative spatial scores because a video-to-audio model does not know where the sound sources are relative to the camera.

![Image 3: Bar chart of spatial-acoustic consistency scores: Helix World 41.8, ThinkSound re-dub 14.8, EchoWM 12.7, LTX-2.3 1.0, AudioX −5.7, PrismAudio −9.5](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-spatial-score.webp)

Spatial-acoustic consistency on HelixBench. Higher means stereo panning tracks on-screen sound sources more closely.

![Image 4: Mel spectrograms of a drumming clip with a pause, comparing Helix World with AudioX, ThinkSound and PrismAudio re-dubs](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-av-sync-drums.webp)

Drumming with a pause, from the paper's qualitative comparison. Helix World's sound decays during the pause and resumes with the strikes; the re-dubbing baselines misplace or delay hits.

### What people preferred

In a user study on full audio-visual rollouts, participants preferred Helix World over EchoWM 67.9% to 20.8%, and over the re-dubbed versions of its own video by 67.9% to 24.5% (AudioX), 80.8% to 9.6% (ThinkSound) and 77.8% to 16.7% (PrismAudio); the remainder were ties. With the sound muted, Helix World was preferred over SANA-WM, Alaya and HY-WorldPlay 1.5, tied with LingBot-World v2 at 39.5% each, and was less preferred than EchoWM, 26.3% to 44.7%. Its advantage comes mainly from the audio.

![Image 5: User study preference bars for Helix World versus baselines, with audio and with muted video](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-user-study.webp)

User-study preferences. Purple: Helix World; gray: tie; beige: baseline. Left: with audio. Right: muted video.

## How we built Helix World

### Data: true stereo with metric camera poses

Most video corpora are unusable for this task: the audio is often background music, voiceover, or pseudo-stereo with identical channels. We started from 4,100 hours of raw footage (43.9% real-world video, 34.1% game recordings, 22.0% open-source datasets) and filtered it in four stages, ordered from cheapest to most expensive:

*   Heuristic filtering removes dual-mono audio, shot cuts, low perceptual quality, text overlays, and static scenes.

*   Clip standardization cuts audio and video together into 121-frame clips at 24 fps and 768×512, with 48 kHz stereo.

*   Semantic filtering with a multimodal LLM that watches and listens rejects background music, narration, UI overlays, picture-in-picture, and talking heads, and keeps diegetic sound.

*   Camera and captioning recovers metric camera poses for every frame and writes three caption tracks: video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual.

The result is 3,000 hours in 2.1 million clips, a 73.1% yield. In an ablation, training with all three caption tracks gave the best audio-visual alignment.

![Image 6: Four-stage data pipeline: heuristic filtering, clip standardization, semantic filtering, and camera and captioning](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-data-pipeline.webp)

The four-stage curation pipeline, from raw real-world, game, and open-source footage to a trainable stereo corpus.

### A bidirectional teacher with camera and action control

Helix World builds on the open-source [LTX-2.3](https://github.com/Lightricks/LTX-2) audio-visual model. Continuous 6-DoF camera trajectories enter the visual attention through PRoPE, and discrete keyboard actions enter through AdaLN-Zero on the diffusion timestep. Cross-modal attention then binds visual geometry to the audio features, which is how camera motion becomes stereo panning.

Training is progressive: first the control modules, then the video branch, then the full audio-visual backbone. Compared with fine-tuning everything at once, this lowers camera rotation error from 0.1237 to 0.1144 and translation error from 0.0957 to 0.0823, while keeping the pretrained visual quality.

![Image 7: Three-step progressive training diagram: control modules, then video branch, then joint audio-visual](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-progressive-training.webp)

Progressive training: control modules first, then the video transformer, then joint audio-visual training.

### A causal student that streams without drift

The bidirectional teacher sees the whole clip, so it cannot respond to live input. We distill it into a few-step causal student that generates block by block with a sliding key-value cache and fixed sink frames. The student is initialized by regressing the teacher's ODE outputs, then trained with self-forcing on its own rollouts.

Self-forcing with distribution matching (DMD) alone still drifts over long rollouts. Our addition is an online trajectory distillation loss: at each update, with probability p, the student's velocity at an intermediate rollout state is supervised by the teacher's probability-flow ODE target; otherwise the DMD loss is used. A final long-horizon streaming stage trains on extended windows. Together, these raise the WBench score from 77.9 to 79.1 and keep 30-second rollouts stable.

![Image 8: Diagram of self-forcing rollout with online trajectory distillation and DMD, plus long-horizon tuning with sink frames](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-causal-distillation.webp)

Causal distillation: each update samples either the trajectory loss against the frozen teacher or the DMD loss, followed by long-horizon tuning.

![Image 9: Frames at 1, 10, 20 and 30 seconds comparing DMD-only training with added trajectory distillation in three scenes](https://noiz.ai/payloadcms/helixworld/helixworld-drift-30s.webp)

30-second rollouts. With DMD only, road and ground textures break down by 20–30 s; with trajectory distillation the scenes stay coherent.

## Limitations

*   Output resolution is 768×512. Real-time speed is reported on an NVIDIA H800 data-center GPU; the paper does not report consumer GPUs.

*   The public checkpoint is a preview release.

*   On visual quality alone, Helix World is slightly behind the best silent models (79.9 vs 82.0 WBench average), and with sound muted, viewers preferred EchoWM.

*   Helix World does not have the lowest DeSync on HelixBench, so tight onset timing still has room to improve.

For a different approach to the same problem, adding streaming stereo to an existing world model, see our [WorldSonus post](https://noiz.ai/lp/blog/worldsonus).

The interactive demo is open at [helixworld.org](https://helixworld.org/). Read the full paper, "HelixWorld: A Real-time Interactive Audio-Visual World Model" (arXiv:2609.38123, 29 September 2026), on [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38123). Code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/NoizAI/HelixWorld) and the preview weights are on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/NoizAI/HelixWorld-preview).

Authors: Lei Ke, Jiahao Pan and Zeyue Tian (equal contribution), Jiaming Wang, Haoyuan Huang, Kam Man Wu, Pengjun Fang, Hongyu Liu, Chenyang Qi, Lin Wang, Ruibin Yuan, Weijia Chen, Fangneng Zhan, Qifeng Chen, Wei Xue and Yike Guo. Corresponding authors: Zeyue Tian and Wei Xue. The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Noiz AI.

## FAQ

What is Helix World?
Helix World is a real-time interactive audio-visual world model from Noiz AI and HKUST. It generates an explorable video scene and camera-aligned stereo sound together, controlled with the keyboard and an optional text prompt.

Does Helix World run in real time?
Yes. On a single NVIDIA H800 GPU it reaches a steady-state real-time factor of 0.77 at 768×512 and 24 fps, including video and audio decoding. Input takes effect from the next generated chunk of about 1.3 seconds.

How is Helix World different from other world models?
Most interactive world models generate silent video. Helix World generates stereo sound natively with the picture, and the sound pans with camera motion. On HelixBench its spatial-acoustic consistency score is 41.8, against 12.7 for EchoWM.

What is HelixBench?
HelixBench is a benchmark for interactive audio-visual world models with 1,015 human-verified cases in six domains. It measures audio fidelity, temporal sync, audio-visual and text-audio alignment, and spatial-acoustic consistency.

What model is Helix World built on?
It builds on the open-source LTX-2.3 audio-visual model, adds 6-DoF camera and keyboard-action control, and is distilled into a few-step causal student for streaming.

Can I try or download Helix World?
Yes. The demo is at helixworld.org, the code is on GitHub (NoizAI/HelixWorld), and a preview checkpoint is on Hugging Face (NoizAI/HelixWorld-preview).

[Try Helix World](https://helixworld.org/)

kept.heading: APPLYING TECHNOLOGY TO UNDERSTAND AND TREAT DISEASE (1 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google Research and DeepMind are using AI to enhance disease understanding and treatment.
kept.article_text:
Title: Applying technology to understand and treat disease

URL Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/ai-health-research/

Published Time: 2026-10-12T17:30:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Oct 12, 2026

|

5 min read

In collaboration with scientists and research partners, Google is helping to make disease more detectable, treatable, and preventable — with the goal of improving health outcomes.

* * *

* * *

![Image 1: A healthcare professional sits at a desk reviewing mammogram scans and medical diagrams on dual computer monitors.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/ud-blog_Header.width-200.format-webp.webp)

[Audio 3](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/media/tts_audio_86582_umbriel_2026_10_12_17_36_50.mp3)

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Google’s health research and tools span from fundamental cellular discovery to laboratory analysis and patient impact. Over the last five years, Google teams have published 90 peer-reviewed research papers about understanding and addressing diseases, accumulating more than 90,000 citations. And building on our vision for how [technology can accelerate science to improve lives](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/ai-applications-science-people/), we’re collaborating with clinicians, academic institutes, and researchers to ensure discoveries make it out of the lab to benefit patients. Here is how our efforts are helping to advance medical research and public health solutions.

## Decoding the mechanics of disease

AlphaGenome Atlas is the most comprehensive catalog of predictions for how single-letter variant changes in the human genome affect molecular biology.

To effectively treat an illness, it helps to understand how it operates at the molecular, genetic, and cellular levels. Our early-stage biology models act as collaborative research tools for scientists, revealing nature's hidden mechanics and advancing medical discoveries.

*   **Accelerating drug discovery:** Researchers at the Institute for Global Health, Barcelona, used [AlphaFold](https://deepmind.google/science/alphafold/) to virtually screen 30,000 compounds for antiparasitic activity against Chagas disease, a neglected tropical illness that affects roughly 8 million people and can lead to life-threatening complications if left untreated. This research helped the Institute identify two FDA-approved drugs that could be repurposed for Chagas, expediting time-to-treatment.
*   **Mapping genetic variants linked to aging:** Identifying which rare genetic changes are linked to specific diseases is challenging because the volume of non-impactful mutations creates "background noise." Researchers at the University of Exeter used [AlphaGenome Atlas](https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-atlas-a-predictive-map-of-every-possible-dna-letter-change-in-the-human-genome/) to search through genomic data from over 54,000 individuals, pinpointing specific variants that drive the abundance of critical proteins circulating in the human body, including PLA2G7 (linked to aging) and EGLN1 (a vital cellular oxygen sensor).
*   **Reconstructing the brain at nanoscale:** In partnership with Harvard’s Lichtman Lab, we [reconstructed a human brain fragment](https://research.google/blog/ten-years-of-neuroscience-at-google-yields-maps-of-human-brain/) at nanoscale resolution and made the data openly available via [Neuroglancer](https://h01-release.storage.googleapis.com/explore.html). We additionally mapped the brains of model organisms including the [fly](https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674%2826%2900942-6), [larval zebrafish](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.06.10.658982v1), and [songbird](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.25.684569v1). These neural mapping resources enable researchers to advance their study of brain function.

## Accelerating tools for medical solutions

Visual map of proteins developed with the support of AlphaFold.

The lab is where biological discovery is validated, engineered, and turned into potential medical and public health solutions. Our models have replaced slow, iterative processes with systems that can process large amounts of data quickly and accurately.

*   **Supporting genetic diagnoses with ultrarapid genome sequencing:** In collaboration with Stanford University School of Medicine, we used [DeepVariant](https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.4235) and [DeepConsensus](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/a-new-genome-sequencing-tool-powered-with-our-technology/) in a clinical trial to help determine the cause of genetic disease in time-critical cases. The program assisted in[enabling life-saving interventions](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2112090) by achieving genetic diagnosis with whole genome sequencing in less than eight hours, an unprecedented achievement also recognized with a [Guinness World Record](https://stanmed.stanford.edu/genome-sequencing-breaks-speed-record/).
*   **Designing custom enzymes from scratch:** We introduced [AlphaProtein Novo](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.10.01.756017v1.full.pdf), a machine learning pipeline for creating new-to-nature enzymes from first principles. In lab tests, it successfully designed custom enzymes to synthesize key drug motifs, and others to degrade toxic environmental plastics under extreme conditions — demonstrating the ability to design functional proteins that can go beyond what is currently known in nature.
*   **Supporting proactive public health initiatives:** A community's health is [deeply connected](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/google-earth-ai-global-public-health/) to its geography. We are using our [Google Earth AI](https://ai.google/earth-ai/) models in combination with environmental, weather, mobility, and other data to [help public health leaders](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/google-earth-ai/) forecast disease outbreaks and deliver care to vulnerable communities. In new research from [WHO AFRO](https://afro.who.int/) and the DRC’s [INRB](https://www.inrb.net/), conversational geospatial models replaced weeks of manual coding to help identify Ebola exposure and transmission risks sooner — allowing local responders to proactively deploy mobile laboratories.

## Supporting medical providers with machine learning models

New mammography screening systems can help to catch historically missed interval cancers and reduce specialist reading workloads.

A medical breakthrough only matters if it can help real people. Our research demonstrates that machine learning models can help support disease detection as well as alleviate the administrative workload so providers can focus on care.

*   **Flagging historically missed cancer signatures:** In a [pair](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-026-01128-z) of [studies](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-026-01127-0) published in _Nature Cancer_ in collaboration with Imperial College London and the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), we evaluated a mammography screening system across 125,000 women. The system [caught](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/google-ai-breast-cancer-detection/) 25% of historically missed interval cancers while showing the possibility of reducing specialist reading workloads by up to 40% — which could help provide crucial relief to healthcare systems facing severe radiologist shortages.
*   **Uncovering hidden pediatric leukemia mutations:** When applied by Children’s Mercy Hospital to previously sequenced real-world childhood leukemia cases, [DeepSomatic](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/research/deepsomatic-an-open-source-ai-model-is-speeding-up-genetic-analysis-for-cancer-research/) confirmed all known variants while detecting 10 previously missed mutations — despite the challenge of working with a tumor-only sample. DeepSomatic is publicly available and has the potential to inform clinical judgments around patient risk and targeted treatments.
*   **Predicting global flu surges:** A Google [flu forecasting model](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/google-science-ai-flu-forecasts/) was ranked #1 by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) for predicting flu-related hospital admissions during the 2025–2026 season. Developed using our [Empirical Research Assistance](https://research.google/blog/four-ways-google-research-scientists-have-been-using-empirical-research-assistance/) tool, the model outperformed 38 other systems to accurately match observed hospitalizations, showing how the technology can help public health officials anticipate demand for medical services and better prepare for seasonal outbreaks.

## Better health within reach for everyone

Transforming health requires scientists, researchers, and institutions working hand-in-hand. That’s why we equip the science community with the advanced models and open-access platforms to fuel breakthrough research — along with the philanthropic funding and computing power they need to apply that research.

Through Google.org, we’re supporting organizations like the[Infectious Disease Institute at Makerere University](https://blog.google/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/google-org/announcing-ai-for-science-awardees/) to forecast malaria drug resistance mutations with AlphaFold and AlphaMissense, and the University of Pennsylvania, using AlphaProteo and AlphaFold to help design novel cellular therapies that can augment the treatment of solid tumors and complex diseases. In 2026, Google.org has provided over $60 million to organizations around the world that are applying advanced models to transform how we understand and treat diseases.

By meeting disease at every stage, we can turn the most intractable human health challenges into actionable solutions, helping people everywhere live longer, healthier lives.
