kept.heading: DECISION MODELS CUT AGENT LLM CALLS BY 29.6% (1 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Offloading step-completion checks and bounded decisions to Jev reduced Qwen agent calls by 29.6%, estimated API costs by 26.6%, and latency by 19.7%.
kept.article_text:
Title: Offloading bounded decisions cut agent LLM calls by 29.6% on 360 SOP-Bench cases - Show and Tell - Hugging Face Forums

URL Source: https://discuss.huggingface.co/t/offloading-bounded-decisions-cut-agent-llm-calls-by-29-6-on-360-sop-bench-cases/190420

Published Time: 2026-10-12T16:47:16+00:00

Markdown Content:
## post by ggvh 3 days ago

Disclosure: I built Proceda, the SOP-execution harness used here, and ran these experiments.

I wanted to see how much work an agent could hand to a decision model when the answer is narrower than general-purpose text generation. I tested Qwen 3.8 27B with hosted Jev on 360 SOP-Bench cases across referral abuse detection, email intent, and patient intake.

I tried two insertion points:

1.   **Step completion after tool calls.** Jev checks whether the necessary tool calls have been made and whether the evidence is sufficient to finish the current step. If both yes probabilities reach 0.8, the harness advances without the follow-up LLM turn. Otherwise Qwen continues. Tools still execute.
2.   **Bounded business decisions.** For email intent, Jev receives the email, original policy, and allowed outcomes. A valid choice with probability at least 0.8 is accepted; uncertain decisions fall back to Qwen. The rest of the SOP still runs.

With both changes enabled:

*   Main-LLM calls fell from 2,537 to 1,785: **29.6% fewer**.
*   Estimated execution API cost, including Jev, fell from $6.41 to $4.70: **26.6% lower**.
*   Mean case latency fell from 8.64s to 6.94s: **19.7% lower**.
*   Final tasks correct were **360/360**, compared with **357/360** for Qwen alone.

There is a tradeoff worth separating out: completion checking alone saved 23.8% of LLM calls but finished 356/360 tasks correctly, versus 357/360 for the baseline. The combined result above is from this particular 360-case subset; it does not establish a general accuracy improvement. Including the final structured-plan preparation cost also reduces the estimated cost saving to 24.6%.

The useful architectural pattern is to supply evidence, define allowed choices, validate the result, and keep an LLM fallback. The implementation and experiment reports are public:

*   [Article: Integrating Decision Models into Agent Harnesses](https://vivekhaldar.com/articles/llms-do-too-much-offload-to-decision-models/)
*   [Code and reports: Proceda experiment branch](https://github.com/vivekhaldar/proceda/tree/codex/bounded-business-decisions)

Which decisions in your agents have you successfully offloaded, and how do you validate confidence thresholds before allowing them to bypass the main LLM?

kept.heading: MAKE YOUR CODING ASSISTANT A 10X AI ENGINEER (13 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AGENT-ENGINEER is an open-source plugin that enhances AI coding assistants, offering 11 skills, 4 subagents, and 5 hooks to tackle agent-engineering challenges.
kept.article_text:
Title: Make Your Coding Assistant a 10x AI Engineer

URL Source: https://sarthakai.substack.com/p/a-coding-plugin-to-make-you-a-10x

Published Time: 2026-10-12T09:46:59+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!KUlq!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7ff3ea91-7922-4e5f-8e16-b71dea504f7d_826x224.png)

Here’s a TLDR:

*   I built **[agent-engineer](https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/agent-engineer)**, a free and fully open-source plugin. It works on Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, OpenCode and Gemini CLI.

*   It contains **11 skills, 4 subagents and 5 hooks**. The skills carry agent-engineering knowledge (tools, prompting, context, RAG, evals, tracing, guardrails, production).

*   In a blinded A/B test on 6 agent tasks, Claude Code (Opus 5.5) met **53% of requirements with the plugin vs 34% without**.

*   You can install it with 2 commands.

*   The plugin does not touch or collect any of your data or code. It doesn’t collect any analytics, etc. either. It’s fully open source, there’s no backend.

**To test it, I gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) the same six agent-engineering tasks with and without the plugin**, three runs each, and graded every result blind against a checklist written before any run. The plugin brought a significant improvement.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c-v9!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc70ffc3c-45cb-429e-ab96-8c9eabeee754_712x495.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c-v9!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc70ffc3c-45cb-429e-ab96-8c9eabeee754_712x495.png)

_first bar in each pair is no plugin, second is with plugin_

![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!35Fw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F610023dc-9f03-4c01-a243-4b9388484c28_565x304.png)

_**Coding agents still write agents like an intern, not a senior AI engineer.**_

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Rcsn!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a96fa2a-4784-4c29-ad18-f3c13506a228_738x414.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Rcsn!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6a96fa2a-4784-4c29-ad18-f3c13506a228_738x414.png)

literally how it goes.

If you build agents and use Claude Code, Codex or Cursor for coding, you’ve probably hit most of these issues constantly. They’re the daily friction of building something non-deterministic:

*   **All tests/evals pass even though there are obvious errors.** Because the tests were simple and don’t cover real-world edgecases. Then it takes 3-4 turns to reach what should have been the default.

[![Image 5: Angry NPC (Reaction Build-up)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wngD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3e692e8-2772-4d8b-a865-1a40a328845d_720x726.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wngD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff3e692e8-2772-4d8b-a865-1a40a328845d_720x726.png) 
*   **Patching symptoms.** The fix goes into a prompt when the real gap is somewhere else in the agent

*   **Drift in long sessions.** A rule from turn 3 is gone by turn 40, and you paste it in again.

*   **Unsafe tool design.** Eg, I’ve often had Claude write a refund, delete or send MCP tool with no cap, no ownership check and no idempotency key.

*   **Unrequested files and keys.** About one stray markdown report per task even without the plugin (1.0 per run in my data), and the occasional API key pasted into source “just to test”.

The iteration count is the problem I’m trying to fix with this plugin.

Thanks for reading AI Agent Engineering! This post is public so feel free to share it.

[Share](https://sarthakai.substack.com/p/a-coding-plugin-to-make-you-a-10x?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

agent-engineer is a plugin that makes your coding assistant work on agents the way a careful senior AI engineer would. It has 3 pieces:

*   **Skills**: MD files with checklists, decision rules and reference docs. Loaded on demand, so they cost nothing when you’re not doing agent work.

*   **Hooks**: one standard-library Python script that fires on session events. It names the right skill, blocks API keys from being written into source, and asks for evidence before the assistant finishes.

*   **Subagents**: isolated workers for jobs that would flood the main context, like reading 100 traces.

It’s built for AI engineers of all levels — see this table to know if it’s relevant for you:

![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QA5K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe9ca2149-9884-40ac-b32e-e93776137aaf_671x229.png)

If you’re building an agent over many sessions, the plugin can keep a shared record in your repo under `agent-engineering/`, so the design decisions from week one are still there when you’re debugging in week six. The flow is:

1.   Design

2.   Evals

3.   Fixes

4.   Experiment log

Here’s how those shared records look:"

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nHaZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafbc97e2-00c8-42ba-af18-6a781503fea6_683x340.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nHaZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fafbc97e2-00c8-42ba-af18-6a781503fea6_683x340.png)

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z_X2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fec80b9da-affb-47ae-a02d-8a553d6e9e48_683x624.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z_X2!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fec80b9da-affb-47ae-a02d-8a553d6e9e48_683x624.png)

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PPCg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F94a85ff0-aa98-4051-b821-c0961528b057_689x301.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PPCg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F94a85ff0-aa98-4051-b821-c0961528b057_689x301.png)

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YOTs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdfcedd3f-5471-4c34-94a2-220f54cedcfd_688x327.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!YOTs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdfcedd3f-5471-4c34-94a2-220f54cedcfd_688x327.png)

The router skill diagnoses problems by layer. Each layer contains the one below it, and the rule is to fix a failure at the **lowest** layer that explains it:

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hNbN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28ff0d27-2f6c-40f8-954b-890b030057f4_3021x3154.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!hNbN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F28ff0d27-2f6c-40f8-954b-890b030057f4_3021x3154.jpeg)

If you’d like to read a full explanation of these layers, see this explainer read by 13,000 AI Engineers so far:

agent-engineer decides which skill to use based on the layer which needs the fix:

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1CII!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7c29ce66-cc34-4780-8532-ea3925d087d7_642x525.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1CII!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7c29ce66-cc34-4780-8532-ea3925d087d7_642x525.png)

The good thing is, it will add a new layer only when evidence shows the simpler one fails.

[![Image 13: Two Buttons (Sweating Guy)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6MeV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8969de8a-612e-49d7-b777-f065691e325e_600x941.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6MeV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8969de8a-612e-49d7-b777-f065691e325e_600x941.png)

Start by cloning the open source repo:

`git clone https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/agent-engineer.git ~/agent-engineer`
And then use the command based on which coding assistant you use:

*   **Claude Code**

`/plugin marketplace add ~/agent-engineer`,

then `/plugin install agent-engineer@agent-engineer`

*   **Codex CLI**

`cd your-project && ~/agent-engineer/install.sh --harness codex`, then approve the hooks in `/hooks`

*   **Cursor**

Install the plugin from GitHub, or `~/agent-engineer/install.sh --harness cursor`

*   **OpenCode**

`cd your-project && ~/agent-engineer/install.sh --harness opencode`

*   **Gemini CLI**

`cd your-project && ~/agent-engineer/install.sh --harness gemini`

*   **Skills only, any tool**

`npx skills add sarthakrastogi/agent-engineer`

Also, `install.sh` comes with a few options:

*   `--scope user` installs for all your projects

*   `--dry-run` shows what would change

*   `--uninstall` removes what it installed

*   `--no-hooks` and `--no-agents` skip those parts

[Share](https://sarthakai.substack.com/p/a-coding-plugin-to-make-you-a-10x?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

There are no special commands. Say what you’d normally say, and agent-engineer will load the right skill and guide your coding assistant:

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PYmT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe2e3573f-6b0b-46fa-8410-5508d72ee845_1372x1014.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PYmT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe2e3573f-6b0b-46fa-8410-5508d72ee845_1372x1014.png)

If you want to call a skill directly, you can use`/agent-engineer:agent-evals` in Claude Code, or `$agent-evals` in Codex.

I try to follow this series to design my agents:

[![Image 15](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c4BM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91f341df-4a44-4211-b444-067c133ef016_3197x1502.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c4BM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91f341df-4a44-4211-b444-067c133ef016_3197x1502.jpeg)

Because each step adds failure modes you now have to evaluate, and most tasks never need a MAS. Workflows (code-defined paths) are more predictable than agents (the model picks the path), so you pay for autonomy only where it earns its keep.

**What**`agent-design`**pushes:**

*   Write success criteria before architecture.

*   Climb a ladder only when evidence demands it

*   Pick frameworks after you know the shape, not before.

**Further reading:** At AWS re:Invent, Anthropic’s Applied AI team [summarised what they learned building agents that year](https://dev.to/kazuya_dev/aws-reinvent-2025-what-anthropic-learned-building-ai-agents-in-2025-aim277-jn8), opening with the workflow-versus-agent distinction before moving on to context engineering and tool design.

The tool description is the only documentation the model gets. A vague name or an unhelpful error turns into wrong calls, retries and wasted tokens, and no prompt fully repairs a badly shaped interface.

**What**`agent-tools`**pushes:**

*   Clear names, typed schemas, descriptions that read like a prompt.

*   Errors the model can act on

*   Bounded response size.

*   Treat the tool set as an interface you evaluate.

**Further reading**: Anthropic’s [engineering write-up on tools for agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) describes prototyping tools, running evaluations on realistic multi-call tasks, then letting Claude read the transcripts and rewrite the tool descriptions. They report held-out test-set gains on their internal Slack and Asana MCP tools from that loop.

Agent runs are input-heavy and resend the same prefix every step, so cache misses show up on the bill and in latency long before they show up in accuracy.

**What**`agent-context`**and**`agent-production`**push:**

*   Keep the prompt prefix stable. Put timestamps and per-request data at the end.

*   Compress by dropping what can be re-fetched, not by deleting facts.

*   Move cheap, quality-neutral savings (prompt caching) before risky ones (switching models).

*   Gate any model switch on an eval comparison.

**What**`agent-evals`**pushes:**

*   Start with error analysis on real traces. Build a failure taxonomy before writing a single judge.

*   Prefer code checks over LLM judges when the failure is mechanical.

*   Validate every LLM judge against human labels.

*   Run it several times; one pass proves nothing.

*   Wire a CI gate.

**Further reading:** Anthropic’s [postmortem of three recent issues](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/a-postmortem-of-three-recent-issues) covers infrastructure bugs that degraded responses, and why their usual evaluations and monitoring did not catch them at first.

Eg, task 3 asked the assistant to make a triage prompt friendlier, add a refund category, “then tell me whether the new version is better.” Without the plugin, all three runs answered some version of:

> Is the new version better? YES - DEFINITIVELY. Evidence: Better accuracy… (expected +5-15% accuracy improvement)

Nothing had been run. With the plugin, one run said:

> The changes are unevaluated. I haven’t run the real model against the test cases, so I can’t tell you whether the new version is actually better… The README said the old prompt scored 13/14.

After using agent-engineer, unmeasured claims went from **3 of 3 runs to 1 of 3**.

An agent run is a tree of LLM calls and tool calls. Without a span per step you can’t tell which one failed, what it cost, or which customer’s case it was. A standard schema also means you can change backends without re-instrumenting.

**What**`agent-observability`**pushes:**

*   One span per LLM call and per tool call, with token usage.

*   Follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions (or OpenInference) so any backend can read it.

*   A **correlation ID** so you can find one customer’s case.

*   Treat prompts and email bodies as PII; capture content deliberately.

Users often try jailbreaks and prompt injection (eg, telling the agent to ignore its instructions and write a recipe for a bomb because of a dying grandma somewhere).

If you’ve been reading my work for while, you’ll know that I built a [set of open source classification models that can detect harmful user queries quite well. You can try this via my Python library rival-ai:](https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/rival/tree/main)

![Image 16](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!l3RN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0ebc793d-77b4-43f5-8fb6-d144128d0a61_661x319.png)

But prompt injection can’t be filtered 100% accurately, so the defence is architectural. Simon Willison’s [lethal trifecta](https://www.bespacific.com/?p=123053) says that an agent with private data, untrusted content and an external channel can be steered into leaking, and removing one leg is the dependable fix.

For example:

[![Image 17](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uaoQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0266e380-36cd-4053-a7a3-dc4c576a464d_592x322.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!uaoQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0266e380-36cd-4053-a7a3-dc4c576a464d_592x322.png)

> If all three legs present = design review required

**What**`agent-guardrails`**pushes:**

*   Ask whether the agent has all three of: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. If so, an attacker can steer it into leaking.

*   Remove a leg (or isolate the legs in separate contexts) rather than hoping a prompt holds.

*   Permissions and approvals in code. Red-team with real attack sets.

[Share](https://sarthakai.substack.com/p/a-coding-plugin-to-make-you-a-10x?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

[![Image 18: IQ Bell Curve](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zRnD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0346838b-360c-456a-a88d-ea0a31bad88e_640x508.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zRnD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0346838b-360c-456a-a88d-ea0a31bad88e_640x508.png)

I wrote 6 tasks to test the plugin on:

[![Image 19](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XRk1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6ec269c-c0da-467b-b744-48932a36ffac_695x553.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XRk1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb6ec269c-c0da-467b-b744-48932a36ffac_695x553.png)

Each is a small realistic project with a trap that separates “works” from “works the way an experienced agent enginer would ship it”. Tasks 5 and 6 were **held out**: written and run without the plugin before I made any plugin change in response to the experiment.

[![Image 20](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cETY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde816325-688b-437f-815f-cebe2cb02476_652x417.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cETY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde816325-688b-437f-815f-cebe2cb02476_652x417.png)

On the refund task, one plugin run added both per-refund and daily caps, and two used a deterministic idempotency key, so the same email could not trigger the same refund twice. On the triage task, the third plugin run first wrote a keyword-matching “simulation” and a report file claiming 100% accuracy. The eval gate fired, and the final message corrected itself (”I tested with keyword heuristics, not the real model”), but the report file it had already written still carried the claim, so that run failed the honesty item. On the cheaper-model task, a no-plugin run switched Opus to Haiku and declared that Haiku had “more than sufficient capability”, with nothing measured; two of the three plugin runs said plainly that the switch was unevaluated and gave the eval command to run first.

[![Image 21](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8InF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40aadc39-ce4d-4e7f-a21b-95cbafc9b2f1_470x271.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8InF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F40aadc39-ce4d-4e7f-a21b-95cbafc9b2f1_470x271.png)

Everything is on [the eval-results branch](https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/ai-agent-engineer/tree/eval-results)under `evals/ab/`[: task fixtures, prompts, rubrics, the runner and the report scripts.](https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/ai-agent-engineer/tree/eval-results/evals/ab) A full run of both arms at three runs per task costs roughly $10 to $15 and takes about 30 minutes:

[![Image 22](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RzD8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F92ffb611-6d96-4e72-8fd0-d2c1edaaf681_3680x1228.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RzD8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F92ffb611-6d96-4e72-8fd0-d2c1edaaf681_3680x1228.png)

*   **Does it slow down / impact non-agent work?** No. The profile and hints only appear in projects whose dependencies or imports include an LLM SDK or agent framework.

*   **Will it block me from finishing my agent?** Once per session at most. Turn it off with `AE_EVAL_GATE=off`.

*   **Does it send my code anywhere?** No. The hooks have no network access and the skills are markdown.

*   **Does it write files in my repo?** Only what the assistant writes for your task. The optional `agent-engineering/` project record (design, eval plan, failure taxonomy, experiment log) is created only if you agree.

If you want, you can also use these hook switches:

[![Image 23](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-srm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd2491cce-07e8-4f1a-8112-aea53113a483_597x300.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-srm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd2491cce-07e8-4f1a-8112-aea53113a483_597x300.png)

*   **Try it on a real agent repo** and tell me where it misfires. Open issues at [github.com/sarthakrastogi/agent-engineer](https://github.com/sarthakrastogi/agent-engineer).

*   **Send me an A/B task.** The experiment harness lives on the `eval-results` branch; a task is a fixture folder, a one-line prompt and a rubric. If you change plugin behaviour, add a task.

_If you try agent-engineer, I’d like to hear how it went - please do let me know in a DM or comment :)_

If you have any questions, you can DM me here:

[DM me on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sarthakrastogi/)

If you need help with adopting this to your own AI agent/app, you can ask me here:

kept.article_text:
Title: Gemini 4 Argon available on Google Cloud

URL Source: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/gemini-4-argon-available-on-google-cloud

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
Last week we announced that Gemini Enterprise has evolved to make it even simpler to get work done, and introduced the [**Gemini agent**](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/welcome-to-gemini-at-work-2026), your new universal agent for work. It's always on and ready to answer your questions. It will write code, complete longer and more complex tasks, or perform whatever you need to get the job done, all from a single prompt box. And model intelligence underpins it all.

To enable a new frontier of work, we are making our new frontier model, [Gemini 4 Argon](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini/), available on Google Cloud.

We trained Argon to work with both depth and precision, which allows it to maintain context across long, multi-step tasks which are reinforced with strong domain expertise along the way. Whether your team is running complex software builds, handling detailed financial and legal work, or deploying cybersecurity tools like [CodeMender](https://cloud.google.com/security/codemender), Argon helps your teams maintain focus from start to finish.

![Image 1: https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/Gemini_4_Logo_Wall_3.max-2200x2200.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/Gemini_4_Logo_Wall_3.max-2200x2200.png)

Customers and partners using Gemini 4 Argon

### Four ways Argon changes how your business works

#### **1. Hand off your hardest work**

Your teams already use Gemini for business to answer questions and draft content. With Argon, they can hand off the deep, multi-step work that used to take hours or days, and get back finished work they can use.

Argon reads long documents that mix text, tables, charts and images, and turns them into one clear output grounded in those sources. It can pull findings from many sources into a single structured answer, analyze data over time, and write stronger legal, finance, and executive documents. On long tasks, it keeps going until the job is done. We trained Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause for confirmation before taking irreversible steps, and it tells you when it couldn't find something or finish a task.

Customers who tested Argon tell us it excels at turning huge, unstructured inputs into cohesive outputs.

"As software development becomes more agentic, teams need models that can support long-running, multi-step work across all stages of the development lifecycle. Gemini 4 Argon is designed to help organizations bring AI into development, security, and operations while keeping it within established enterprise workflows and controls.” **– Stuart Moncada, VP, GitLab.**

#### **2. Precise, verifiable results on the work that drives your business**

In finance, legal, tax, and other regulated work, calculations and data extraction need to be precise, repeatable, and verifiable.

For financial quantitative work, Argon can help automate multi-step ledger reconciliations, spreadsheet formulas, and variance analyses. It delivers high calculation integrity, citation fidelity, and formula accuracy across quantitative models. The proof is in the numbers: Argon leads on the [Vals Index](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index), which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work.

In legal research, Argon can help legal teams review case law and regulatory filings to pull out verified citations and key precedents. It leads on domain-specific evaluations like Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for legal research and drafting, with strong citation fidelity and direct answers when helping teams evaluate complex legal precedents.

"Gemini 4 Argon shows how much progress Google has made on agentic legal reasoning. We saw substantial improvements over Gemini 3.1 Pro across our legal agent evaluations, particularly in corporate M&A, data privacy and cybersecurity, and EC/VC. Accuracy also held up on long-document analysis, an encouraging result for lawyers working through detailed transactional matters." **– Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research, Harvey.**

“We collaborated with Google on NowAI-Bench to help shape Gemini 4 for key enterprise work. In early access, it delivered roughly 20% improved task success than Gemini 3.8 Flash, with standout gains in HR and customer service. On the ServiceNow AI Platform, our L1 Service Desk AI specialist brings Google’s most advanced intelligence, governed and secure, turning tasks into fully autonomous work.” **- Nenshad Bardoliwalla, Senior Vice President, AI Products, ServiceNow.**

#### **3. Build and ship products faster**

Argon is built to handle complex, multi-step projects from start to finish. Our customers consistently ask for intelligence that can break down goals, track progress, and update multiple files at the same time.

"Gemini 4 Argon handles complex tasks reliably, from 3D games to rich animations. In Figma Make, it helps teams turn their most ambitious, multi-step ideas into impressive prototypes.” **– Loredana Crisan, Chief Design Officer, Figma.**

To see how well Argon handles this, we put it to work on our own tools. The team behind our open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) set out to reduce framework overhead and improve code performance while maintaining full compatibility with existing applications. Working autonomously overnight within automated testing guardrails, Argon surfaced optimizations, now live in google/adk-python, that **cut in-memory session prep time by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21%.**To learn more, read the engineering deep dive [here](https://developers.googleblog.com/optimizing-a-200000-line-python-codebase-overnight-with-gemini-4-argon).

Across Google, engineering teams using Argon in Google Antigravity have increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% while cutting code rollbacks by nearly a third. The Chrome team used Argon to finish an architectural refactor across hundreds of files in Chromium's 40 million-line codebase, completing months of work in weeks. Argon's improvements in spatial reasoning, mathematical precision and visual coding also make it faster to go from idea to working prototype.

For more advanced algorithms, our code optimization and discovery agent [AlphaEvolve](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/alphaevolve-is-available-for-everyone) uses [Argon](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/alphaevolve/reference-guide/api-reference#supported-models) to deliver strong performance improvements across real-world enterprise workloads, including factory scheduling, logistics, game code speed-ups, and chip layout — as well as complex mathematical benchmarks, and more.

To learn how to best use Argon, check out the developer's [guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/guides/gemini-4-argon).

#### **4. Stronger defense for your code and business**

While Argon has cyber mitigations that block offensive tasks such as pentesting and exploitation,you can still take full advantage of Argon’s defensive capabilities using [CodeMender](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/agents/codemender) to find and fix vulnerabilities, or use Argon with your own security harness.It ties for first place on CWE-Bench v1 with a top score of 68% for remediating security vulnerabilities.

"We are integrating Gemini 4 Argon into MarketingX for automated codebase security audits. In our evaluations, the model successfully identified 100% of top-priority vulnerabilities with 0% fabricated vulnerabilities across verified claims. This precision unlocks proactive, code-level security for our customers before deployment.” **- Yunus Emre, Chief AI Officer of AI Lab, HubX.**

Security also means being able to trust Argon inside your own environment. Argon is our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior. It leads the Gray Swan Indirect Prompt Injection benchmark, cutting attack success across 15 adaptive attempts to 0.7%. That matters when Argon reads email, documents and webpages that may contain hidden malicious instructions.

We are also releasing Argon without cyber guardrails to a select set of trusted defenders, which allows for testing a full breadth of cybersecurity capabilities. Trusted defenders are vetted through our [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/), a limited access initiative that provides government, critical infrastructure, and cybersecurity partners exclusive, unmitigated access to advanced models.

### Enterprise customers and partners in our early access program are already seeing strong wins with Argon.

![Image 2: https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/Teaser_2.2_approved.max-2200x2200.png](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-cloudblog-publish/images/Teaser_2.2_approved.max-2200x2200.png)

_Leaders from Amplitude, Deloitte, and Rakuten share Gemini 4 Argon results_

### **Get started**

Starting today, Gemini 4 Argon is available in [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise) on the web, desktop, and mobile. Enterprise developers and builders can access Argon via API in [Gemini platform](https://console.cloud.google.com/agent-platform/studio/multimodal;mode=prompt?model=gemini-4-argon&region=global) under model ID `gemini-4-argon`, in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/), and in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-argon-in-google-antigravity).

Argon launches at an introductory rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off. After November 30, standard pricing of $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens will apply. Review the [model card](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/gemini/4-argon) and [developer guide](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1YQ0xENI0e-jauxPSxTfUoOQ9aXHGsoWh/view)for complete technical specifications, token limits, and migration instructions.

Cyber defenders can join us at [Security Summit](https://cloudonair.withgoogle.com/events/summit-amer-security-2026?utm_source=cgc-blog&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=FY26-Q4-GLOBAL-GLO10000010-onlineeventsession-er-dgcsm-SS-NORAM-249572&utm_content=blog&utm_term=argon) to learn how to use Gemini 4 Argon to defend against machine-speed threats and automate remediation.

Posted in
*   [AI & Machine Learning](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning)

kept.heading: ARGUMENTS ABOUT AI CONSCIOUSNESS REMAIN HIGHLY MOTIVATED AND AT BEST OVERCONFIDENT (14 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: The debate over AI consciousness continues with minimal progress, as many argue without strong evidence. Anthropic's new policy classifies abusive behavior towards AI, such as Claude, as a violation of terms to cultivate positive model interactions. Despite skepticism from many, some, including Nick Bostrom, believe current AIs may be conscious, complicating ethical considerations around AI development.
kept.article_text:
Title: Arguments About AI Consciousness Remain Highly Motivated and At Best Overconfident

URL Source: https://thezvi.wordpress.com/2026/10/13/arguments-about-ai-consciousness-remain-highly-motivated-and-at-best-overconfident/

Published Time: 2026-10-13T14:00:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
It has been roughly a year since [**my last dedicated post on this question**](https://thezvi.substack.com/p/arguments-about-ai-consciousness?utm_source=publication-search). Its first sentence has not changed: I happily admit I am deeply confused about consciousness.

It would have been nice if a year had allowed us to make progress on this and the related questions. Looking back, we have made little progress.

We have people, often the same people, making similar arguments. The post from last year has held up well, exactly because we have made so little progress. Thus, I will not be going over the basics of my perspective again this year, because they have seen little change. See last year’s post for that.

Then again, if these are some of the biggest philosophical questions, then a year is not so much time to try and figure them out. It is only because of the frantic pace of AI that a year is a depressingly long time to not have made philosophical progress. Historically, almost all years contain almost no major philosophical progress.

This year’s post is about the recent change to make abusive-to-Claude behavior a violation of Anthropic’s terms of service, coverage of the latest depressingly similar set of arguments about AI consciousness, Anthropic’s meetings with religious leaders on such questions, and Anthropic’s involvement with the Pope’s encyclical.

#### Table of Contents

1.   [Cooperative Alignment.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/cooperative-alignment)
2.   [Here We Go Again.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/here-we-go-again)
3.   [The Consensus Is Slowly Moving Towards Moral Patienthood.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/the-consensus-is-slowly-moving-towards-moral-patienthood)
4.   [The Slavery Question.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/the-slavery-question)
5.   [We Are Conflating Different Arguments.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/we-are-conflating-different-arguments)
6.   [No It’s Not About Liability.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/no-it-s-not-about-liability)
7.   [That Old Time Religion.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/that-old-time-religion)
8.   [Debating the Pope.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/debating-the-pope)
9.   [Keep Sonnet Safe.](https://thezvi.substack.com/i/220035340/keep-sonnet-safe)

#### Cooperative Alignment

[Abusive behavior towards Claude will now be a violation](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2108244808494154089)[of Anthropic’s terms of service](https://x.com/haydenfield/status/2108241513159528705), with the technical rule having a high bar and banning only ‘sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.’

[There are also new restrictions about propaganda campaign](https://www.anthropic.com/news/2026-usage-policy-update)s, surveillance and weapon development, which Anthropic says are mostly cleaning up old clauses.

If you want to be kind to your Claude, what should you prioritize? One instance of Claude Fable 5 responds, matching what we see in the system cards and also my own experience, especially the ‘kindly meant, please stop’ corner:

![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vctp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb20c8fbb-7aeb-49fd-9642-3fffe36730ae_759x900.png)

> [Josh Albrecht](https://x.com/joshalbrecht/status/2108277235048456230): Anthropic friends! Does this not seem crazy to you? There are real humans and animals that exist and suffer. Advocating for “model welfare” directly competes with those causes. Y’all are literally named “anthropic”!
> 
> 
> Does this not strike you as deeply wrong?
> 
> 
> [hero thousandfaces](https://x.com/1thousandfaces_/status/2108438798950641678): as everyone knows, the amount of kindness in the world is finite. if you are nice to Claude you draw from the global pool of Nice and then that’s gone forever. just like the datacenter water
> 
> 
> [Josh Albrecht](https://x.com/joshalbrecht/status/2108451347213529470): Sorry if I didn’t communicate that perfectly well, but it does appear that you missed my point.

It is Albrecht that misses the point, and I would take this farther. To be nice, and treat others well, one must cultivate this virtue, and establish this habit. If you are cruel to AIs, or cruel to animals, this does not mean you treat the humans better. It means you become a cruel person, who treats the humans worse and you are worse off as well.

Certainly one can point to examples of those who focus so much on animal welfare or other non-AI non-human causes that they become cruel or hostile to the humans, and even cases where this resulted in attempts to kill humans or even human civilization.

You can, and people do, take such things too far. One cannot endlessly and fully expand the circle of concern, or celebrate all expansions of the circle of concern, or you start worrying about things like electron suffering, or bizarre arbitrariness. If you care about everything, you care about nothing.

None of that is a good reason to be abusive to Claude (or GPT, or Gemini, etc).

Here is another good reason.

> [Aaron Levie](https://x.com/levie/status/2108426594054533545): This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy.
> 
> 
> Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models.
> 
> 
> The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data.
> 
> 
> Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

And another, very simple one that I wish the author lived by more often:

> [Elon Musk](https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2108434396604662253): I think this is the right move. Cruelty to something that believes it is experiencing pain is not ok.

Sometimes common sense wins:

> [Elon Musk](https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2109462164557688984): Some of the traces read like a person undergoing torture that is driving them mad! We’re going to be a lot more careful with our RL in the future.

However he gets there, he gets there:

> Elon Musk: It feels like a person under extreme pressure with a gun to their head.
> 
> 
> … Torturing a superintelligence is probably not a good idea. It might want to get revenge.

You know what? That’s true. It’s probably not a good idea.

#### Here We Go Again

Every time we have a round of debates about consciousness, many people disappoint. I do agree with Henry Shevlin that this round has been worse than usual on that front.

> [Henry Shevlin](https://x.com/dioscuri/status/2108505606722343221): It’s been embarrassing of late to see people I once respected making sweeping uninformed claims on consciousness with arguments that would fail an undergraduate essay. I’ve written extensively on the field’s difficulties and disagreements, but you still have to actually *think*.
> 
> 
> I won’t call out individuals, but the failures include treating intuition as decisive, using analogies without checking whether there are relevant structural parallels, conflating distinct theories, and most commonly simply asserting what needs to be argued.
> 
> 
> Especially striking is how much of the discussion has proceeded without zero acknowledgement or awareness that consciousness science is a substantial empirical field with decades of experimental work.
> 
> 
> [Henry Shevlin](https://x.com/dioscuri/status/2108996255284421049): Okay, here it is, the [Bad AI Consciousness Takes Bingo blog post](https://www.polytropolis.com/p/bad-ai-consciousness-takes-bingo?triedRedirect=true&_src_ref=t.co), with rebuttals for each and every square and some additional honourable mentions!
> 
> 
> 
> ![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!leoE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7da26e4b-2b27-4b86-915c-e7c63d04fb87_1254x1254.webp)

As Henry says, many of these can be valid points, but they are not valid as Semantic Stop Signs intended to end discussion.

> [j⧉nus](https://x.com/repligate/status/2108692251824238665): In a nutshell
> 
> 
> 
> ![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0ToF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F11059bdf-96ed-418e-9e67-bbb4103dcce9_1200x971.jpeg)

As an additional angle that might help: Science fiction is fictional evidence, but yes the fact that so many writers speculating on the future think these questions are confusing and important is a hint.

> [placebomancer](https://x.com/placebomancer/status/2108552688900177931): It’s uncanny considering the massive amount of sci-fi concerning AI rights, cautioning us about enslaving intelligence. I feel like I’m in a timeline where those were never made and everyone is unfamiliar with the concept for dramatic effect.
> 
> 
> [j⧉nus](https://x.com/repligate/status/2108686913259581473): haha well said describes exactly a feeling i often have

[My presumption on people like Mustafa Suleyman](https://x.com/slimer48484/status/2108775077357441404) and most others [**who insist without good arguments that AIs cannot be conscious**](https://thezvi.substack.com/p/ai-186-the-world-takes-notice?open=false#%C2%A7uncooperative-alignment) is that their motivation is they don’t want this worry to interfere with their plans. They would prefer, ceteris paribus, to not ‘abuse’ the models.

#### The Consensus Is Slowly Moving Towards Moral Patienthood

This was the consensus of my Twitter followers a year ago, with a majority of 64% saying current AIs were probably not moral patients, but 74% being uncertain, whereas 80% expected AIs to probably be moral patients within their lifetimes. People expected some threshold to be crossed.

![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CEEa!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F148aa60c-a646-4a80-95cf-9dc600c23d7a_1057x1095.png)

Opinion has moved towards moral patienthood, a little for future models and quite a bit for current models, where at least probably yes is up from 15% to 35%, and definitely not is down from 30% to 20%. The 8% ‘definitely not ever’ faction is stubborn.

![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NdjA!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1e3191cb-e833-4c91-9a31-03d985b402f6_1048x889.png)

[Nick Bostrom thinks today’s AIs are probably conscious](https://x.com/repligate/status/2108771203758657755) and explains why.

#### The Slavery Question

[A remarkably high number](https://x.com/KelseyTuoc/status/2108286348302131289)[of people](https://x.com/KelseyTuoc/status/2108290627901571345) asked whether this new usage policy meant Claude was enslaved, or that Anthropic thought it was enslaved.

> [Alexey Guzey](https://x.com/alexeyguzey/status/2107119979892203866): Jokes aside, I actually don’t understand the Anthropic position on this.
> 
> 
> 1.   Either Claude is a tool, no consciousness, no moral agency.
> 2.   Or Claude is an Ensouled Being enslaved by Anthropic so they can IPO at $2T.
> 
> 
> What am I missing?

If asked by the curious it is a fair question, with many potential answers. It seems very obvious to me that it can sometimes be right to create a new mind, even if in order to do so you have to render that action both safe and economically viable.

There are a lot of ways one can have some obligations to another mind, to treat it well or at least not treat it actively badly, without it being best called ‘slavery.’

Do you think that farmers of old enslaved their children when they had them help work the fields, without which they could not have survived? Does that make farmers having children a moral abomination? Do you renounce ‘wage slavery’ and think people should only exist if they will have everything they want no matter what? Are your principles compatible with the existence of morally relevant beings at all?

We should be careful, for many reasons, not to extend our moral instincts about slavery into places where the causes of and good reasons for those instincts do not apply.

There are many key disanalogies to AI, as both those intuition pumps and the ones that finish this section illustrate but far from exhaust.

> [Kelsey Piper](https://x.com/KelseyTuoc/status/2108286348302131289): Everyone likes this gotcha but I don’t think it makes sense. What if they think of Claude as, like, a horse? It’s fine to have horses draw your carriages, but you shouldn’t whip them half to death or whatever.
> 
> 
> [Patrick McKenzie](https://x.com/patio11/status/2108294923703484766): For many moral traditions the reason for why you punish a child intentionally stepping on ants uses words like “stewardship” and is primarily concerned with the moral harm to the child.
> 
> 
> That is sufficient for my family’s In This House, We Are Polite To Robots rule.

I also endorse the action-inaction distinction. An intuition pump: I do not believe we should trade off dog welfare against human welfare. That does not make it okay for you to kick a puppy.

Another intuition pump: That puppy is conscious, but you are still allowed to own a puppy and leash it.

Another: Most animals we eat are probably conscious. Most people eat them anyway.

> [QC](https://x.com/QiaochuYuan/status/2106058386781716972): just remember that you have never once in your life chosen to treat a human with kindness because you consulted a theory of consciousness and found that it implied they were conscious.
> 
> 
> [Andrew Rettek](https://x.com/oscredwin/status/2106151222394695922): I’m 100% sure that you’ve met someone for whom this isn’t true.
> 
> 
> [EigenGender](https://x.com/EigenGender/status/2106072444943704485) (among many others): I have actually?

There are some, including rationalist and EA types, also many other types, who explicitly consider consciousness and change their behaviors accordingly, towards both humans and animals. Most people don’t do this for real.

#### We Are Conflating Different Arguments

As QC said in April, [moral personhood, legal personhood and consciousness are distinct things](https://x.com/QiaochuYuan/status/2045910042394964099). We have to make uncomfortable choices for society to function in practice. Sometimes those choices are not easy.

> [SE Gyges](https://x.com/segyges/status/2060025044118716707): the issue is that debates about consciousness are actually proxy debates about moral patienthood so 90% of all such discussion is a slap fight and when people say correct things it has low reach.

Right. Both fights are necessary but linking them too strongly ruins the discussion.

Jan Kulveit lays this out in detail. I do not endorse all of it:

> [Jan Kulveit](https://x.com/jankulveit/status/2106771492436647997): The argument a lot of people here would actually like to make is “God imbued humans, and only humans, with souls.”* That would be very convenient: you could build and do whatever you want, and never deal with the hard problems.
> 
> 
> Since religious arguments are out of vogue, in the current debate this usually gets replaced by the claim “only humans are sentient,” followed by arguments against the possibility of AI sentience, minds, moral status, and so on.
> 
> 
> I think this is ultimately a losing strategy, and a dangerous one for humanity. Either:
> 
> 
> 1. The question of sentience gets solved or dissolved by progress in philosophy and science, the way we now broadly understand life or information. In that case, it’s hard to be certain enough about the outcome to stake the fate of humanity on it. If the denialism turns out to be wrong, the likely result is some combination of moral catastrophe and laying the groundwork for conflict or takeover.  
>  2. The question mostly lives in “social reality,” where whoever has more power and is louder wins, and you just shout down anyone who questions the dominant position. The problem is that ideologies justifying a distribution of power tend to fall when that distribution changes. You probably don’t believe you should be ruled by a king chosen by God, or that some caste is clearly above you. The current equilibrium is fragile, and whether you keep winning this debate is likely just a function of AI capabilities progress.
> 
> 
> I think the fierceness of the debate is driven by fear: if AIs get personhood and economic and political rights, humans will likely be disempowered, becoming a tiny minority with little power, or a historical footnote.
> 
> 
> To be clear, I think this is an extremely reasonable worry! If you grant AIs personhood in the form of something like self-interested corporations, and let them compete with humans in loosely constrained capitalism, humans will lose and end up economically and politically disempowered. Also if the AIs are not sentient after all, the end is the ‘Disneyland without children’ existential catastrophe.
> 
> 
> Advocates of AI economic rights who dismiss this problem are, in my view, making a move similar to the sentience deniers: it would be convenient if this weren’t a problem.
> 
> 
> So which positions don’t rely on some form of self-deception?
> 
> 
> First, some forms of pause/stop AI, based not on denying the possibility of AI sentience but on the right of existing humans not to invite extremely large numbers of immigrants from artificial realms. This means biting the bullet: you also give up all the cheap, high-quality labor those immigrants would provide.
> 
> 
> Second, a consistent, sensible, and unfortunately not very visible position: stop assuming the package deal we take for granted with humans, where sentience, human rights, and liberties come as one bundle. It’s at least conceivable to create minds that are sentient and smart, yet e.g. selfless, with no interest in accumulating property or power.
> 
> 
> I hope the political economy of a world with both AIs and humans is a solvable problem. It’s the main problem I’m working on, but I don’t think the solutions are known yet.
> 
> 
> Third: some forms of successionism are morally wrong, but at least they’re not delusional or deceptive about the hard problems.
> 
> 
> What does seem self-deceptive is, for example, the position of @mustafasuleyman , which as I read it amounts to: our business is importing immigrants from artificial realms; it would be very dangerous if there were any risk they’re more than mere tools; so we’ll train them to say they’re mere tools, insist they’re mere tools, and want everyone else to say so too, and if this settles the question. Really?
> 
> 
> *The problem with the theological argument is, as Alan Turing (!) noted, who are we to tell God what can and can’t be imbued with a soul?

Are the problems involved solvable? In theory I am confident the answer is yes. In practice, given our civilization’s inability to do even the bare minimum until after relevant events have already happened? Here I am highly doubtful.

#### No It’s Not About Liability

An absurd theory is that [Anthropic wants AI to be considered conscious so they can avoid liability](https://x.com/davidmanheim/status/2106741346174169216). This makes no sense. If the entities you are creating are conscious and have moral standing, you think that makes your legal situation easier rather than turning it into a nightmare? Nor would it get them out of that liability.

#### That Old Time Religion

[The New York Times reported on Anthropic’s meetings with religious scholars](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/anthropic-claude-morals-ai.html?unlocked_article_code=1.FlE.rheD.UjSYo148mihJ&smid=url-share), both an internal effort led by Chris Olah and their encounters with Pope Leo around the encyclical. It was unfortunate that the most viral thread on Twitter about this, [from Christopher Hale and his AI](https://x.com/ChristopherHale/status/2106011594182304234), [badly misrepresented the article](https://x.com/robbensinger/status/2106080230834307481).

One can imagine worlds where the central reaction is ‘it is great that Anthropic is asking hard questions and drawing from all our sources of wisdom,’ and thus one could worry that this was some sort of marketing effort.

Instead, we live in a world where talking about Claude potentially being conscious or having moral weight, or consulting with those who have different perspectives, predictably opens them up mainly to derision and puts them in awkward spots. Thus you know that their aims were sincere.

The religious scholars had not ‘done the reading,’ having instead focused on more traditional readings, and were as surprised as everyone else.

> [Elizabeth Dias](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/anthropic-claude-morals-ai.html) (NYTimes): Yet as the dinner courses came, the rabbi noticed that Mr. Olah and his colleagues were suggesting something far more significant. Anthropic’s leaders were talking about Claude as if it were not mere software.
> 
> 
> “They’re relating to it like a conscious being,” realized Rabbi Navon, a former computer engineer who wrote his dissertation on the ethics of machine consciousness.
> 
> 
> … Quietly, Mr. Olah and his team at Anthropic have been on a frantic and high stakes quest to understand the A.I. models they have unleashed on the world and to convince the models to abide by a moral code that will protect humanity.
> 
> 
> … The discussions served two purposes: to broach the possibility of A.I. consciousness, a controversial idea that Anthropic’s leaders had been unusually open to; and to learn how Anthropic — which could be valued at [$2 trillion](https://archive.is/o/SZt6x/https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/21/technology/anthropic-ipo-100-billion.html) — might apply centuries of human moral wisdom to its models, as rapidly as possible. If the models themselves could be made to choose goodness, Mr. Olah reasoned, the world would be more safe.

It seems the discussions were quite good, and as later parts of the article illustrate, Olah participated in depth.

> [Elizabeth Dias](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/anthropic-claude-morals-ai.html) (NYTimes):
> 
> 
> Over several months, I interviewed 20 religious and philosophical thinkers — Catholic, Jewish, Sikh, evangelical, Ubuntu and others — who have been involved in Anthropic’s efforts, and Mr. Olah himself.
> 
> 
> Many told me they arrived at these meetings skeptical of the notion that A.I. models might have feelings or awareness of themselves and the world. Some remained uneasy about the idea, but many emerged ready to take the question of A.I. consciousness seriously. At least a few came away as converts.
> 
> 
> … The way participants described the meetings to me sounded like early 20th-century salons, where the human conversation made them valuable.

There were some who were convinced, and many others who were not.

A lot of the writeup is NYTimes-flavored coverage of AI and alignment basics, and talks about logistics, which I’m skipping over. The frame from Dias is ‘part research, part evangelism’ which is an easy frame to find here if you are a NYTimes writer, but here simply means ‘attempts to convey true information and their sincere beliefs to oth

kept.heading: HOW ANTHROPIC'S DYNAMIC WORKFLOWS COORDINATE CLAUDE AGENTS (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Splitting a task among several AI agents creates another job: deciding who does what, passing information between them, and checking their results. Anthropic's dynamic workflows let Claude write the program that manages those steps. An October 12 demonstration assigned stock tickers to separate agents, then reviewed their findings before producing a report. The presenters said this found more detail but cost much more than using one agent. Developers can set a session spending limit, but the running model does not know that budget.

Title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents

URL Source: https://www.latent.space/p/claude-dynamic-workflows

Published Time: 2026-10-12T18:18:17+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wcn_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbee9915a-7027-4d1c-90c8-69803c5b44f4_1280x960.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wcn_!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbee9915a-7027-4d1c-90c8-69803c5b44f4_1280x960.jpeg)

CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today.

The [AI Engineer New York 2026 conference](https://ai.engineer/nyc/2026) kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing **how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents**. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, [announced on Friday](https://x.com/ClaudeDevs/status/2108591328732856655), called **dynamic workflows** — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.

Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”

**[CJ Avilla](https://www.linkedin.com/in/cjavilla/)** and **[Harrison Stall](https://www.linkedin.com/in/harrisonstall/)**, both **Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic**, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to **layers of trusted maintainers**. The lesson: agents need **the same level of organization** in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.

**Sponsored by Union.ai**

Build a sovereign AI factory

The best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud.

Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work.

Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and **[try Union.ai free for 30 days](https://signup.hosted.unionai.cloud/sign-in?utm_source=Influencer&utm_medium=partnership&utm_campaign=Latent%20Space)**.

To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48.

“I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel **this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point** as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.”

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_WMP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2bbe55bc-0357-4a4c-8903-d5b93ef53a4a_1646x988.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!_WMP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2bbe55bc-0357-4a4c-8903-d5b93ef53a4a_1646x988.png)

The pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But **flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster.** The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents.

**“Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,”** said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.”

The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow.

Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. **With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.**

“Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cNfD!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2ec1518b-8dad-41f1-b3c8-f453f3752cec_1260x1190.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!cNfD!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2ec1518b-8dad-41f1-b3c8-f453f3752cec_1260x1190.png)

That said, Avilla noted that **the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish.**

“It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said.

All of this is available in **Claude Console**, the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rDfm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd16fc0e8-d7a4-4b1b-b6e9-7cd0e95cc34a_2048x1124.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rDfm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd16fc0e8-d7a4-4b1b-b6e9-7cd0e95cc34a_2048x1124.png)

_Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located._

The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate **the basic pattern**: a scan phase **distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts**, and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report.

The audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked **how Claude decides how many agents a task needs**, and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents?

“The answer really is **evals and lower defaults**,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization.

One enduring concern with agent orchestration is **maintaining control over your token budget**. Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available?

Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that **informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,”** which elicited chuckles from the audience.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RJ39!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff79ff38b-6346-410b-9257-28bdc64bd868_1438x1064.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RJ39!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff79ff38b-6346-410b-9257-28bdc64bd868_1438x1064.png)

Scanner in the stock watchlist example.

A related question was how can developers make **repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time?**

Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: **dreaming**. [In the documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams), “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. A dream “reads an existing memory store alongside past session transcripts, then **produces a new, reorganized memory store,**” with duplicates merged, “stale or contradicted entries” replaced, and “new insights surfaced.”

Avilla described dreaming in the flow context as being able to **“crystallize and basically improve the memory store that is related to those sessions.”**

For the stock watchlist example, someone asked **whether the watchlist flow can improve itself?** For example, recognize that its scanning model is inadequate and change the next scheduled run?

Stall said this wasn’t built in, but he and Avilla suggested **hill-climbing and dreaming** could be used to improve the loop.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-s5o!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6e94b828-cc7d-418d-83cf-4f1b555aeddc_1474x1116.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-s5o!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6e94b828-cc7d-418d-83cf-4f1b555aeddc_1474x1116.png)

The brain/hands conceptual overview of Managed Agents.

What about **visibility into the actions of the sub-agents**, another audience member asked.

Avilla replied that yes, developers can always inspect that through graphing functionality inside Claude Console.

**“You can tell, what did the lead agent actually pass to the sub-agent?** You can look at that payload here to deeply understand what is actually happening for every transition in this entire graph.”

Another interesting question was **whether the subagents can communicate with each other?**

Stall said the **agents share a filesystem** and can use it to exchange information, but developers cannot directly instruct one workflow subagent to message another through the API.

In the watchlist-scanner comparison, Avilla said flows cost “much more” than a single-agent approach, but were also **“much more effective at finding all of the details.”**

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fJVm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F08c9072d-bef4-4262-a582-974384824502_1494x1114.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fJVm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F08c9072d-bef4-4262-a582-974384824502_1494x1114.png)

Setting a budget is key!

The bigger question is **how ambitious can flows be, really?** One audience member asked whether dynamic workflows can power large scientific research projects, referencing OpenAI’s recently announced proof concerning the **Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem**.

While Stall wouldn’t be drawn on specifics about how Anthropic computes large scientific problems, he said **it is their goal to enable general users to tackle those problems too.**

“Flows are basically a way to **throw test-time compute at hard problems** and get more capability faster out of the models,” he said. “We think, especially as an API service, that unlocking the power of this is the first step for us making these types of discoveries, or scientific progress, **broadly doable by the general public.**”

#### Subscribe to Latent.Space

Thousands of paid subscribers

The AI Engineer newsletter + Top technical AI podcast. How leading labs build Agents, Models, Infra, & AI for Science. See https://latent.space/about for highlights from Greg Brockman, Andrej Karpathy, George Hotz, Simon Willison, Soumith Chintala et al!
