Title: NVIDIA Run:ai Is Now Open Source as Part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform

URL Source: https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform

Published Time: 2026-10-13T14:19:40+00:00

Markdown Content:
NVIDIA is making the full [NVIDIA Run:ai](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/run-ai/) platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx/) by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs.

Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference.

By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.

This post details the open source release, which includes the complete [NVIDIA Run:ai platform](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai) and four components that can also be adopted independently: [KAI Scheduler,](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-scheduler#readme)[GPU Fractioning Operator](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-gpu-fractioning#readme), [KAI Resource Management](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-resource-management), [Workload Map](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/karta). Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements.

## How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#how_to_adopt_open_source_nvidia_runai)

NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open-source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings.

### Deploy the open source platform directly[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#deploy_the_open_source_platform_directly)

The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the [NVIDIA Run:ai repository](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai) within the [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory). Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently.

The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on [NVIDIA NGC](https://catalog.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/nvidia/runai/collections/run-ai-self-hosted/-) as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack.

Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included.

### Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#adopt_open_source_nvidia_runai_through_nvidia_dsx_ecosystem_partners)

Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements.

*   [Crusoe](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/run-ai-open-source-release) integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure.
*   [Mirantis](http://mirantis.com/blog/mirantis-k0rdent-ai-integrates-open-source-nvidia-run-ai-for-full-stack-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-operations/) extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization.
*   [Nebius](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/nvidia-run-ai-open-source-nebius-applications) offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes.
*   [OpenNebula](https://opennebula.io/blog/product/nvidia-runai/) Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds.
*   [Rafay](https://rafay.co/ai-and-cloud-native-blog/rafay-open-source-nvidia-runai-nvidia-dsx-ai-factories) is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs.
*   [Saturn Cloud](https://saturncloud.io/blog/saturn-cloud-nvidia-runai-integration/) integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing.
*   [Spectro Cloud](https://www.spectrocloud.com/blog/paletteai-nvidia-run-ai-integration) integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure.
*   [vCluster](https://www.vcluster.com/blog/stronger-tenant-isolation-for-nvidia-run-ai) provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet.

For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering.

For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently.

## Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#modular_open_source_components_of_the_nvidia_runai_platform)

This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements.

### KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#kai_scheduler_the_scheduling_engine_behind_nvidia_runai)

[KAI Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-scheduler#readme) is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and [contributed it to CNCF](https://github.com/cncf/sandbox/issues/372) as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale.

KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating:

*   Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly
*   Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams
*   Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level
*   GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HaMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning)
*   Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support

To learn more about key features, visit the [kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler#key-features) GitHub repo.

Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform.

Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the [kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler#key-features) GitHub repo.

### GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#gpu_fractioning_an_operator_for_gpu_fractions_on_kubernetes)

The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation.

GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in [CUDA 13.4](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-toolkit-release-notes/index.html)[.](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-toolkit-release-notes/index.html) The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what [GPU Fractioning Operator](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-gpu-fractioning#gpu-fractioning-operator) provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic.

Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers.

GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the [GPU Fractioning Operator documentation](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-gpu-fractioning#install).

### KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#kai_resource_management_the_organizational_layer)

While the scheduler decides how work is placed, [KAI Resource Management](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-resource-management) governs who gets what:

*   **Projects and departments:** The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them.
*   **Resource management with an organizational hierarchy:** The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics.
*   **Node pools:** Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources.

Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee.

Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters.

Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the [KAI Resource Management documentation](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-resource-management/tree/main/docs).

### Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#workload_map_a_workload-management_contract_for_kubernetes)

[Workload Map](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/karta) is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management.

In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status.

Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle:

*   Describing pods, components, and roles
*   Submitting and configuring
*   Scheduling with gang and topology awareness
*   Observing status and health consistently
*   Applying policy at admission or runtime

This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD.

Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters.

Learn more in the [dsx-ai-factory/workload-map](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/karta) GitHub repo and check out the [adopter projects](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/karta/blob/main/ADOPTERS.md).

The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components.

### Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#model_streamer_reducing_cold-start_latency)

Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models.

Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors.

#### Inference engines

Model Streamer is integrated upstream in [vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/models/extensions/runai_model_streamer/) and [SGLang](https://docs.sglang.io/docs/advanced_features/object_storage), where it can be enabled with the `--load-format runai_streamer` flag, as well as in [ModelExpress](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/modelexpress). Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below.

#### Clouds

Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance.

*   **AWS**: Model Streamer ships in the [vLLM Deep Learning Container](https://gallery.ecr.aws/deep-learning-containers/vllm) and is the recommended fast path in the official [EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/ml-inference.html), with [tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/ml-inference-fast-model-loading.html).
*   **Google Cloud**: [Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/nvidia-runai-model-streamer-supports-cloud-storage), including [GKE documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/persistent-volumes/run-ai-model-streamer) for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory.
*   **Microsoft Azure**: Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers. [Published benchmarks](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/azure-sdk/eliminate-llm-cold-starts-load-models-up-to-6x-faster-with-azure-blob-storage-and-runai-model-streamer/) on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path.

#### **Storage platforms**

Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results:

*   [WEKA](https://www.weka.io/article/model-loading-that-is-faster-than-local-node-nvme-with-nvidia-runai) loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment.
*   VAST Data measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe
*   [DDN](https://www.ddn.com/blog/improving-ai-efficiency-how-fast-model-loading-slashes-gpu-costs/) streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage.

Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck.

### Grove: One API, any inference architecture[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#grove_one_api_any_inference_architecture)

Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs.

Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On [NVIDIA GB200 NVL72](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/gb200-nvl72/), it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML.

Grove is a modular part of [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo) that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress.

Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements.

## Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai[](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/nvidia-runai-is-now-open-source-as-part-of-nvidia-dsx-ai-factory-platform#get_started_with_open_source_nvidia_runai)

NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources:

*   [NVIDIA Run:ai](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/run-ai) full platform
*   [KAI Scheduler](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler) scheduling engine
*   [KAI Resource Management](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-resource-management) for projects, departments, quotas, and node pools
*   [GPU Fractioning Operator](https://github.com/kai-scheduler/kai-gpu-fractioning) for CUDA GPU fractions on Kubernetes, with per-pod metrics
*   [Workload Map](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/karta) workload-management contract

Related open source projects include:

*   [Model Streamer](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/runai-model-streamer) for fast model weight loading
*   [Grove](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/grove) for multicomponent inference orchestration

We’re excited to bring this work to the community and to build the next generation of AI workload and GPU orchestration in the open. We welcome your contributions, issues, and feedback.

kept.heading: FRONTIER MODELS FOR EVERY ROBOT (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Physical Intelligence is making its latest models available for training and inference through the Pi API beta. The Pi API adapts the latest and most powerful robotic foundation models to each application, dealing with ML infrastructure, compute, and complex data pipelines. Users just upload data, launch fine-tuning on managed compute and infrastructure, and access the fine-tuned models via a hosted gateway to run inference.
kept.article_text:
Title: Frontier Models for Every Robot

URL Source: https://www.pi.website/blog/api-beta

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
Published

October 13, 2026

We are making our latest models available for training and inference through the [Pi API beta](https://www.pi.website/waitlist).

Deploying robots is challenging. Besides identifying the right use case and building the right hardware, developers need models intelligent enough to perform the task at hand. General-purpose robotic foundation models such as [π 0 and π 0.5](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi) offer a promising way to tackle this challenge. They provide a strong foundation of physical knowledge and capabilities, substantially reducing the data and effort needed to adapt to new tasks, environments, or robots. But adapting them still requires ML infrastructure, compute, and complex data pipelines, which are difficult in their own right. What if the latest and most powerful robotic foundation models could be adapted to each application through a simple and ready-made API?

The Pi API does that for you. You upload data, launch fine-tuning on compute and infrastructure we manage, and access fine-tuned models via a hosted gateway to run inference. The latest model available through the API already provides more data-efficient fine-tuning and improved capability for our partners. Since Pi can update the models underpinning the API rapidly, we plan to continue enabling access to our latest and most capable models. Launching the beta is our first step in providing the physical intelligence foundation the community can build upon and enabling end-to-end autonomy.

To ensure that the API supports diverse applications, we sought to answer two key questions. First, do our models support a broad range of applications and robotic hardware in diverse industries? Second, how easily does the API enable developers to iterate toward useful, practical autonomy?

### Supporting a broad range of applications in diverse industries

To discover how broadly our models can adapt, we work closely with companies deploying robots to build autonomy systems for their applications. These collaborations let us validate how well our models perform across different tasks, hardware, and operating environments.

![Image 1](https://website.pi-asset.com/api/logos/actor.png)

#### Actor

Actor deploys autonomous heavy machinery. Their autonomous wheel loader scoops material and loads it into a dump truck during a real commercial deployment without any operator inside the machine.

### Enabling independent iteration towards practical autonomy

Across these initial collaborations, a common pattern emerged. The challenges differ from task to task: an inside-out garment, an ingredient that wouldn’t stay in a scoop, a manufacturing part that landed in the wrong position. But the process for improving performance was much the same: collect demonstrations, train a model, test it on the robot, and use the failures to decide what data to collect next. We built the API to let developers run this iteration loop themselves, using our latest models.

**API workflow:** Upload your data, fine-tune a π model, and run it on your robot through hosted inference. Use evaluation data to guide the next iteration.

We gave a small number of companies early access to the API to test whether they could improve autonomy on their own. We were impressed by how quickly they got started and began making progress. Their experiences offer a glimpse of what you could do with your own robots and data.

![Image 2](https://website.pi-asset.com/api/logos/almond.png)

#### Almond

Almond builds Axol, a dual-arm robot for physical AI builders. Their goal is for Axol to build itself. Here, Axol deburrs spacers used in its own assembly, running a model the team obtained after iterating with the Pi API for four days.

Most applications shown above, from Japan to Switzerland to deployments across the United States, ran with cloud-hosted inference through the API. These early deployments spanned a range of environments and tasks and highlighted areas for improvement, including network connectivity challenges for some.

### Improving from feedback

The more our models are used, the more we learn how to improve them: by understanding the potential and limitations of our current models in real-world applications, we can make the next generation of models more broadly applicable, and make tangible progress toward truly general physical intelligence. But the range of real-world tasks is enormous, and understanding the broad range of tasks that robots could do requires making our models available for these tasks. Real-world robotic applications are not easy: tackling robotic construction, robotic surgery, or warehouse automation each requires an entire company. If each such application requires solving the physical intelligence problem from scratch, the challenges become insurmountable. By making our models available through the API, we accelerate the growth of the robotics ecosystem and, in the process, advance our own understanding of physical intelligence.

The examples above show that the models we develop can be used for real, useful applications, and that our partners are able to use the API to independently iterate on policies and improve autonomy on their tasks. We’re still early, and feedback from developers will help shape future releases.

If you would like to participate in the beta, please [tell us](https://www.pi.website/waitlist) what you want to build.

If you would like to help develop the models and tools behind this work, [we’re hiring](https://www.pi.website/join-us) across research, infrastructure, hardware, people, and operations.

kept.heading: LFM2.5-24B-A2B (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with 2B active parameters, is designed for fast, private on-device agents. It outperforms or matches larger models like Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on five out of eight benchmarks and runs up to 1.7x faster due to its efficient architecture. Available on Hugging Face, it supports extensive inference frameworks, making it suitable for tasks needing swift local inference and tool usage.
kept.article_text:
Title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for Fast On-Device Agents

URL Source: https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-24b-a2b

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
Today, we release **LFM2.5-24B-A2B**, a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from [LFM2.5-230M](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-5-230m) to [LFM2.5-24B-A2B](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B).

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B) and [our Playground](https://playground.liquid.ai/chat?model=LFM2.5-24B-A2B). Check out our [docs](https://docs.liquid.ai/lfm/models/lfm25-24b-a2b) on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

## What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous [LFM2-24B-A2B](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-24b-a2b) release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

**Architecture.** It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the [in-place tokenizer expansion](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/tokenizer-expansion), which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

**Pre-training** was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

**Mid-training** has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

**Post-training** turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as [OpenClaw](https://openclaw.ai/), [Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/), [Pi](https://pi.dev/), and [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/).

Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository's git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

This behavior looks emergent but might be explained by training data containing similar patterns. We tightened our sandboxes in response, and all reported results below come from sealed evaluation environments.

## Benchmarks

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B across 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. Despite being the smallest model in total and active number of parameters, it is competitive with, and often outperforms, larger MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.

**Benchmark****LFM2.5-24B-A2B****Qwen3.6-35B-A3B****Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it****Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B)**

Table 1: LFM2.5-24B-A2B benchmark performance*.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), with its widest margin on AutomationBench, where it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode.

The results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B an ideal foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. For knowledge-heavy workloads, we recommend pairing LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength.

## Fast inference everywhere

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem:

*   **llama.cpp** — GGUF checkpoints for efficient edge inference
*   **MLX** — Optimized inference for Apple Silicon
*   **vLLM** — GPU-accelerated serving for production throughput
*   **SGLang** — High-performance GPU serving framework
*   **ONNX** — Cross-platform inference across diverse accelerators

All runs were collected on [Pipette](https://pipette.liquid.ai/), the same benchmarking infrastructure behind Liquid AI's public device performance data.

**Edge inference.** Due to the efficient LFM2 architecture, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs at reading in prompts and generating answers. It decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

**GPU inference.** To demonstrate the competitiveness of LFM architecture we compare the GPU inference throughput to other similarly sized MoE models. We measure GPU throughput (total output tokens / wall time) on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU using a sustained-load setting: at each concurrency level, we continuously maintain the target number of in-flight requests, replacing each completed request immediately.

We benchmark each model with SGLang 0.5.22, 1,024 input tokens, up to 256 output tokens, in BF16. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency.

## Run local agents with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B’s size, speed, and capabilities make it a great choice for agents that run continuously on your own hardware. In the demo below, we run it inside Hermes Agent on an M5 Max MacBook Pro, where it plans, calls tools, and works through a real task entirely on-device, without any cloud API calls.

[Video 3](https://aypchzzf9pftwuto.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/lfm2.5-24b-a2b-zweMxBhXyXQrk7RsPzPJHuOc9BgDS3.mp4)

Video 1: Local Hermes Agent with LFM2.5-24B-A2B creating a morning briefing about trending models on Hugging Face and responding to follow up questions.

The point of the demo is not the individual tools. It is that the tool-dispatch loop feels interactive on consumer hardware: ask, propose, confirm, run, repeat, all in well under a second per dispatch, with full audit trails and your data never leaving the device. Check out [our local agent guide](https://docs.liquid.ai/examples/agent-harnesses) for how to serve the model locally and connect it with the agent harness of your choice.

## Get Started

Start building today with LFM2.5-24B-A2B, available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B).

For API inference, you can also sign up for [Liquid Console](https://console.liquid.ai/) where you'll receive $2 in credit to get started. The model is priced at $.10/1M input tokens (at $.05 for cached input) and $1.00/1M output tokens.

With LFM2.5, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:

*   **Open-weight** — Download, fine-tune, and deploy. See our [model license](https://www.liquid.ai/lfm-license).
*   **Fast from day one** — Native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, Qualcomm, and Nvidia hardware
*   **A complete family** — From base models for customization to specialized audio and vision variants, one architecture covers diverse use cases

We can't wait to see what you build.

kept.heading: OPENCODE 2.0 (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: OpenCode 2.0 contains quite a lot of new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes. The server now automatically runs as a single background process. Programmatic clients will autodiscover the local service and just work. OpenCode can now be used as a library with the SDK package. More details about the update are available in the article.
kept.article_text:
Title: OpenCode 2.0

URL Source: https://anoma.ly/notes/opencode-2-0/

Published Time: 2026-10-12

Markdown Content:
OpenCode 2.0 is a major over haul.It draws on mil lions of daily users'expe ri ence to deliver a system that can flex to every thing an agent needs to be.There are quite a lot of new fea tures,per for mance improve ments,and bug fixes but here are some of the more impact ful user-facing changes.

## The Service

From the begin ning OpenCode adopted a client/server model.However,this was not some thing it took advan tage of by default and was mostly used by power users.

In 2.0 this server now auto mat i cally runs as a single back ground process on your machine.When you open up a TUI,the web inter face or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process.

opencode pid 48213 Running

Sessions

Fix flaky test

Add dark mode

Review changes

If you're using the pro gram matic client`@opencode/client`to make your own scripts,they will autodis cover the local service and just work.This is par tic u larly useful for sched uled tasks.You can also call it via CLI by using`opencode``api`com mands.

You can expose it to other hosts and run`/pair`or`opencode``pair`to connect it to other appli ca tions.We have native apps in the works that take advan tage of this flow.

## The API

The old API grew hap haz ardly as we and the world col lec tively learned what agents are and should be.It was bad.

We started from scratch and exam ined all the weird use cases across the mil lions of users who use OpenCode every day.It now sup ports nearly any thing you need to be able to do.

OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git work tree when start ing new work.

Session New session

OpenCode

~/app

Fix flaky upload test interrupted

Migrate config loader tab closed

New session this session

~/worktrees/rate-limit

We've also shipped a new client package`@opencode/client`that con tains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect.

review.ts

```
import { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client"
import { Service } from "@opencode/client/service"

const endpoint = await Service.ensure()
const client = OpenCode.make({
  baseUrl: endpoint.url,
  headers: Service.headers(endpoint),
})

const session = await client.session.create({
  location: { directory: process.cwd() },
})

await client.session.prompt({
  sessionID: session.id,
  text: "Review the current changes",
})
```

## Code Mode

The models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advan tage of that more than any other coding agent.We've built a minimal JavaScript inter preter in the`@opencode/codemode`package.

Session

Code Mode

MCP servers

github

linear

sentry

This package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI end points,con vert ing them into func tions that the agent can call in a script.It can run these scripts natively without the com plex ity of Node.js VMs or embed ding com pli cated solu tions like QuickJS.

This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool,map over the results and call another tool.Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time.

All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into code mode by default.This means you can add a thou sand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will dis cover and compose them to get things done.

## Background Tasks

The latest batch of models are incred i bly good at orches tra tion and it is impor tant for har nesses to let them express the full extent of that capa bil ity.

Session

Background

First,we've added back ground sub agents.This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it con tin ues.

This happens auto mat i cally but you can also trigger it man u ally-even with a dif fer ent model.It lets you do things like“spawn a back ground fable sub agent to review this code”while you keep prompt ing.

Second,we've added back ground shell com mands.The shell tool can be invoked asyn chronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent.It'll be noti fied when things are com plete.

If any fore ground shell command or sub agent takes longer than you expect,you can hit a hotkey to move them to the back ground so you can keep prompt ing.

## Plugins

Although OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system,it never got the atten tion it needed.To correct that,we forced our selves to imple ment nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an inter nal plugin and there are now 80+of them.This guar an tees that the Plugin API stays well main tained.

We've also pro moted TUI plugins from exper i men tal to stable.Since it is all powered by OpenTUI,you can build nearly any thing.Here is an example of some thing useless.

We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded.So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away-we covered the design of this in a[previous blogpost](https://anoma.ly/notes/opencode-reloaded).

You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to.But if you do want to read the docs,they are available[here](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins).

## The SDK

OpenCode can also now be used as a library with the`@opencode/sdk`package.This is the exact same code that powers our CLI.

This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in spe cial ized envi ron ments like Durable Objects.And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the stan dard OpenCode server pro to col.

It also has an optional Effect-based API.

This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can[already use it](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk).

## Upgrading

To upgrade the CLI,make sure you're on the latest 1.x release,then run`opencode``upgrade``--major`.

To upgrade your desktop app,download the latest[here](https://opencode.ai/download).

There are some break ing changes.

1.0 plugins will not work in 2.0

Server API is completely different

tui.json config is moved to json

There are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible.It is worth pointing OpenCode at[this doc](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1/)so it can migrate things for you.

kept.article_text:
Title: An Update on Character.ai

URL Source: https://blog.character.ai/an-update-on-character-ai/

Published Time: 2026-10-13T03:52:33.000Z

Markdown Content:
Oct 12, 2026 2 min read

![Image 1: An Update on Character.ai](https://storage.ghost.io/c/ad/34/ad34888f-5b63-4d5f-a358-18cf16489b83/content/images/size/w960/2026/10/oct-blog-header.jpg)

![Image 2](https://storage.ghost.io/c/ad/34/ad34888f-5b63-4d5f-a358-18cf16489b83/content/images/2026/10/oct-blog-header-1.jpg)
Today, we’re sharing that Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to facilitate a court-supervised sale of the company.

Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders.

We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down.

As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority.

**What This Means for Our Community**

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time.

We know that this news may raise questions for some of you. To learn more, please see our FAQs below. And if you need support, you can find helpful resources[here](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/42649759119003-Resources-You-Can-Turn-To?ref=blog.character.ai).

**1. Why did Character.ai file for Chapter 11?**

Over the past year, we have taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.

After a comprehensive review of available options, we determined the best path forward was to begin a Chapter 11 case to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets. We believe that this court-supervised process both maximizes the value of our business and provides the best opportunity for continued service to our platform users.

**2. How long is the sale process expected to take?**

We currently expect that the court-supervised sale process will be complete by the end of November or perhaps early December 2026.

**3. What does this mean for users?**

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community.

**4. Is my paid subscription still active?**

Yes, your subscriptions remain active, and billing is unchanged for now. If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance.

**5. What happens to user data and chats?**

Your information continues to be protected under our[Privacy Policy](https://character.ai/privacy?ref=blog.character.ai), and our data privacy and security practices are unchanged. As a reminder, you can [delete your account](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/15063461160475-How-do-I-delete-my-account?ref=blog.character.ai)or [export your data](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/56967715028891-How-do-I-download-my-data?ref=blog.character.ai) through the app or the Character.ai website.

To learn more, you can read the full press release [HERE](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261012656385/en/Character.ai-Initiates-Voluntary-Chapter-11-Proceeding-to-Facilitate-Value-Maximizing-Sale-Process?ref=blog.character.ai). Court filings and additional information relating to Character.ai’s Chapter 11 case can be found [HERE](https://cases.stretto.com/chartech?ref=blog.character.ai), a website administered by Character.ai’s claims and noticing agent, Stretto, Inc.

Title: Drama 3 – Direct Every Line of AI Voice | Fish Audio

URL Source: https://fish.audio/drama-3

Markdown Content:
Drama 3 Preview

## Direct the performance,not just the words.

## One line, five directions

## Try a roast with Uncle Roger

Uncle Roger's licensed voice, directed by Drama 3. Pick a kitchen crime, hear his verdict, then write your own roast.

## More from Uncle Roger

Every take on this page is a Drama 3 generation of the exact text shown.

## Five ways to direct, one script

Mix them freely in the same line. Every direction is plain text you can read, edit, and reuse.

[warm and relaxed, like talking to an old friend] It's been a while.

### Describe it in your own words

Try natural-language directions, beyond the preset tags: emotion, intent, pacing, who they're talking to.

Alright, [sigh] let's try again.

### Add a sound, emotion, or pause

Put a sigh, a laugh, a breath, or a short pause where you want it, and nowhere else.

I'm fine. Really. <whisper>Go on without me.</whisper>

Control selected words

### Control exactly which words change

Select a few words and pick a scoped tag. Paired tags apply only to the words you select.

[像是在强忍着眼泪，却努力笑着]

[conteniendo las lágrimas, pero sonriendo]

[涙をこらえながら、無理に笑って]

I'm fine. Really. Go on without me.

### Direct in your own language

Write tags and directions in English or your own language. The performance follows the direction, whatever language it's written in.

I was home. Asleep.

Auto Tag

[defensive, slightly uneasy tone] I was home. [pause] Asleep.

### Start with Auto Tag

Need a starting point? Auto Tag adds directions to your script. Keep what works and rewrite the rest.

## Write the scene. Auto Tag directs it.

Give each speaker a voice, write plain dialogue, and let Auto Tag add the directions. Drama 3 performs the whole scene in one pass.

Detective: Adrian · Suspect: Delia · Generated in one pass

## Direct from the API

Set the model header to drama-3 and send your script as it is. Directions, sounds, and paired tags all work in API requests.

[Read the docs](https://docs.fish.audio/api-reference/introduction)[Read the docs](https://docs.fish.audio/api-reference/introduction)

## Your script deserves a performance

Drama 3 is available now in Text to Speech.

## Drama 3 FAQ

Drama 3 is a text-to-speech model from Fish Audio built for direction. Alongside your script you can describe how a line should be performed, add sounds and pauses, and limit an effect to specific words.

Put a direction or a sound in square brackets where it should happen, for example [sigh] or [barely holding it together]. To change only some words, select them and pick a scoped tag such as Whisper or Slower from the Tags menu; the editor wraps them in a paired tag.

Yes. Write tags and directions in English or your own language.

Yes. Add speakers in the Text to Speech editor, give each one a voice, and Drama 3 generates the whole dialogue together.

Drama 3 is still improving. Results vary between takes, so generate a few and pick the best. We will keep updating the model while it is in preview.

Yes. Call the Text to Speech API with the model header set to drama-3. The same tags work in API requests.

# SpaceXSI bundles X Premium, Grok, and Cursor into one subscription

In a bid to attract more subscribers, the company now known as SpaceX Super Intelligence is [bundling](https://x.com/Subscriptions/status/2109783614879650158) all its subscriptions, including X Premium, Grok, and Cursor, into one [plan](https://t.co/xmtWC8apyd) called simply “The X Subscription.”

The idea is that the combined offering could potentially attract more subscribers than any single subscription, given the competitive paid AI subscription market, where SpaceXSI faces rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and others.

With The X Subscription, users can gain access to Grok for AI-powered chat, with support for voice, images, video, and the API. Grok’s agentic AI Bot is also available, as is Cursor for AI coding and the paid features that come with an X Premium subscription, like the blue verified checkmark, creator tools, and fewer ads.

There are five plans available on the new subscription: free, Plus ($8/month), Premium ($30/month), Super ($100/month), and Ultra ($200/month), with AI usage caps increasing as you move up through the tiers. The free plan will only offer limited chat and agent usage, and Premium or higher is required to access the latest Grok models.

There’s another draw for existing X Premium+ subscribers: The comparable plan on the new X subscription costs the same or less, the company noted.

Existing users can either switch from their subscription settings on X to upgrade to the new bundle, or maintain their current plan. The option to upgrade will roll out gradually, so interested customers will need to keep an eye on their billing settings for the offer to upgrade.

kept.heading: MOONDREAM IS JOINING PRIME INTELLECT (4 MINUTE READ)

kept.article_text:
Title: Moondream is joining Prime Intellect

URL Source: https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
## Moondream is joining Prime Intellect

We’ve acquired Moondream. Founders Vik Korrapati and Jay Allen are joining Prime Intellect to lead and scale inference, and to accelerate our work on multimodal models, including vision and computer use.

Moondream was one of our earliest customers, and we’ve long admired what Vik and Jay built with a tiny team. They've shipped state-of-the-art open-weight vision-language models with millions of monthly downloads.[1](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-1) They also built Photon, an inference engine that compiles each model into a single GPU program, along with custom GPU kernels and the megakernel compiler behind them.[2](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-2)

“Moondream is proof that small, efficient models can beat giant ones at specific tasks. Prime is building for that same future: many specialized models that companies own. We were Prime customers long before we joined. Now Photon can power far more than our models, and our models get Prime’s full training stack.”

![Image 1: Jay Allen](https://www.primeintellect.ai/_next/image?url=%2Fblog%2Fmoondream%2Fjay-allen.png&w=3840&q=75&dpl=dpl_B4tp3yFHpAy5ZcFn76XssY6553nG)

Jay Allen

co-founder of Moondream

Moondream 3.1 leads on object detection, aerial images, charts, and crowded scenes like store shelves. It does this at 34 requests per second, about 24x faster than the next most accurate open model.[3](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-3) Compared with Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder, Moondream 3.1 reaches 80% of its accuracy at pointing at objects in photos, at about 1/1000th of the cost.[4](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-4)

Much like Prime Intellect, Moondream made the bet that a model and its underlying infrastructure have to be built together, and that a specialized, efficient model running on the right infrastructure beats a generalist at a given task. We’re excited to double down on this together and help everyone train, deploy and serve frontier multimodal models across video, image, voice and computer use.

## Why inference

We launched Prime Inference because serving is where a model’s usefulness gets decided: inference dictates how fast a model responds and what it costs to run.[5](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-5)

This is where Moondream’s systems work pays off: answers come back in tens of milliseconds, often 40x+ faster than calling a frontier API. On a single H100, Photon runs more than 60 Moondream inferences per second, which is fast enough for live video.[6](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-6) Put together, Moondream’s models get Prime’s full training stack, Photon gets to power far more than Moondream’s models, and Prime customers get a multimodal stack that was built as one system rather than assembled from parts.

Photon and Moondream’s kernel work are being integrated into Prime’s stack. It is a commitment to having the fastest inference on the market and making our customers run models as well as they train them.

## Building together

Moondream built exceptional models and a specialized inference engine. Prime’s open superintelligence stack connects evaluation, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and inference. Together, we combine our training platform with efficient serving and bring on Vik and Jay’s deep expertise in vision and computer use.

We’ve already started shipping. Moondream 3.1 is now available through Prime Inference and powered by Moondream’s Photon engine. Clef and Clef Flash are also live through Prime Inference and OpenRouter, with Clef priced at parity with Jev and Clef Flash at half the price.[7](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fn-7)

![Image 2: Prime Inference model catalog showing Clef, Clef Flash, and Moondream 3.1](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream/prime-inference.png)

In the next few days, every customer of Moondream Cloud will receive credits on our platform, usable for Moondream models and our broader training and inference offerings. Moondream will remain our brand for small, efficient multimodal models.

Our mission is to make open superintelligence accessible to every company. If you’re building vision models, computer-use agents or need the fastest inference on the market, we’d love to work with you.

## References

1.   Korrapati, Vikhyat. [“moondream2.”](https://huggingface.co/vikhyatk/moondream2) Hugging Face. Accessed October 13, 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-1)

2.   Moondream. [“Photon: Official Moondream Inference Engine.”](https://moondream.ai/photon) Accessed October 13, 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-2)

3.   Moondream. [“Moondream 3.1: Beyond Benchmarks.”](https://moondream.ai/blog/moondream-3-1-beyond-benchmarks) Moondream Blog, 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-3)

4.   Prime Intellect. “Pointing Accuracy and Cost per 1,000 Images: Moondream 3.1 and Frontier Models.” Unpublished internal evaluation, October 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-4)

5.   Prime Intellect. [“Prime Inference: Fast, Reliable Serving for Frontier Open Models.”](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/prime-inference) Prime Intellect Blog, 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-5)

6.   Moondream. “Photon Serving Benchmarks, NVIDIA H100.” Unpublished internal measurements, October 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-6)

7.   Vigliarolo, Brandon. [“Cloudflare Tries to Outplay Jev with Open-Weight Clef Models.”](https://www.theregister.com/a/5300649/) The Register, October 1, 2026. [↩](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/moondream#user-content-fnref-7)
