kept.article_text:
Title: Introducing CLiF: Continual Learning from Full-Stack Trajectories

URL Source: https://www.copilotkit.ai/blog/introducing-clif

Published Time: 2026-10-13T15:04:04.172Z

Markdown Content:
Today we're releasing [CLiF](https://go.copilotkit.ai/clif-page) - Continual Learning from Full-Stack Trajectories in early access!

CLiF turns the work your customers and employees already do in your product into the skills, evals, and fine-tuning data your agents need to do that same work reliably in production. It's fully self-hostable, and everything it produces is yours to export.

Your agents could already learn from their own conversations in [CopilotKit Intelligence](https://www.copilotkit.ai/copilotkit-intelligence). CLiF now securely captures both sides of the work (agent trace and user actions) through the AG-UI protocol.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QOrT6sWeirw)

To see what CLiF can do for your product, [book a demo](https://go.copilotkit.ai/clif-page), and our engineers will run it live on your use case.

Here's why we built it, and why every agentic product will need full-stack trajectories.

## Why agents stall before production

Agents like Claude and Codex now take on whole tasks by themselves. Your users want the same in your product, from your built-in agent or any external agent they bring.

But even agents using top-tier models like Fable and Astra struggle to carry out complex, end-to-end tasks in your product consistently enough to deploy, at a cost and speed that make sense.

At companies shipping agents at scale, the pattern is the same. You grind out evals for the flows that matter most, often thousands of cases, each written by hand. Then you improve the agent bit by bit until it passes enough of them to go live.

![Image 1: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/00d6fa6bc189a75ade14afe639cc52c59d29a9ae-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

That work is slow and expensive:

*   **Prompts** grow with every edge case.
*   **Harness** code fills up with special cases: hardcoded step orders, extra checks, custom retries.
*   **Memory** piles up with every conversation, and the agent can't tell which parts matter.
*   **Fine-tuning** comes last, if at all, because the right data is hard to collect.

Even after launch, users find themselves nudging the agent. Guiding it, correcting it, adding context it was missing. Then the next conversation starts, and it needs the same help again.

Meanwhile, the people using your product do this exact work every day.

## Your users already do the work in your product

Your customers and employees already know which actions to take, and in what order, to get the job done. They've done it hundreds of times. Your agent has to deduce all of that from prompts, skills, and hundreds of tools and APIs, so it guesses, retries, or hands the task back.

> Say you run a support platform. A rep gets a ticket: "I was charged twice." They check the plan, find the duplicate charge, and since the customer is on an annual plan, they issue an account credit instead of a refund, because that's what their team does. No doc or prompt says so.

You could add that rule to a prompt. But there are hundreds like it, and you only find the missing ones when the agent gets them wrong.

![Image 2: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/50448227098062eb953647ffa437f89247b703fb-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

Products already record clicks, funnels, and session replays for people reading dashboards. To teach an agent the job, you need trajectories, securely captured as they happen: the full record of every action taken to complete a task, whether by a person or an agent.

In your product, that's a product trajectory: every click, API call, and agent conversation behind a task.

With product trajectories:

*   Your agent improves every day from how your customers and employees actually work.
*   The problems that come up most get fixed first.
*   You approve every change before your agent uses it.

By hand, you would make one or two fixes a day, usually after a customer has already complained. Teams using product trajectories can see a significant drop in repetitive tasks, up to 80%, within the first two weeks.

## Continual learning from full-stack trajectories

[CLiF](https://www.copilotkit.ai/clif) is part of [CopilotKit Intelligence](https://www.copilotkit.ai/copilotkit-intelligence) and learns from full-stack trajectories captured over [AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol)](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui). AG-UI is the open protocol that connects agents to user-facing apps, supported by Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and most of the ecosystem.

AG-UI sits between your agent and your users on any surface, so it sees both sides of the work:

*   **Agent trajectory (agent trace):** every run, tool call, and state change your agent made, and what it returned.
*   **Product trajectory (user actions):** what was on your users' screens, the buttons they clicked, and the server requests they triggered.

Together, that's a full-stack trajectory.

![Image 3: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/e6f7d927e966c534ceb5ba84331c47ef80df0fd6-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

Because it runs on AG-UI, CLiF works with any agent harness and any model under the hood, whether your agent lives in your web app, mobile, Slack, or Teams.

![Image 4: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/8b1e493f44f3f2c17008b386bbdc084da70b858d-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

CLiF reviews new trajectories on a schedule and finds the patterns, including the friction people silently work around. That friction often repeats across thousands of sessions and shows your agent exactly what to learn next.

CLiF turns those patterns into proposed skills, and once you approve them, they reach your agent without redeploying.

Skills are where it starts. From there, we want every team to own the full cycle:

1.   Securely capture every agent and user action as trajectories.
2.   Use agents to make sense of that data at scale.
3.   Turn it into evals and environments.
4.   Review the results together, agents and humans.
5.   Fine-tune smaller, faster open models for your most important tasks.

See how CLiF works on a real product at [copilotkit.ai/clif](https://go.copilotkit.ai/clif-page).

![Image 5: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/a29bb41e07b11b60774d2fa1532e63ad93872371-3200x2000.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

## What you get from full-stack trajectories

CLiF turns them into:

*   **Skills** for your agent or MCP server, built from patterns across your trajectories.
*   **Production-based evals**, built from what your users actually do and ready for the eval platform you already use.
*   **Fine-tuning datasets** for smaller models that run faster and cheaper on your most important tasks.
*   **Full-stack trajectories** you can export to any observability platform.

All of it works with your existing observability and evals stack.

![Image 6: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/a90d479f1b452e226c06a95f60d0d9c90acc9896-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

The more your product gets used, the more of its work your agents can take on.

## Learning from agent trajectories, available today

Every conversation with your agent is an agent trajectory, stored in [AG-UI Streams](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/threads): the messages, tool calls, generative UI, state, and more. When a user corrects the agent, asks for a different format, or adds context it was missing, that becomes a signal CLiF can learn from.

In CopilotKit Intelligence, you organize these trajectories into [learning containers](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/learning), for example, one for expense review and another for onboarding. A container only learns from its own threads, so a skill learned from expense reviews stays with expense reviews.

Every learning run surfaces Product Insights: the recurring requests and friction in those conversations, each linked to the threads behind it. When the evidence supports a reusable lesson, CLiF proposes it as a skill.

Each proposed skill is a `SKILL.md` you review, approve, and can ship with your project. Approved skills reach your agent without a redeploy, and each one stays readable and reversible.

![Image 7: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/76304102caa1a257f5ffc0c7835a2cc701dceee2-3200x2000.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

Around that loop, Intelligence lets you:

1.   **Import the threads you already have** from a LangGraph Server or LangSmith Deployment, so you don't start from zero.
2.   **Run the analysis manually**, or on a schedule once a container has at least 15 eligible threads.
3.   **Deliver skills automatically** through adapters for LangGraph (Python and TypeScript), Mastra, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, and CopilotKit's built-in agent. Setup is one prompt you paste into your coding agent.
4.   **Download published skills with the CLI** as plain `SKILL.md` files for any other agent.

![Image 8: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/fad6cb13851c67820b6608d48f50ea169f6a12c7-3200x2000.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

## Fully self-hostable

CLiF is fully self-hostable, so your data stays inside your own network. You can [self-host CopilotKit Intelligence](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting) on your own Kubernetes cluster with our Helm chart, or on AWS ECS/Fargate.

You bring your own Postgres, Redis, and identity provider, such as Okta, Azure AD, or Keycloak, and keep secrets in the store you already use. Your trajectories, skills, and everything learned from them stay inside your VPC or on-prem. You can also send traces to your own OpenTelemetry collector.

![Image 9: __wf_reserved_inherit](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/y3fjfzcd/production/2f0e34dfecc3422a02996afdbe5e3b035a281d77-3200x1800.png?w=750&fit=max&auto=format&q=85)

Learning from agent trajectories also runs on our [managed cloud](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/managed-intelligence-platform) for the fastest setup.

Our engineers can help you set it up. If you're planning an enterprise self-hosted deployment, [book a call](https://copilotkit.ai/talk-to-an-engineer) and we'll walk through it with you.

## Get started

Learning from agent trajectories works today, and product trajectories are in [early access](https://intelligence.copilotkit.ai/?early_access=automatic_learning).

Want to see CLiF on your product? [Book a demo](https://go.copilotkit.ai/clif-page), and we'll take your use case and show how full-stack trajectories generate the exact evals and skills to get your agents' success rates above the line.

We're also hosting a live session on CLiF on October 15 at 9 AM PT. [Sign up here](https://luma.com/copilo-sxr2).

To learn more:

*   CLiF: [copilotkit.ai/clif](https://go.copilotkit.ai/clif-page)
*   Learning docs: [docs.copilotkit.ai/learning](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/learning)
*   Self-hosting Intelligence: [docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/intelligence/self-hosting)
*   AG-UI: [docs.ag-ui.com](https://docs.ag-ui.com/)

The agentic ecosystem is moving from agent trajectories to full-stack trajectories. The products whose agents learn from how work actually gets done will pull ahead.

Follow CopilotKit on [Twitter](https://go.copilotkit.ai/socials-twitter) for updates. If you get stuck, reach out in the [CopilotKit](https://go.copilotkit.ai/discord) or [AG-UI](https://go.copilotkit.ai/AG-UI-Discord) communities.

kept.heading: GROK VOICE 3.0 (3 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: xAI announced Grok Voice 3.0, a speech-to-speech model with sub-second latency and improved customer-support performance.
kept.article_text:
Title: Introducing Grok Voice 3.0

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/sfLO2d

Published Time: 2026-10-14T00:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
Today, we’re announcing Grok Voice 3.0, the world’s most intelligent speech-to-speech model. It sets a new record for resolving customer support calls, has class-leading latency at under one second, and costs less than other frontier models. Grok Voice powers millions of conversations a day across Tesla and SpaceX, and is available today in the API at the same price as its predecessor.

## [The Most Accurate Voice Model](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/sfLO2d#the-most-accurate-voice-model)

In Artificial Analysis’s independent testing, Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #1 on the Speech-to-Speech Index, with a score of 86.9. The Index combines speech reasoning, τ-Voice, and preference and task success from blind head-to-head calls. Grok Voice 3.0 also scores 97% on Full Duplex Bench, a measure of how naturally it handles pauses, turn-taking, and interruptions.

Speech-to-speech benchmark comparison between Grok Voice 3.0 and competing models, per Artificial Analysis.| Benchmark | Grok Voice 3.0 (this release) | Grok Voice 2.0 | GPT-Live-1(Astra, Medium) | Gemini 3.8 Live(Ext. Thinking, High) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Overall AA Speech-to-Speech Index | 86.9 | 81.3 | 83.2 | 82.6 |
| Speech Reasoning Big Bench Audio | 98.5% | 97.2% | 90.1% | 97.7% |
| Human Preference Speech Agent Arena Elo | 1070 | 1011 | 1048 | 990 |
| Task Completion Task Success Rate | 94.8% | 94.6% | 87.4% | 89.1% |
| Conversational Dynamics Full Duplex Bench | 97.0% | 95.1% | 94.9% | 91.9% |

τ-Voice measures how well agents handle support calls with diverse accents, background noise, and interruptions. Grok Voice 3.0 scores 71.6%, comparable with GPT-Live-1 (Astra), but at 40% lower latency, setting a new frontier in agent intelligence versus responsiveness.

It's also cheaper to run than comparable models. Artificial Analysis measures what each model costs to complete a task in its Big Bench Audio run, and Grok Voice 3.0 comes in under both GPT-Live-1 (Astra, Medium) and GPT-Realtime-2.1.

Lower cost per task than comparable models

Average cost per task on Artificial Analysis's Big Bench Audio run, USD. Lower is better.

On [EVA-Bench](https://servicenow.github.io/eva), ServiceNow’s benchmark for enterprise voice agents, Grok Voice 3.0 achieves the highest accuracy score at 74% and is the best-performing model when jointly scored across accuracy and customer experience.

> “Grok Voice 3.0 sets a new Pareto frontier on EVA-Bench, ServiceNow’s open-source benchmark scoring voice agents on accuracy and experience across 200+ realistic enterprise scenarios. It pairs top accuracy with a natural, responsive conversation, setting a new standard for what enterprises can expect from AI on the front line of customer service.”

Nitin Aggarwal, Senior Director of Product Management, Agentic Evals and RAI, ServiceNow

## [Used by Millions of Customers at Tesla & SpaceX](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/sfLO2d#used-by-millions-of-customers-at-tesla--spacex)

Grok Voice 3.0 handles millions of conversations a day in Tesla vehicles. Drivers can use Connectors for simple requests like checking their calendar or answering an email, and Grok Bot for bigger tasks like ordering a coffee or booking dinner—all completely hands-free ([see it on X](https://x.com/Tesla/status/2102430656349544590)). Grok Voice 3.0 also powers Grok Bot’s voice mode.

Starlink call centers use Grok Voice to answer 20,000 customer calls every day across multiple languages. Roughly 70% are resolved with no human in the loop, and one in four sales calls ends in a purchase before the caller hangs up. A single agent built on Grok Voice 3.0 verifies customers, troubleshoots hardware, issues credits, and ships replacement equipment.

## [Pricing and Availability](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/sfLO2d#pricing-and-availability)

Grok Voice 3.0 is available today in the Voice Agent API at [$0.08 / min ($4.80 / hr)](https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing?campaign=voice-3-blog#voice-api-pricing), the same price as Grok Voice 2.0. Agents using `grok-voice-latest` have already been switched over automatically, with no changes needed.

## Start building with Grok Voice

[Try It Free](https://console.x.ai/team/default/voice/agents?campaign=voice-3-blog&utm_source=website&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=voice-3-blog)[View Docs](https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/audio/voice?campaign=voice-3-blog)

kept.heading: JEV: FOR THE BUILDERS AND DREAMERS (5 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Jev 1.14.0 features image support, a new type, and longer context. Multimodal support has also been turned on for Jev 1.13.0. Both models perform worse on multimodality than on pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. The new 'box' type returns a single bounding box. It is a preview of TypeSafe's explorations beyond simple decisions and into what else System One Models can support.
kept.article_text:
Title: Jev: For the builders AND dreamers - TypeSafe AI Blog

URL Source: https://typesafe.ai/blog/jev-1-14

Markdown Content:
_TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the_`danger zone`_at your own risk. 🔥_

## Our philosophy

A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.

To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.

On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.

Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.

### Composable Images

Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love (`jev-1.13.0`) was multimodal all along!

Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in `assets`. You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the `state`, `instructions`, or even `criteria`! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.

As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.

`TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true`

Check out docs: [docs.typesafe.ai/go/images](http://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images)

### Types Beyond Decisions

We’re introducing another new type as well: `box`. It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.

We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for `jev-1.14.0` (spoilers).

Check out docs: [docs.typesafe.ai/go/box](http://docs.typesafe.ai/go/box)

### Size _does_ matter, apparently 💅

We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod.

We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to:

`TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true`

Check out docs: [docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length)

### Opt-in to help us

We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases.

![Image 1](https://framerusercontent.com/images/9xWPxly4HZ7S43IpAEGS2VOFM.png?width=1528&height=1078)

## jev-1.14.0

We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under `jev-preview`! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to _everything_. Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support.

Model releases should generally also be strict improvements, but we’re well aware of how much developers hate updating their dependencies. `jev-latest` will be updated to `jev-1.14.0` in a week. `jev-1.13.0` will be available for a while.

We intend to give 60 days warning before `jev-1.13.0` is formally deprecated, and 30 days for `jev-1.14.0`. We’ll release a deprecation policy prior to this.

### Measuring Intelligence

As you all know, we [dislike public benchmarks](https://typesafe.ai/blog/antibenchmaxxing). However, we have our own internal best guesses on how to measure the form factor of intelligence that matters most for developers.

We’re trying something new out here: we’re going to treat you guys like adults and share this with you all.

##### Some nuance

*   This measurement is our best guess and will continue to evolve. If ever we show you our internal numbers again, don’t expect them to be consistent.

*   Don’t believe it entirely. Always favor your own experimentation and evals with your use cases.

*   We’re including only open weight models because we guard our validation set very closely and are spooked out about the data policies of our model providers.

*   This is likely biased towards our models. Feel free to ignore our model, and instead focus on the relative ranking of open source models.

![Image 2](https://framerusercontent.com/images/IMAdGJMIKQYl8JkqnebGaIB3g.png?width=2136&height=1372)![Image 3](https://framerusercontent.com/images/TmIsBzc45HeG5x98MZM5oHM.png?width=2136&height=1372)![Image 4](https://framerusercontent.com/images/UHjjLTnHvk90WzLkGbrDdbSHkM.png?width=2136&height=1372)

## What’s next

Lots of people love to ask what kind of sci-fi we’re releasing next. While we are working on some mindblowing stuff, expect most releases to be beautifully boring (like we think AI should be): small improvements across the board, better stability, and features for real deployment.

kept.heading: MORE AGENTS, SAME MYTHICAL MONTH (18 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: AI has made producing code cheap. This moves the bottleneck of software delivery to deciding, verifying, and coordinating. AI amplifies whatever coordination an organization already had. Adding more agents will not fix weak coordination, just as adding more developers never did.
kept.article_text:
Title: More Agents, Same Mythical Month

URL Source: https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/caghQc

Published Time: 2026-10-14T18:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: More Agents, Same Mythical Month](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/_astro/heroImage.DMZvwBb5_ZQHHCM.jpg)
A delivery date is slipping. The backlog is long, the team is tired, and someone in the planning meeting points out that the work no longer has to wait for people. _Agents are cheap. We can start ten more tonight, or a hundred, and let them work through the queue while we sleep._ The proposal sounds modern and reasonable, and some vendors make it feel natural: Moonshot AI [markets its Kimi K2.5 model](https://www.kimi.ai/blog/kimi-k2-5) on its ability to direct a swarm of up to a hundred sub-agents. The assumption that more agents simply means better results is common enough that [a Google Research study](https://research.google/blog/towards-a-science-of-scaling-agent-systems-when-and-why-agent-systems-work/) set out to test it.

The instinct is older than the agents. Fred Brooks described it in 1975, in _The Mythical Man-Month_:

> Oversimplifying outrageously, we state Brooks’s Law: Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.

The reasons behind it apply to agents with surprisingly few changes. [An earlier post of mine](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/your-ai-platform-will-inherit-your-engineering-culture/) argued that an AI platform inherits the engineering culture it is built on. This one looks at what happens when we try to scale that culture with agents.

AI has made producing code cheap, which moves the bottleneck of software delivery to deciding, verifying and coordinating - capabilities that were always largely organisational. **AI amplifies whatever coordination an organisation already has.** Adding more agents will not fix weak coordination, just as adding more developers never did.

## What changed: code got cheap

In early 2026 Cursor [ran hundreds of agents on a single codebase](https://cursor.com/blog/scaling-agents), and in close to a week they produced a web browser of more than a million lines. Anthropic had a team of parallel agents [build a C compiler](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler) that builds many real projects - Doom among them, and a Linux kernel that boots - though not all of them. Steve Yegge built [Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown), an orchestrator for fleets of coding agents.

Their authors are also honest about what these projects are. Cursor’s engineer described the browser as a research experiment that was [never meant to be production software](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jan/23/fastrender/). Anthropic’s write-up says plainly that the compiler is not yet a drop-in replacement for a real compiler. Yegge [wrote](https://yegge.ai/essays/the-shape-of-things-to-come/) that he only ever ended up using Gas Town to build Gas Town. These are experiments about how far output can scale, and on that question they are convincing: output scales. But it scales only when someone designs a structure for the agents to work in - a hierarchy, a single design authority, written intent, and a test suite strong enough to tell the agents when they are wrong.

![Image 2: Workers on the assembly line at Ford's Highland Park plant](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/_astro/Assembly_line_at_the_Ford_Motor_Companys_Highland_Park_plant_LCCN2011661021.Ds_db8Yy_Z2kLkMR.jpg)
_The assembly line at Ford’s Highland Park plant, 1913. Public domain, Library of Congress, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Assembly\_line\_at\_the\_Ford\_Motor\_Company's\_Highland\_Park\_plant\_LCCN2011661021.jpg)._

Agent-written software also creates real value. Claude Code is [reportedly written almost entirely by Claude Code](https://fortune.com/2026/06/11/anthropic-claude-boris-cherny-doesnt-write-code-by-hand-anymore/), and Anthropic reported Claude Code’s run-rate revenue at [over $2.5 billion in February 2026](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-raises-30-billion-series-g-funding-380-billion-post-money-valuation). Lovable, where people build applications by describing them, passed [$600 million in annualised revenue in September 2026](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/24/lovables-annualized-revenue-crosses-600m-as-vibe-coding-takes-off/). It would be wrong to say that agents produce output but no value.

Code has become cheap and abundant, but cheap code is not the same as correct, working software. Verification and quality are still partly technical problems, and we will come back to them as part of the correction mechanisms that have to keep up. The rest of the argument depends on one point: when one input becomes cheap, the constraint moves to the inputs that do not.

## What did not change: Brooks’s mechanism

Others have drawn the Brooks parallel before. Murat Demirbas argued that multi-agent systems [do not escape Brooks’s law](https://muratbuffalo.blogspot.com/2026/01/agentic-ai-and-mythical-agent-month.html), and Wes McKinney that coordination [changes shape rather than disappearing](https://www.oreilly.com/radar/the-mythical-agent-month/). What this piece adds is a step past both the Brooks parallel and the finding that AI amplifies what a team already is. Cheap output makes hidden coordination and value failures visible, as review queues and unused features, faster than our correction loops can respond.

Brooks’s law is about late projects, while the agent question is about throughput in general, so the comparison needs some care. Twenty years after the book, Brooks still described his law as a rule of thumb rather than a law of nature. What carries over is the mechanism he gave for it.

The first part is partitioning. Months and workers are interchangeable only when a task can be split into pieces that need no communication between them. When a task has sequential constraints, more effort does not shorten it. His example was childbirth: some work takes the time it takes, no matter how many people are assigned. Agents do not escape this. A controlled study of agent configurations, using small teams of three or four agents on benchmark tasks, found that every multi-agent setup it tested made sequential planning 39–70% worse, while a multi-agent setup improved performance by about 80% on a task that could be split cleanly ([published January 2026](https://research.google/blog/towards-a-science-of-scaling-agent-systems-when-and-why-agent-systems-work/)). Agents help where the work divides and hurt where it does not: Brooks’s rule, restated.

![Image 3: Telephone exchange operators connecting calls by hand](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/_astro/Telephone-operators-Japan-1902.CW45uw2s_Z23Dmaw.jpg)
_Telephone exchange operators in Yaesu, Japan, 1902. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Telephone-operators-Japan-1902.jpg)._

The second part is communication. Brooks counted the pairwise channels between workers, _n(n-1)/2_, and noted that coordination effort quickly overtakes the time saved by dividing the work. Cursor ran into the same problem. Its first design let agents coordinate as equals, with no hierarchy, and Wilson Lin reported the result:

> Twenty agents would slow down to the effective throughput of two or three, with most time spent waiting.

The fair reply is that Cursor then fixed it. A hierarchy of planner agents and worker agents let hundreds of agents work in parallel, and the field is building more of these tools every month: orchestrators, merge queues, review agents, written specifications. This is the strongest objection to the argument here - that coordination is a distributed-systems problem, and engineering is solving it.

The answer is that the fixes are Brooks’s own. A single planner that decides the shape of the work is his surgical team, in which one chief programmer makes the key decisions and the others support that person. One design authority that keeps the parts consistent is his conceptual integrity, the idea that a design must come from one mind, or from a very small number of agreeing minds. These fixes work, and they solve coordination among the agents. What they cannot reach is the coordination among the people who decide what the agents are for - the goal, the trade-offs, the definition of done. That kind of coordination does not get easier with more agents, and the rest of this piece is about it.

The third part is training, and this is where agents differ most. Brooks wrote:

> Each worker must be trained in the technology, the goals of the effort, the overall strategy, and the plan of work.

Human ramp-up largely disappears: an agent can take in a codebase far faster than a new hire. But the second half of Brooks’s sentence does not disappear. The goals, the strategy and the plan still have to be transmitted, and with agents they become context and specification that someone must write and keep consistent. The recurring cost is keeping that written intent current as goals change. Requirements engineers see the same effect from their side: AI [magnifies the quality of the documentation it is given](https://www.clarityisrare.com/blog/documentation-quality-bottleneck/), good or bad. [Written conventions](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/the-renaissance-of-written-coding-conventions/) and agent skills are this training in written form, and they matter for the same reason [conventions matter in large, distributed teams](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/the-power-of-coding-conventions-in-large-distributed-teams/).

Agents have no careers or egos, so their failures have partly different causes, even where they take the same shapes as human ones: [a study of failures in multi-agent systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657) sorted them into poor specification, misalignment between agents, and missing verification. The coordination problem also does not shrink when the human team does. A small team directing hundreds of agents still meets it: in how the agents are organised, in the customers and other teams it works with, and in the limits of its own attention. One engineer at OpenAI, whose team [grew from three to seven engineers](https://openai.com/index/harness-engineering/) while shipping about a million lines of agent-written code, [described the team’s synchronous attention](https://www.latent.space/p/harness-eng) as the only fundamentally scarce resource.

## What is new: speed outruns self-correction

Every working software organisation already corrects its own mistakes, through code review, testing, small releases, retrospectives and talking to users. Self-correction is the “verifying” from the thesis, seen at the scale of the organisation. Tom Johnson made this point well in [a review of Yuval Noah Harari’s _Nexus_](https://idratherbewriting.com/blog/review-harari-nexus-scms-and-alien-intelligence): software methodology is already built on self-correction. That is right, and the real question is whether those mechanisms were built for the speed they now face.

One of Harari’s observations fits here directly:

> as a network becomes more powerful, its self-correcting mechanisms become more vital.

Our correction loops were calibrated to human pace. A reviewer could read most of what a team produced in a week. A product manager could watch a feature in use before the next one was built. Kief Morris observed in March 2026 that [agents can now generate code faster than humans can inspect it](https://martinfowler.com/articles/exploring-gen-ai/humans-and-agents.html), and others have pointed out that many of our engineering habits were [built around the assumption that code is expensive](https://simonwillison.net/guides/agentic-engineering-patterns/code-is-cheap/). When that assumption breaks, the habits do not adjust themselves.

There is a fair counterpoint. Cheap code also makes experiments, tests and automated reviews cheaper, and teams running many agents already use review agents and verifiers to speed up correction. That helps, but it does not settle the question: someone still has to decide what counts as wrong, and that decision is the part that does not speed up.

The same speed mismatch has another side. Problems that used to stay hidden for months now become visible artefacts within days. Weak coordination used to show up as a vague sense that the team was slow. Now it typically shows up as a queue: pull requests waiting for review, features delivered that nobody asked for, several agents solving the same problem in different ways.

A flawed understanding of value used to be a matter of opinion in a planning meeting. Now it is something you can point at in the repository. AI makes these failures visible faster than our correction mechanisms can respond; it did not create them. The requirements-engineering blog Clarity Is Rare [puts it in one line](https://www.clarityisrare.com/blog/what-organizations-must-change/):

> AI doesn’t make uncertainty disappear. It makes its consequences arrive faster.

## Output is not value

The clearest statements come from the people who build the tools. In February 2026, [Dario Amodei](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/dario-amodei-2), Anthropic’s chief executive, was asked about his earlier prediction that AI would write 90% of the code. He called the share of lines a poor measure of what matters:

> But that’s actually a very weak criterion.

His point was that the share of code written by AI says little about how much faster a company actually delivers. AI writing most of the code and a company needing far fewer engineers are, in his view, two very different claims, and the first does not imply the second. He estimated the overall speed-up from coding models at the time at perhaps 15–20%.

Amodei himself expects the speed-up to keep growing, and models to do software engineering end to end within a year or two, which makes the narrower point stronger: even by the builders’ own account, value depends on more than code. In February 2026 [Boris Cherny](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Feb/14/boris/), who leads Claude Code, described what engineers at Anthropic - a company still hiring engineers - now spend their time on when Claude writes their code:

> Someone has to prompt the Claudes, talk to customers, coordinate with other teams, decide what to build next.

[A study of the company’s own engineers](https://www.anthropic.com/research/how-ai-is-transforming-work-at-anthropic), from December 2025, found that most of them could fully hand over only 0–20% of their work. The rest still needs a person in the loop.

At the level of whole organisations the picture is mixed. [Faros AI](https://www.faros.ai/blog/ai-software-engineering) analysed telemetry from more than 10,000 developers in 2025 and [summarised the result](https://www.faros.ai/ai-productivity-paradox) this way:

> Engineers are completing twice as many code changes, but company metrics remain flat.

In its [2026 dataset](https://www.faros.ai/blog/key-takeaways-from-the-dora-report-2025), median time in pull-request review rose by 441%, compared with a 91% rise in the previous year’s dataset. DORA’s survey-based research is more encouraging: its [2025 report](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report) found a positive relationship between AI adoption and both throughput and product performance, while the relationship with delivery stability stayed negative. A year earlier, DORA had [estimated](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/devops-sre/announcing-the-2024-dora-report) that rising AI adoption came with a 1.5% drop in delivery throughput and a 7.2% drop in stability.

Both sources are correlational, and they do not agree. Controlled [field studies](https://laweconcenter.org/resources/ai-productivity-and-labor-markets-a-review-of-the-empirical-evidence/) have also found real productivity gains at the level of individual tasks; those gains turn into delivery gains only if review, decisions and coordination can absorb them. What the organisation-level data shares is that more output does not reliably or evenly turn into more value. These studies measure AI adoption in general, not fleets of agents, so they cannot settle the agent question directly. But if broad AI adoption already amplifies weak coordination, it would be surprising if more agents did the opposite - and Brooks’s mechanism suggests why.

![Image 4: A chimpanzee seated at a typewriter](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/_astro/Chimpanzee_seated_at_typewriter.C8fq0crb_Z11ngb.jpg)
_A chimpanzee at a typewriter, New York Zoological Society, around 1906. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chimpanzee\_seated\_at\_typewriter.jpg)._

There is an old image for output without aim: the infinite monkey theorem, in which monkeys at typewriters, given infinite time, will eventually type Shakespeare. The image is a deliberate stretch. Agent output is usually locally competent and often good, far from random. The problem is aim, not quality - or, as requirements engineers describe the same pattern, analysis that is [locally correct but globally wrong](https://www.clarityisrare.com/blog/failure-modes/). Output that is locally competent but not aimed at shared intent is, with respect to that intent, as good as random. That is why the finite version applies. [When researchers calculated the odds in 2024](https://phys.org/news/2024-10-monkey-unable-hamlet-lifetime-universe.html) for a finite universe, they found that random typing would almost certainly never produce the complete works of Shakespeare before the universe ends, even with every chimpanzee on Earth at a keyboard. Real projects have budgets, not infinite time, and my reading is that output not held to shared intent will not add up to a working product before the budget runs out.

## What gets amplified: the organisation

Deciding, verifying and coordinating live in the organisation, and [DORA’s AI research](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report) describes the effect plainly: AI amplifies what is already in a team rather than fixing it. Its [AI Capabilities Model](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/introducing-doras-inaugural-ai-capabilities-model) adds a warning that reads like a summary of this whole argument:

> But, when users aren’t the focus, AI-assisted development teams may just be moving quickly in the wrong direction.

Melvin Conway made the structural point in 1968: organisations [produce designs that copy their own communication structures](https://www.melconway.com/Home/Committees_Paper.html). My [previous post](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/your-ai-platform-will-inherit-your-engineering-culture/) argued this for AI platforms. Agents work inside the organisation’s communication structure, and they inherit its gaps. When goals are unclear, agents implement the unclear goals faster. When ownership is fragmented, agents produce fragmented systems faster. Amplification also works in the positive direction: Clarity Is Rare [observes](https://www.clarityisrare.com/blog/amplification/) that the value from AI concentrates in the teams that redesigned their workflows, not in the ones that only adopted the tools.

[A large international survey of requirements engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.10288) found that hidden requirements and frequently changing goals were among the most common problems teams reported, and that they were linked to project failure. Incentives make the problem worse. Researchers who studied [Résumé-Driven Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12703) found that job adverts and CVs both overemphasise fashionable technologies, and described how the two can feed each other in a self-sustaining loop. However this is a story about structure rather than bad people: people do what the structure rewards, and when it rewards visible activity over value for customers, AI makes visible activity very cheap. The same structures that leave large teams [feeling powerless](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/learned-helplessness-in-software-teams/) or [divided by culture and hierarchy](https://links.tldrnewsletter.com/blog/navigating-cultural-clashes-in-global-software-teams/) will shape what a fleet of agents produces.

## Change the structure, and the mindset follows

We have seen this pattern before. Agile spread through the industry as a set of values and practices, and in many companies only the ceremonies arrived - stand-ups, sprints and boards - without the change in thinking behind them. Martin Fowler called the result [faux-agile](https://martinfowler.com/articles/agile-aus-2018.html): agile in name, without the practices or the values. AI adoption can follow the same path, with agents, dashboards and adoption targets standing in for the shift it needs: from measuring output to owning intent and value.

[Craig Larman](https://www.craiglarman.com/wiki/index.php?title=Larman%27s_Laws_of_Organizational_Behavior)’s observation explains why the shift is hard to achieve by persuasion alone:

> (in large established orgs) Culture follows structure.

Structure and incentives come first, because the rest follows from them. That points to three concrete changes.

The first is to judge AI work by value rather than output - by changes in what customers do, not by lines, pull requests or agent hours. This matters more than it may seem: Microsoft’s experimentation team reported that [only about a third of tested ideas improved the metric they were designed to improve](https://www.exp-platform.com/Documents/2015%20Online%20Controlled%20Experiments_EncyclopediaOfMLDM.pdf). Cheap output with good validation finds more of the winners; without validation, it mostly multiplies the other two thirds.

The second is to invest in shared, written intent before scaling the number of agents: what we are building, for whom, and what good looks like - with [named owners for that documentation and a validation step](https://www.clarityisrare.com/blog/what-organizations-must-change/) before AI output drives decisions.

The third is to match review and validation capacity to the new speed of production, rather than letting the queue grow.

None of this rejects technical work. Tests, verifiers and version control are part of the correction mechanisms, and they matter more now, not less. The claim is not that AI in software development has no technical side; it is that the technical part became cheap, and the expensive part is everything that turns code into value.

## The man-month, revisited

Brooks’ central point was never really about headcount. It was that effort and progress - his word for what this piece has called value - are different things, and that the man-month, as a unit, confuses them. Cost scales with people multiplied by months. Progress does not.

The cheap agent-hour makes the same confusion easier: we can now buy effort almost without limit. What we cannot buy is the shared intent that turns effort into progress: knowing what to build, agreeing why, and noticing quickly when we were wrong - deciding, coordinating and verifying. Those were always the scarce part of software development, and AI has made them much harder to hide. So the next time a late project meets the offer of a hundred more agents, the better question is not how many to start, but whether we know what we want them to build.

## Used resources

*   [The Mythical Man-Month (essay text) - Frederick P. Brooks, Jr.](https://phoenix.goucher.edu/~kelliher/f2010/cs245/theMythicalManMonth.pdf)

kept.article_text:
Title: Agent observability on the Claude Platform

URL Source: https://claude.com/resources/articles/agent-observability-on-the-claude-platform

Published Time: 2026-10-14

Markdown Content:
Claude Resources

Announcing OpenTelemetry traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs on the Claude Platform.

You can now send OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs to any OTel tool, and follow each step your agents take. If you already send Claude Code or Cowork traces to your observability tool, the agents you build on the Claude Platform can also show up in the same place.

## Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

Trusting an agent with more access starts with tracing its model calls, tool use, and MCP server calls. Review its traces, then widen its access as it proves reliable.

Add a destination in the Claude Console, and every agent turn, model call, and tool use arrives in your observability tool as a standard OpenTelemetry trace, with latency, tokens, and IDs.

![Image 1: How OpenTelemetry traces work](https://assets.claude.com/28fe34519808d40faa51162351234a3790230860.png)
## Works with your observability tools

Claude traces follow the [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai/), so data from Claude and other providers works in the same tools and dashboards.

*   **Debug agents next to the rest of your stack**. In [Grafana Cloud](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana-cloud/observe-and-act/agent-observability/guides/send-claude-platform-traces/), [Honeycomb](https://docs.honeycomb.io/send-data/use-cases/claude-platform), [Sentry](https://sentry.io/cookbook/trace-claude-platform-with-opentelemetry/), and [Splunk](https://agent-observability-docs.splunk.com/sdk-api/third-party-integrations/claude), agent traces sit beside your logs and metrics, so you can see which service a slow or failed step came from.
*   **Improve agents with production data**. With [Arize AI](https://arize.com/docs/ax/integrations/platforms/claude-managed-agents/claude-managed-agents-tracing), [Braintrust](https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/integrations/ai-providers/anthropic#export-opentelemetry-traces-from-the-claude-api), [Datadog](https://docs.datadoghq.com/llm_observability/instrument/otel_instrumentation/?tab=python#using-claude-managed-agents), [Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/integrations/model-providers/claude-platform), [LangSmith by LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/langsmith/trace-anthropic), [New Relic](https://newrelic.com/blog/news/anthropic-otel-ai-observability), and [PostHog](https://posthog.com/docs/ai-observability/installation/anthropic?tab=Claude+Platform&utm_source=anthropic&utm_campaign=anthropic-otel), you can turn real traces into evals, catch quality issues, and measure whether a change helped.
*   **Track usage across your organization**. Send traces to [Databricks Unity Gateway](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ai-gateway/unified-trace-table) so platform and security teams can see token usage by team and flag unusual activity.

Claude traces also work with any other OpenTelemetry tool that accepts a standard OTLP endpoint.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tok8ncWJ7l4)

## Get started

OpenTelemetry traces on the Claude Platform is available in public beta. Managed Agents and the Messages API need a destination in the Claude Console, while Claude SDKs export traces automatically.

See the [docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/opentelemetry) to get started.

![Image 2: FloQast](https://assets.claude.com/37eab59899ee1b3f95d9bd8106e2708f2db42680.svg)

> “Agents that touch a company’s books have to show their work, the same way an accountant does. Our agents run on the Claude Platform and our telemetry lives in Grafana Cloud, and native OpenTelemetry export from Claude puts each model call in the same trace as the reconciliation or journal-entry workflow it ran inside. We see the prompt version, tool calls, latency, and token spend alongside the rest of our stack, so when an auditor asks what an agent did and why, we can answer from one timeline.”

![Image 3: Foxglove](https://assets.claude.com/59150536fe838e40bd470d19ad4ab74ec3fa2d61.svg)

> “At Foxglove, we’re building agents that help robotics teams debug their robots. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform lets us analyze agent interactions in PostHog alongside product usage data. That helps us evaluate how our agents perform in practice, identify where they fall short, and prioritize improvements for robotics teams.”

![Image 4: Ramp](https://assets.claude.com/6db782273272dd89f11df7b54089328994fe718e.svg)

> “Claude powers some of Ramp’s most capable internal and customer-facing agents. We built Reflect, an agentic system that scores their Langfuse traces, finds recurring failures, and proposes fixes. On some agents, we’ve already cut token usage by 10–20% and made sessions 30% faster. But Reflect can only improve what it observes. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude API can feed high-fidelity instrumentation directly into that improvement loop, with no extra steps.”

![Image 5: Sterling Labs](https://assets.claude.com/0e7434aa92b7dbc6ea6bd4109a0b3602bcb2a22c.svg)

> “At Sterling Labs, we tune our systems like a race team tunes its engine. For agents analyzing live markets 24/7, Langfuse is our pit wall. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform streams every trace straight in with no custom instrumentation, so my team can focus on the edge, not the wiring.”

1/4

kept.heading: ANALYZING TECHNICAL DOCUMENTS WITH DEEP REVIEW (12 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Google's Deep Review is an agent AI system engineer designed to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. It was initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, but its capabilities have since expanded to reviewing documents across many domains. Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, but support for multi-file inputs will arrive soon. Google believes that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.
kept.article_text:
Title: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review

URL Source: https://research.google/blog/analyzing-technical-documents-with-deep-review/

Markdown Content:
Generative AI has accelerated many technical fields. It is now common for AI to play some role in writing scientific papers and technical documents, running code, designing experiments, and drafting proposals. However, accelerating content creation has created a review challenge: the human capacity for verification has remained largely fixed amid this rapid increase in AI-generated content. Reviewing complex documents like long scientific manuscripts or complex legal agreements requires specialized expertise and advanced subject knowledge. This imbalance creates a [validation bottleneck](https://deepmind.google/public-policy/conjecture-machines-ai-agents-and-the-new-validation-bottleneck-in-science/), where information is being generated faster than it can be rigorously reviewed.

Today, we’re excited to announce the public release of [Deep Review](https://research.google/deepreview/), an agentic AI system engineered to provide rigorous feedback and technical verification on complex documents. Initially designed for computer science academic paper analysis, the system’s capabilities have expanded to review documents across many domains, such as legal and finance. It can be used as both an iterative improvement tool during the drafting process and a tool for the scientific process verification, claims, and evaluation during the review process.

Deep Review represents the evolution of our Paper Assistant Tool (PAT) — an experimental initiative developed to help researchers stress-test manuscripts prior to conference submission. Over the past year, we partnered with four flagship computer science conferences ([STOC 2026](https://research.google/blog/gemini-provides-automated-feedback-for-theoretical-computer-scientists-at-stoc-2026/), [ICML 2026,](https://blog.icml.cc/2026/03/30/retrospective-on-pat-x-icml-2026-ai-paper-assistant-program/)[NeurIPS 2026,](https://blog.neurips.cc/2026/04/21/neurips-supports-authors-with-googles-paper-assistant-tool-pat/) and [ICLR 2027](https://blog.iclr.cc/2026/09/10/making-googles-paper-assistant-tool-pat-available-to-iclr-submitters/)) to provide private, pre-submission feedback to authors of more than 16,000 manuscripts who opted in. Further details on PAT and these pilots can be found in our manuscript, [Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google’s Paper Assistant Tool](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28277).

With this release, Deep Review is now accessible worldwide:

*   **Tiered access and scalable API**: Every user receives two complimentary document reviews per week. Users with high-volume workflows can connect their [Gemini API key](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/api-key) for higher usage limits and programmatic integration via the Deep Review API.
*   **Format flexibility**: Deep Review will initially support PDFs and plain text as input formats, with support for multi-file inputs coming soon.
*   **Privacy and data policy**: Documents uploaded to Deep Review are never used to train, fine-tune, or improve Google models. Uploaded documents are stored for one year for the sole purpose of display to the user in the Deep Review UI.

## Deep Review accelerates technical validation

One of the most significant examples of the validation bottleneck is in academic peer review. This can be seen in the uptick of submissions to academic publication venues, especially venues for AI research itself, which have seen a dramatic rise. This year, there were over 74,000 submissions to three major AI conferences ([ICLR](https://blog.iclr.cc/2026/03/31/a-retrospective-on-the-iclr-2026-review-process/), [NeurIPS](https://csconfstats.xoveexu.com/?conf=NeurIPS), and [ICML](https://media.icml.cc/Conferences/ICML2026/ICML2026_Fact_Sheet.pdf)) [up from approximately](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.28277) 45,000 in 2025, 32,000 in 2024, and 23,000 in 2023. Each of these submissions requires multiple high-quality reviews to ensure the integrity of the peer review process, which can place a larger burden on human experts.

Deep Review aims to help alleviate this expanding burden on human reviewers across technical fields. By providing detailed, objective evaluations of documents, Deep Review checks logical consistency and mathematical statements, suggests improvements, grounds facts, and compares with existing work. It addresses some of the most cognitively burdensome facets of review, while leaving higher-level judgements to humans.

## A proven track record for scientific review

Deep Review has been extensively tested and deployed under its experimental name, the [Paper Assistant Tool](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28277) (PAT), in four pilot partnerships with the flagship computer science conferences STOC 2026, ICML 2026, NeurIPS 2026, and ICLR 2027. During these pilots, authors were able to opt-in to receive feedback and analysis on their paper via PAT in the weeks before the submission deadline. The goal was to provide authors with actionable feedback to help improve the quality of papers in submission. This feedback was completely decoupled from the official conference review process. PAT did not collect any of the data for training, and papers were deleted from Google systems promptly after each program concluded.

Author reactions to the tool have been extremely positive, and reflect continued improvements to both underlying models and the PAT harness. With the addition of Gemini 4 Argon support in Deep Review, the underlying capabilities of the tool have further increased beyond the older iterations of PAT described below.

## How Deep Review works

Single-prompt LLM calls often fail when evaluating long, complex documents due to exhausting their token reasoning budget, overlooking long-context cross-section dependencies, or accepting nuanced claims without fully scrutinizing them. Deep Review solves these challenges through a four-stage agentic pipeline:

1.   **Document segmentation**: The document is first ingested and autonomously decomposed by a segmenter agent into logical segments (e.g., Introduction, experiments, methodology, etc.). These segments can be overlapping, and must cover all the content of the input document.
2.   **Adaptive budgeting**: Not all sections require equal cognitive depth. The pipeline inspects information density and dynamically allocates a compute budget, along with a specialized inference scaling pipeline for each section. For instance, sections with dense mathematical proofs may receive more compute than an introduction or a related work section in an academic paper.
3.   **Deep parallel verification**: Specialized reasoning agents scrutinize each segment in parallel. Each agent has access to the full document context to track cross-references, but focuses its reasoning power specifically on the task of reviewing its specific target section. This ensures both that reviewing tasks are manageable for each review swarm, and that parallel swarms are properly coordinated.
4.   **Global synthesis and agentic grounding**: A dedicated synthesis agent consolidates the segment-level reports, and does final consistency checks between sections, rerunning logical checks if required. The agent further performs external grounding checks and tool calls as a final preventative measure against hallucinations.

## Universal verification and review: Beyond research papers

While Deep Review originated in academic paper reviews, long-context review is generalizable: reasoning mechanisms used to check whether a mathematical proof holds up in a research paper can also help surface logical gaps and inconsistencies in other types of documents, where claims must be backed by evidence. Therefore, Deep Review can be used to bring structured critique to a broader range of everyday workflows.

Users can now apply Deep Review to analyze complex documents across many domains. For instance, it can be run on:

*   **Design documents:** Catch unstated architectural assumptions, spot edge cases, and suggest concrete improvements.
*   **Presentations:** Ensure slide transitions flow logically and bulleted takeaways match visual charts.
*   **Legal and financial documents:** Check internal consistency across clauses and data tables, flag ambiguous terms or downstream consequences, and ground claims against supporting evidence.

## Deep Review meets Antigravity

We’re also introducing the [Teamwork Deep Document Review Pattern](https://antigravity.google/docs/teamwork/#execution-paths)**,** a document review implementation pattern inspired by Deep Review built into [Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/) using the [Teamwork multi-agent orchestration framework](https://antigravity.google/blog/teamwork-when-ai-becomes-a-research-partner). This pattern is designed systematically to evaluate research papers, manuscript drafts, and technical proposals using a multi-agent hierarchy with self-correction and segment-based rubrics. Antigravity users can invoke this pattern using the `/teamwork-preview` command.

## Making thorough, high-quality technical reviews widely accessible

Comprehensive pre-submission critique in computer science has generally depended on access to extensive review networks — like senior faculty, well-resourced academic laboratories, or extensive peer advisory networks. Providing reliable, automated logical verification can help many academics stress-test their assertions, identify avoidable flaws, refine and strengthen their documents based on verified foundations, and present their work in a review process with more confidence.

## Get started

We invite researchers, engineers, and creators everywhere to explore Deep Review:

*   **Try Deep Review:** Visit the [Google Research Portal](https://research.google/deepreview) to review your first documents.
*   **Integrate with the API:** Access programmatic verification in your continuous integration and drafting workflows using your [Gemini API key](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/api-key).
*   **Read the research:** Read the [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28277) to explore the underlying methodology and pilot evaluations.

## Conclusion and looking ahead

Given the utility it demonstrated during our pilot programs with academic conferences, we believe that tools like Deep Review will play a significant role across the peer review process in the coming years by empowering both authors and reviewers.

Moving forward, we are continuing to expand the platform’s capabilities. With the rollout of Gemini 4 Argon support, Deep Review’s underlying capabilities further improve, delivering even higher quality feedback and analysis to authors. Additionally, with multi-file support coming soon, users will also be able to run these same consistency checks across entire sets of related documents, spreadsheets, and exhibits simultaneously. We hope these advancements will make high-quality technical reviews more widely accessible for knowledge workers everywhere.

## Acknowledgments

_Deep Review is a collaborative effort across Google Research, Google DeepMind, and Google Cloud. We thank our core contributors and research collaborators — Santiago Balseiro, Taylan Cemgil, Tommaso D'Orsi, Kirk Draheim, Lindi Emoungu, Ayse Erduran, Palash Goyal, Caroline Hartnell, Shobana Kannan, Amy Keeling, Siyi Kou, Bridget Lee, Ian Li, Anoushka Mazumdar, Taylor Montgomery, Mouad Naciri, Uche Okonkwo, Mihir Parmar, Anthony Phalen, Rory Pilgrim, Sarah Presotto Post, Rob Tierney, Drew Tyler, Vishnu V., Vahab Mirrokni, Laura Vardoulakis, Johannes Welbl, David Woodruff, Yunhan Xu, Jinsung Yoon — as well as our executive sponsors Katherine Chou, Corinna Cortes, Burak Gokturk, Vahab Mirrokni, Tomas Pfister, Yossi Matias and the Program Chairs of STOC, ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR for their partnership._

kept.heading: GOOGLE HARNESS² FOR RECURSIVE SELF IMPROVEMENT (GITHUB REPO)
kept.blurb: Google Research's Harness² lets agents iteratively improve their prompts, tools, memory, and orchestration without changing model weights. It refines the harness for each task and then carries evidence-backed lessons forward to improve future tasks.
kept.article_text:
Title: GitHub - google-research/harness2

URL Source: https://github.com/google-research/harness2

Markdown Content:
### [![Image 1: Harness²](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/raw/main/assets/Harness2-wordmark.png)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/assets/Harness2-wordmark.png)  
 Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#----recursive-agent-harnessing-for-an-open-world)

[![Image 2: Paper](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/7c3b852da96a84347c73a3c750918bff5e8dadbda901570676b34d47e8c4219f/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f50617065722d61725869762d4541343333353f6c6f676f3d6172786976266c6f676f436f6c6f723d7768697465)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.14224)[![Image 3: Website](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/acdb42e32d126f3c3f3ca51e0cde3851fa71ee689b66b2174a9f57674bf3b404/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f576562736974652d6861726e657373322e6769746875622e696f2d3432383546343f6c6f676f3d676f6f676c656368726f6d65266c6f676f436f6c6f723d7768697465)](https://harness2.github.io/)[![Image 4: Benchmark guides](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/aa5839f0b4446acc25c139ad60945bc46d8830ab16e09e4ff048ffa8bc07c1c5/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f446f63732d42656e63686d61726b2532306775696465732d464242433034)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md)[![Image 5: License](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/85290ad5095410a2382190dcba74633fe0b35a5cede547d6a90e69cb80498c5e/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f4c6963656e73652d417061636865253230322e302d333441383533)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/LICENSE)

[![Image 6: Install, set up, and run JobBench: uv pip install -e '.[render]', harness2-setup jb, then harness2 --bench jb --k 1 --mode parallel. Click for prerequisites and commands.](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/raw/main/assets/harness2-setup.gif)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#jobbench)

A **harness** is the system around a model that enables it to act as an agent: prompts, tools, memory, skills, orchestration, and more. **Harnessing** is the process of optimizing that system.

Harness² is a plug-and-play framework for **recursive agent harnessing** in an open world, where agents encounter tasks unseen during harness design. It connects two levels of recursion while keeping model weights fixed:

*   **Task-level recursion** refines the execution harness for the current task through a contrastive **Propose–Probe–Compose** step: propose edits, probe their effects on the same task, and compose a refined harness from behavioral contrasts between executions, without ground-truth feedback.
*   **Harnessing-level recursion** updates a persistent _improvement harness_ with adopted harnesses and evidence-supported lessons from each task to guide future refinement.

[![Image 7: Harness² pipeline. Task-level recursion: an agent executor runs the initial harness, a harness editor proposes invariant and domain edits, candidate probes execute them, and a harness composer combines them into the final harness. Harnessing-level recursion: an experience reflector reflects on the step and updates the improvement harness used for the next task.](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/raw/main/assets/harness2_pipeline.png)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/assets/harness2_pipeline.png)

Across three professional benchmarks and four model–harness configurations, a single Harness² step improves GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, with gains of up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8 percentage points on LAB's partial pass rate. Increasing the task-level recursion budget brings further gains.

The release supports **parallel and sequential recursion**, **OpenCode and Codex executors**, and **JobBench, LAB, and WorkBuddy-Bench**.

## Video overview

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#video-overview)

harness2-video.mp4[Video 3](https://private-user-images.githubusercontent.com/63894509/669252828-76b10548-b14b-4c8f-9aa5-a93662df4d56.mp4?jwt=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..PiRjNj0rzZKuEiJVm5IW8RzGxSAQg8pympSwuA320Q8)

## Contents

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#contents)
*   [Video overview](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#video-overview)
*   [Harness components](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#harness-components)
*   [Install](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#install)
*   [Run a benchmark](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#run-a-benchmark)
*   [Experiments](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#experiments)
*   [Web access](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#web-access)
*   [Results and resume](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#results-and-resume)
*   [Citation](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#citation)
*   [Contributing](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#contributing)
*   [License](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#license)
*   [Disclaimer](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#disclaimer)

## Harness components

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#harness-components)
Harness² exposes eight editable components around the model: **system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, and plugins**. They control context construction, the tool interface, delegation, and behavior inside the tool loop.

[![Image 8: Eight harness components grouped by runtime role: system prompt, guardrails, memory, and skills construct context; tool guidance and scripts define the tool interface; subagents orchestrate delegated work; plugins control middleware.](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/raw/main/assets/components.png)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/assets/components.png)

## Install

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#install)
Use **Linux, Python 3.12, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)**. From the repository root:

uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[render]'
harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2

The local demo runs both recursion modes with deterministic editors and real Python executions. It requires no model credentials.

For model-backed benchmarks, install **Node.js 20+, the Google Cloud CLI**, and the [benchmark dependencies](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/SETUP.md#requirements). LAB needs Pandoc and Poppler; WorkBuddy-Bench needs Docker. Then configure your models:

cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env with your Vertex AI project and model IDs.
gcloud auth application-default login

See the [setup guide](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/SETUP.md) for model settings, authentication alternatives, and the [Codex executor](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/SETUP.md#codex-executor).

## Run a benchmark

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#run-a-benchmark)
The following example installs LAB and runs one task, then evaluates and reports its result. Model-backed runs incur API costs; start with a small task selection.

harness2-setup lab
harness2-check --bench lab
harness2 --bench lab --k 1 --mode parallel \
  --only-domains antitrust-competition --max-tasks 1
harness2-judge --bench lab --k 1 --mode parallel
harness2-report --bench lab --k 1 --mode parallel

Sequential recursion runs the same commands with `--mode sequential`. `--k` is the task-level recursion budget; see [Experiments](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#experiments). Judging and reporting must use the same benchmark, executor, subset, `--k`, `--mode`, and seed as the refinement run. Add `--dry-run` to `harness2` to preview task selection without model calls.

| Benchmark | Tasks | Install | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JobBench | Professional work | `harness2-setup jb` | [JobBench](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#jobbench) |
| LAB | Legal work | `harness2-setup lab` | [LAB](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#lab) |
| WorkBuddy-Bench | Office, web, and code | `harness2-setup wb` | [WorkBuddy](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md#workbuddy-bench) |

Choose one benchmark per command. WorkBuddy also takes `--subset office`, `--subset web`, or `--subset code` on every command after setup. The [benchmark guides](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/BENCHMARKS.md) cover each one's data, domains, and grading.

## Experiments

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#experiments)
Scale task-level recursion in two ways: **parallel recursion** explores multiple candidate harnesses and composes refinements from their execution evidence; **sequential recursion** carries the refined harness and accumulated evidence through successive Propose–Probe–Compose steps.

[![Image 9: Two ways to scale task-level recursion. Parallel: probe k general and k domain-specific candidate harnesses, then produce k compositions from the shared evidence. Sequential: carry the refined harness and accumulated evidence through k Propose–Probe–Compose steps.](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/raw/main/assets/harness2_recursion_modes.png)](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/assets/harness2_recursion_modes.png)

_Parallel recursion explores wider; sequential recursion refines deeper._

| Option | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `--k 1` | One Propose–Probe–Compose step |
| `--k K --mode parallel` | Probe `K` general and `K` domain-specific candidates, then produce `K` compositions |
| `--k K --mode sequential` | Refine the harness through `K` successive steps |
| `--substrate cx` | Use Codex instead of the default OpenCode executor |

After each task, harnessing-level recursion retains the adopted harness and evidence-supported lessons to guide future refinement. See the [experiment guide](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/EXPERIMENTS.md) for task selection, concurrency, reproducibility, and baseline comparisons.

## Web access

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#web-access)
Executor network access is unrestricted, and Codex runs with its sandbox disabled. Public benchmark rubrics may be accessible online. Before evaluation, configure [network restrictions](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/EXPERIMENTS.md#web-access) to prevent access to benchmark answers and grading criteria.

## Results and resume

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#results-and-resume)
Results are saved under `runs/`, organized by benchmark and subset where applicable. They include task summaries, deliverables, adopted harnesses, reflection notes, and evaluation results.

Repeat the same command to resume. Use a new `HARNESS2_RUNS_DIR` when changing models or task selection. See [results and resume](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/docs/EXPERIMENTS.md#results-and-resume) for details; each command also supports `--help`.

## Citation

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#citation)

@article{xu2026harness2,
  title   = {Harness$^2$: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World},
  author  = {Xu, Ruiyao and Chen, Yanfei and CuiZhu, Zhongying and Dalvi Mishra, Bhavana and Ming, Yifei and Yu, Han and Han, Rujun and Lee, Chen-Yu and Pfister, Tomas},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.14224},
  year    = {2026},
  url     = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14224}
}

## Contributing

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#contributing)
See [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

## License

[](https://github.com/google-research/harness2#license)
Harness² is licensed under [Apache 2.0](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/LICENSE). Third-party code under [`third_party/`](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/third_party/README.md), benchmarks, and datasets retain their upstream licenses; see [third-party notices](https://github.com/google-research/harness2/blob/main/dependencies/README.md).
