kept.heading: ROUTERS ARE A NEW AI PRIMITIVE (13 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Routers have emerged as a new primitive of the AI stack. They promise to handle the complexity of model management and help companies benefit from new models without revisiting model selection across every application themselves. Every router shares the same fundamental design, but they differ in how they decide. This post provides an independent comparison of current routers and looks at how today's routers compare with single models on quality and cost.
kept.article_text:
Title: Routers Are a New AI Primitive

URL Source: https://www.vals.ai/blogs/routers-new-ai-primitive

Published Time: 2026-10-14

Markdown Content:
## Partners

[![Image 1: fireworks](https://www.vals.ai/Partners/fireworks.svg)](https://fireworks.ai/)

[![Image 2: notdiamond](https://www.vals.ai/Partners/notdiamond.svg)](https://www.notdiamond.ai/)

[![Image 3: openrouter](https://www.vals.ai/Partners/openrouter.svg)](https://openrouter.ai/)

[![Image 4: router-by-ramp](https://www.vals.ai/Partners/router-by-ramp.svg)](https://ramp.com/router)

Every few months, frontier models unlock harder problems and new domains. No company can afford to sit that out, but few can afford frontier prices on every request. Which model should handle each piece of work, and when does the performance of frontier models justify their cost?

At Vals, we evaluate models from across the major labs on their ability to carry out complex work across domains such as finance, software engineering, law, and tax. The [Vals Index](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vals_index) brings these evaluations together to measure AI’s potential economic impact. From that vantage point, the frontier is jagged: five different models hold the top spots on the Index’s eight benchmarks, and no model ranks in the top three on all of them. Choosing only one model means compromising performance on some tasks.

On real work, the frontier is jagged
The five models that hold the top spots on the Index’s eight benchmarks, and their rank on each, out of 48 models.

| Benchmark | Argon Gemini 4 Argon Google | Sonnet 5.5 Claude Sonnet 5.5 Anthropic | Opus 5.5 Claude Opus 5.5 Anthropic | Fable 5.1 Claude Fable 5.1 Anthropic | Muse Spark 1.2 Muse Spark 1.2 Meta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vals Index Vals Index (overall) | #1 | #2 | #3 | #4 | #33 |
| Finance Agent Finance Agent v2 | #1 | #11 | #10 | #8 | #3 |
| Excel Modeling Excel Modeling | #4 | #3 | #2 | #1 | #34 |
| Tax Agent Tax Agent Bench | #2 | #5 | #11 | #1 | #39 |
| Terminal-Bench Terminal-Bench 4.0 | #6 | #2 | #1 | #4 | #40 |
| Vibe Code Vibe Code Bench | #2 | #1 | #5 | #6 | #25 |
| Code Migration Code Migration | #2 | #1 | #3 | #8 | #34 |
| Legal Research Legal Research Bench | #4 | #10 | #6 | #1 | #20 |
| HLAB Harvey’s Legal Agent (HLAB) | #5 | #35 | #33 | #25 | #1 |

*    #1 
*    Top 10% 
*    Top 25% 
*    Top half 
*    Bottom half 

Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 rank second and third overall but 35th and 33rd on Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, which Muse Spark 1.2 tops from 33rd overall. Vals Index v2.1, published scores.

The range of models to choose from is continuously and rapidly expanding. This past month alone, ten developers released 16 language models tracked by Vals. Each release raises another set of decisions for companies: which workloads would benefit, whether the improvement is worth the cost, and whether it should replace a model already in production. Sticking with one model can mean missing better options; maintaining separate model choices across many workflows is an operational burden requiring continuous engineering and evaluation effort.

Routers have emerged as a new primitive of the AI stack, promising to manage that complexity and help companies benefit from new models without revisiting model selection across every application themselves. The value is both better use of today’s models and a way to keep benefiting from progress across labs.

Every router shares the same fundamental design. It sits in front of a pool of models and, for each request, decides which one should answer, right-sizing the intelligence to the task by weighing quality, cost, and latency. Where routers differ is in how they decide. Some judge the prompt itself, such as the type of task or how hard it looks. Others draw on external signals like benchmark scores or usage statistics. Increasingly, routers make this call at every step of an agent’s work rather than once per task.

An ensemble of models, used well, can beat any single model on the frontier. To measure by how much, we calculated the performance of an oracle router, one that picks the perfect model for every task in hindsight. **On the Vals Index, that oracle would beat the best single model by 14 points while costing about 40% less.**

Perfect hindsight is impossible, of course, but it shows the full potential of choosing the right model for each task. The real question is how much of that potential today’s routers capture in practice, and existing benchmarks weren’t built to answer it. Most academic router benchmarks score a single choice on a single public question, often from datasets frontier models have long since saturated. When every model in the pool gets the answer right, a router that always picks the cheapest one looks perfect. But routers today are asked to do something much harder, choosing a model at every step of agent work that can run for hours.

Router providers have begun publishing serious evaluations of their own, and we think the natural next step is an independent comparison, with every router run through the same harness on private, long-horizon tasks across real professional domains. Vals has always set out to chart the frontier of AI performance, which is why we’re now measuring how today’s routers compare with single models on quality and cost, with the task-level oracle as a reference point.

## From isolated prompts to agent workflows

Academic benchmarks have established a foundation for evaluating model routers. [RouterBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12031) (Hu et al., 2024) helped establish an early framework using precomputed model outcomes. [RouterArena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00202) (Lu et al., 2025) broadened comparisons across domains and difficulty levels, while [LLMRouterBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.07206) (Li et al., 2026) brought routing methods into a shared framework that includes tool-use and software tasks. More recently, [TwinRouterBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18859) (Yang et al., 2026) introduced live coding-agent evaluation, selecting a model at every call and measuring task success and actual API spend.

Today’s agents complete complex work over dozens of steps, where each routing decision affects the context and choices that follow. A cheaper model may save money on one call but introduce an error that takes several more calls to recover from, while a weak routing decision can derail the rest of the task. Predicting how a task will decompose into subtasks is another challenge, and any decision to switch models must account for the cost of losing the existing prompt cache. For long-running sessions, switching to a cheaper model does not automatically bring cost savings.

Isolated prompts miss these consequences, and TwinRouterBench’s live evaluation remains focused on coding. Difficulty matters too: Stanford’s [2025 AI Index](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2025-ai-index-report/technical-performance) identifies benchmarks such as MMLU and GSM8K as saturated, making them less revealing of the accuracy sacrificed for cheaper models. Newer benchmarks address parts of this gap, but public tasks still carry a risk of prior exposure.

The next step is to bring these requirements together: challenging, realistic work across professional domains, live execution that exposes the consequences of each routing decision, and private test data to reduce contamination risk.

## What router providers are already measuring

Router providers are also evaluating how their systems perform in practice. [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/benchmarks/routers) compares its own and third-party routers against single models on quality, time, and cost.

The way an agent session unfolds affects its cost. [Fireworks](https://fireworks.ai/blog/introducing-firerouter-with-opus) evaluated FireRouter through randomized A/B tests on live sessions, accounting for the cost of lost prompt caching when switching models. [Not Diamond’s coding-agent evaluation methodology](https://www.notdiamond.ai/blog/interactive-benchmarks-a-new-methodology-for-evaluating-model-routing) uses simulated users to model long sessions and pauses between user interactions, capturing the costs of growing context and cache expiration.

Benchmarks also shape routing decisions themselves. [Ramp’s Benchmark Routing strategy](https://ramp.com/blog/router-launch) lets customers select and weight benchmarks, then routes requests to the model with the highest weighted score. The relevance of those benchmarks to the customer’s work therefore matters to the routing decision.

These efforts provide useful evidence about router performance. An independent comparison can build on them by running router products through the same harness on shared, private tasks across professional domains, with each product’s configuration documented.

## Evaluating routers on the Vals Index

The Vals Index was built to measure the impact of AI on real-world agentic tasks—the very things routers are now aiming to optimize.

The Vals Index is **agentic and long-horizon**. All eight components evaluate tool-using agents spanning finance, coding, legal, and tax work: [Finance Agent v2](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/fabv2), the [Excel Modeling Benchmark](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/emb), [Terminal-Bench 4.0](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/terminal-bench-4), [Vibe Code Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/vibe-code), [Code Migration](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/code-migration), [Legal Research Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/legal_research), Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark ([HLAB](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/hlab)), and [Tax Agent Bench](https://www.vals.ai/benchmarks/tax_agent_bench). Many of these tasks are long: the median Terminal-Bench 4.0 task is estimated at four hours of expert work, each Excel Modeling task takes an expert five hours or more, and on Legal Research Bench, some models work for upwards of an hour on certain tasks.

The Index is **expert-written and mostly private**. Six of its eight benchmarks are private, and their tasks, answers, and grading rubrics are written by people who do this work professionally: financial analysts for the finance benchmarks, practicing lawyers for Legal Research Bench, and tax professionals for Tax Agent Bench. Coding tasks are graded by running tests against what the agent actually built. Our private test set has never been released, and our evaluations are run with ZDR (Zero Data Retention) policies in place, meaning that model providers cannot retain or train on our prompts.

Importantly, **no single model leads every component**. The model that tops Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark ranks 40th on Terminal-Bench 4.0, different models lead other components, and of the top two models, the second costs about 36% more per task than the first. This kind of spread is the opportunity routing can exploit.

Finally, the Index is **continuously updated**. We regularly evaluate frontier models on it with consistent harnesses, and retire components as they saturate. This means every router can be compared against single-model baselines run in the same harness, along with an oracle that keeps pace with the models being routed between.

Choosing a model to answer a trivia question is a very different problem from choosing a model for every step of a corporate tax research task, and we think router evaluations should reflect that. Concretely, good router evaluations put each router through live, end-to-end agent runs. The router takes the place of a model in the same harnesses and is consulted on every model call, allowing it to retain the current model or select another as the task unfolds. Prompts, tools, and graders stay fixed. Each router runs as shipped, with its default model pool and settings, and that configuration is documented for every run. Task outcomes, cost per task, cache usage, and completion time are compared against baselines run in the same harness (the best and the cheapest single model in the router’s own pool), with the task-level oracle as a reference point.

## Beyond picking a single model

If routers are judged primarily on isolated public questions, evaluations will reward a narrower set of capabilities than production agentic work requires. As routing increasingly determines what AI work costs, we believe it deserves to be measured on that work, with the same care as the models themselves.

That is what our router evaluation is designed to do, and we will publish results on a public leaderboard soon. If you build a router and are interested in having it evaluated, [get in touch with us here](mailto:contact@vals.ai).

## References

kept.heading: IT AIN'T AGI UNTIL H100S GO FOR $30 AN HOUR (7 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Stratospheric GPU prices will be one of the easiest indicators of AGI to monitor and trade on. A 10x price jump in the price of AI compute will be the clearest sign that agents can finally outperform humans at most economically valuable work. The price would need to rise to an estimated $30 per H100-hour to reach this point. Supply will always be limited to the amount of available compute in the world, so something has to give.
kept.article_text:
Title: It Ain't AGI Until H100s Go for $30 an Hour | Kyle Corbitt

URL Source: https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Nvidia H100 rental price over the past year, about $3.50 an hour, with a hand-drawn line sweeping up to $30 an hour labeled AGI](https://corbt.com/blog-images/h100-agi-chart.png)

_Kyle Corbitt with Claude Opus_

## Sparks of AGI

Greg Brockman [claimed](https://fortune.com/2026/09/03/openai-debuts-gpt-6-astra-computer-use-greg-brockman-says-start-of-agi/) that GPT-6 Astra marks the start of the “AGI era.” We may be in the AGI era, but if AGI means an agent that can “[outperform humans at most economically valuable work](https://openai.com/charter/)” it isn’t here yet. You’ll know it is when the price of AI compute jumps 10x from where it is now.

I’ve included a calculator below to visualize my assumptions of where the supply and demand of compute equalize based on different assumptions about the world. I’ll walk through them below.

Demand

An AGI agent will be as productive as a worker earning

$

an hour.

Supply

An AGI-complete agent needs

×

as much compute as

.

Anthropic

's current inference margin is

%, with compute costing

$

per H100-hour.

At today's

$3.52

, AGI agents would want about

28

× more compute than exists. The price rises until demand falls back to the supply.

1 Agent-hour at list price Opus 5.5 at $8.21 × 1× compute$8.21

2 Compute cost of an agent-hour$8.21 × (1 − 50% margin)$4.11

3 H100-hours per agent-hour$4.11 ÷ $3.52 per H100-hour 1.17

4 Agents each H100 can run 1 ÷ 1.17 0.86

5 What an H100-hour is worth at AGI 0.86 agents × $35.00 wage$30.01

## Tokenomics with AGI Characteristics

In October 2026 you can rent an H100 for about [$3.52 an hour](https://getdeploying.com/gpu-price-trends). That’s up 18% on the year, which is surprising since old compute usually becomes less valuable over time. But it’s nothing compared to where prices are going as we start deploying real AGI.

Let’s do some basic math:

**Supply:** By [AI 2040’s estimates](https://ai-2040.com/econ-explorer/model-explanation), there’s enough compute today to run AGI agents that could replace about 95 million full-time workers.[1](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-1)

**Demand:** The top 95 million earners in the world make at least $35 an hour.[2](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-2) So an AGI that can really do one of these jobs must be worth at least $35 an hour. (Many white-collar jobs in today’s economy pay far more. That’s just the floor price!)

How much compute will one of these agents use? The most capable publicly available model today is Claude Opus 5.5, which tops the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://officechai.com/ai/claude-opus-5-5-creates-5-point-lead-over-gpt-6-astra-jumps-to-top-spot-on-artificial-analysis-intelligence-index/). Run as a full-time agent, it costs about $8.21 an hour at unsubsidized API prices.[3](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-3) The cost of reaching a given level of capability has been [falling 5–10x a year](https://epoch.ai/gradient-updates/how-persistent-is-the-inference-cost-burden), and we’re already close to the AGI threshold. So it’s reasonable to assume an AGI-complete agent will run on a hardware footprint no larger than Opus 5.5’s today.

Let’s further assume Anthropic spends half of that $8.21 on compute[4](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-4) and is paying near-market prices.[5](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-5) At $3.52 an hour, that’s 1.17 H100-hours for each hour of agent time. In other words, a production deployment can support about 0.86 agents running constantly for each H100-equivalent GPU in it.[6](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-6)

If each of these agents becomes capable enough to truly replace a white-collar worker, but **supply is still limited** by the amount of available compute in the world, something has to give. We already know demand for these workers is high: at least $35 an hour. With supply fixed, either (a) compute gets rationed (frontier labs stop selling externally entirely), or (b) prices rise until supply and demand balance.

How far would the price need to rise? On the conservative assumptions above, to about **$30 per H100-hour**: 0.86 agents at $35 an hour. If we make less conservative assumptions, such as that Anthropic’s API margins are well above 50%, that AGI only requires the same hardware as a cheaper model like GPT-6.1 Sol, or that employers will pay what a worker actually costs them with taxes and benefits, you can make a compelling case that prices will rise as high as **$75 per H100-hour**.[7](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fn-7)

Stratospheric GPU prices won’t be the weirdest thing we see on the way to AGI. But they may be one of the easiest to monitor and trade on.

## Footnotes

1.   **Workers the compute could replace.** AI 2040 estimates about 20M H100-equivalents of AI compute at the start of 2026, growing about 3.3x a year ([AI 2040](https://ai-2040.com/econ-explorer/model-explanation)). That’s roughly 50M by October. Big AI companies spend roughly half their compute on R&D ([AI 2040](https://ai-2040.com/)), leaving about 25M to serve customers. At 0.86 agents per H100, running around the clock (8,760 hours a year, against 2,000 for a full-time worker), that’s about 95M full-time workers. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-1)

2.   **The wage floor.** US figures are measured: among people who worked at least 40 weeks in 2023, 27.9M earned $100,000 or more (about $50 an hour) and 75.8M earned $50,000 or more (about $25 an hour) ([DQYDJ, from Census CPS data](https://dqydj.com/salary-percentile-calculator-for-the-united-states-in-2024/)). I couldn’t find a global count. I estimate another 20–40M people outside the US earn $50 an hour or more, and assume the same shape below that. That puts the 95-millionth highest-paid worker at about $31–40 an hour. All earners stand in for white-collar workers here. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-2)

3.   **Cost per agent-hour.** I assume an agent reads 1,000 input tokens and writes 80 output tokens a second, with 90% of input served from cache: 288,000 output and 3.6M input tokens an hour. At [Opus 5.5 list prices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) ($20 per million output tokens, $0.20 cache reads, $5 cache writes), that’s $5.76 + $0.65 + $1.80 = $8.21. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-3)

4.   **Margins.** This is a wildly conservative assumption. SemiAnalysis estimates Anthropic’s API gross margin is above 80%, and its margin across the whole business is in the mid-60s even including heavily subsidized subscription plans ([Crypto Briefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/anthropic-inference-margins-semianalysis-88-percent/), [KuCoin, relaying the WSJ](https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/semianalysis-anthropic-q3-2026-profit-to-exceed-10-billion)). Higher margins make each H100 more valuable. At 80% margins one H100 runs 2.1 agents. The fleet then covers about 240M workers, reaching down to a wage floor near $19 an hour, and an H100-hour is worth about $41. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-4)

5.   **Market prices.** We don’t know Anthropic’s blended cost of compute, but based on its xAI deal it may in fact be paying above-market prices to secure large blocks of supply on short notice. That deal reportedly costs about $1.25B a month for Colossus 1 ([Let’s Data Science](https://letsdatascience.com/blog/anthropic-pays-musk-1-25-billion-month-colossus)), which by my rough math is $6–7 per H100-equivalent hour. If Anthropic is paying that much and _still_ getting good inference margins, that makes my math even stronger. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-5)

6.   **“H100” is just a convenient price unit.** It means compute that rents for $3.52 an hour today. Anthropic serves on TPUs, Trainium and newer Nvidia chips. A literal H100 may rise less than the newest chips. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-6)

7.   **The less conservative case.** More agents per H100 means the fleet replaces more workers and reaches further down the wage ladder, so I lower the floor using the distribution in note 2. [GPT-6.1 Sol](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gpt-6-1-sol) ($2 per million input tokens, $0.10 cached, $10 output) costs $3.92 per agent-hour. At a 50% compute share that’s 1.8 agents per H100, a fleet of about 200M workers and a floor near $22 an hour. Employers’ full cost is about 1.43 times wages, since wages and salaries are 70% of private-industry compensation costs ([BLS](https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/compensation-costs-for-private-industry-workers-averaged-46-89-per-hour-worked-in-june-2026.htm)). Counting full employer cost, Opus at 80% margins gives about $58 per H100-hour, Sol at 50% about $57, and Sol at 80% about $75. [↩](https://corbt.com/posts/it-aint-agi-until-h100s-go-for-30-an-hour#user-content-fnref-7)

kept.heading: PUSH-BASED KV TRANSFER TO IMPROVE TTFT AND TPOT FOR DISAGGREGATED INFERENCE IN VLLM (15 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path, resulting in improved application responsiveness, particularly at high request rates.
kept.article_text:
Title: Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM

URL Source: https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector

Published Time: 2026-10-14

Markdown Content:
[vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm) is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. [Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_prefill/) runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).

One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) [connector](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/nixl_connector_usage/), which moves KV blocks over RDMA-capable interconnects such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ([AWS EFA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa.html), the low latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On [supported instance types](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa.html#efa-instance-types), AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA, enabling NIXL to transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is **pull-based**: After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.

![Image 1: Pull-mode timeline: router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to first token.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/pull-mode-timeline.png)

Pull-mode timeline: router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to first token.

This post introduces a **push-based** NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. For customers running disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, this can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.

In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30% better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the [Performance data](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector#performance-data) section) for Qwen3-32B model; results depend on workload and configuration.

We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an AWS p5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.

## Push-based KV transfer

### Architecture overview

Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:

1.   **It removes the serialization of the pull model** by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer's blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side identifier-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
2.   **It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance.** That setup — preparing the NIXL descriptors and submitting the transfer — runs on the prefill side and on a background thread, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.

The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.

The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance, which registers its target blocks up front; the prefill instance, which matches each request and issues the transfer; and a dedicated background thread that carries the KV write off the engine's forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.

![Image 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture overview: the decode instance registers its blocks with the prefill instance, which pushes KV to the decode instance with a NIXL WRITE.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/push-architecture.png)

Push-based KV transfer architecture overview: the decode instance registers its blocks with the prefill instance, which pushes KV to the decode instance with a NIXL WRITE.

### Implementation details

The protocol has three logical steps.

**1. Registration (decode side).** When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.

**2. Rendezvous (prefill side).** The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request's blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by identifier, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.

**3. Transfer (prefill side).** Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder's registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it, and treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.

### Threading model

The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.

The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request's KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.

![Image 3: Sequence diagram of one request through the push path, showing the main-loop and background-thread handoffs on the prefill and decode instances.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/push-request-flow.png)

Sequence diagram of one request through the push path, showing the main-loop and background-thread handoffs on the prefill and decode instances.

### Timing comparison: Pull vs push

The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.

![Image 4: Timing comparison of pull and push modes on the path to first token.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/timing-pull-vs-push.png)

Timing comparison of pull and push modes on the path to first token.

The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.

## Performance data

For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse decode node's local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.

The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates 1–8 QPS. At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.

![Image 5: Four-panel TTFT comparison of push and pull KV transfer for Qwen3-32B on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA. Test configuration: 1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, and prefix caching disabled on the Decode node.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/ttft-push-vs-pull.png)

Four-panel TTFT comparison of push and pull KV transfer for Qwen3-32B on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA. Test configuration: 1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, and prefix caching disabled on the Decode node.

This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is never starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.

![Image 6: Four-panel TPOT comparison of push and pull KV transfer for Qwen3-32B on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA. Test configuration: 1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, and prefix caching disabled on the Decode node.](https://vllm.ai/blog-assets/figures/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/tpot-push-vs-pull.png)

Four-panel TPOT comparison of push and pull KV transfer for Qwen3-32B on Amazon EC2 P5en instances with EFA. Test configuration: 1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, and prefix caching disabled on the Decode node.

## How to run benchmark

To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the [Reproducing our results](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector#appendix-reproducing-our-results) guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.

## Conclusion

In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30% improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use `NixlPushConnector` instead of `NixlConnector`.

Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, allowing users to select the approach that best fits their deployment.

As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations; we have opened a pull request ([#45211](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/45211)) to explore this.

*   [vLLM disaggregated serving guide](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/disagg_prefill.html)
*   [AWS EFA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa.html)
*   [Push-mode NIXL KV connector](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/nixl_kv_push_connector/)

## Acknowledgements

We thank the vLLM community for their support in maintaining this feature.

## Appendix: Reproducing our results

The topology is two p5en GPU nodes (prefill on `:8100`, decode on `:8200`) with EFA enabled, plus a third smaller node that runs the proxy and the benchmark client. Three scripts ship with this post: [`serve_pd.sh`](https://vllm.ai/assets/repro/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/serve_pd.sh) launches either leg in either mode, [`run_sweep.sh`](https://vllm.ai/assets/repro/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/run_sweep.sh) drives the sweep, and [`cleanup.sh`](https://vllm.ai/assets/repro/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/cleanup.sh) tears everything down. [`plot_push_vs_pull.py`](https://vllm.ai/assets/repro/2026-10-14-nixl-push-connector/plot_push_vs_pull.py) redraws the two figures above from the result JSONs.

### Test environment

Both GPU nodes were configured identically:

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Instance type | `p5en.48xlarge` (8x NVIDIA H200), one for prefill and one for decode |
| Region / AZ | `ap-south-1` (Mumbai), `ap-south-1b` (AZ ID `aps1-az3`), both nodes in the same AZ |
| Placement | No cluster placement group; both instances launched into a targeted On-Demand Capacity Reservation, default tenancy |
| AMI | Public AWS ParallelCluster 3.14.2 image for Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, `aws-parallelcluster-3.14.2-ubuntu-2404-lts-hvm-x86_64-202602121713` (`ami-0133f195033a4baae` in `ap-south-1`; AMI IDs differ by region). It ships kernel `6.14.0-1018-aws`, NVIDIA driver 570, and CUDA 12.8, so upgrade the driver, CUDA toolkit, and EFA installer to the versions below. |
| OS / kernel | Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, `6.14.0-1018-aws` |
| NVIDIA driver / CUDA | Driver `580.126.16` (CUDA 13.0 driver API); CUDA toolkit 13.0 |
| EFA interfaces | 16 per instance, one per network card (cards 0-15, all interface type `efa`), 200 Gb/s each for 3.2 Tb/s total. 8 interfaces sit on each NUMA node, and each GPU shares a PCIe switch with 2 of them. |
| EFA software | EFA installer `1.50.0`, EFA kernel module `3.3.0g`, libfabric `2.6.0amzn1.0`, rdma-core `64.0amzn0` |

**EFA device selection by NIXL.** The LIBFABRIC backend opens all 16 EFA devices as rails with the `efa` provider. It then registers each GPU's KV cache only on the 2 rails that share that GPU's PCIe switch, so every transfer stays PCIe-local. No NIXL or libfabric device overrides were set; this is the default selection. To confirm it on your own nodes, launch the servers with `NIXL_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` and check the registration lines:

`grep -E "Created rail [0-9]+ \(device=|mapped to rail" server.log`

### 1. Provision the nodes

Install the EFA userspace stack on both GPU nodes and confirm the provider is present. We used installer `1.50.0`:

```
curl -O https://efa-installer.amazonaws.com/aws-efa-installer-1.50.0.tar.gz
tar -xf aws-efa-installer-1.50.0.tar.gz && cd aws-efa-installer
sudo ./efa_installer.sh -y
fi_info --version         # libfabric 2.6.0amzn1.0
fi_info -p efa            # verify the EFA provider is present
```

The two GPU nodes must reach each other on `8100`/`8200` and on the NIXL side channel (`5600`).

### 2. Install vLLM and NIXL

On both GPU nodes:

```
python3.12 -m venv ~/vllm_env && source ~/vllm_env/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install vllm==0.29.0      # any build that includes the NIXL push connector
pip install nixl==1.4.1       # NIXL with the libfabric/EFA backend
```

On the proxy node (no GPU runtime needed):

`pip install vllm aiohttp fastapi uvicorn pandas datasets`

### 3. Download the model

```
export HF_HOME=/shared/huggingface     # a large shared volume
hf download Qwen/Qwen3-32B
```

### 4. Launch the P/D pair

Run `serve_pd.sh` once per GPU node. The only difference between the two modes is `kv_connector`: `NixlConnector` for pull, `NixlPushConnector` for push. Ports, engine IDs, roles, and ranks stay the same.

```
# on the prefill node
PREFILL_IP=<PREFILL_IP> DECODE_IP=<DECODE_IP> ROLE=prefill MODE=pull ./serve_pd.sh
# on the decode node
PREFILL_IP=<PREFILL_IP> DECODE_IP=<DECODE_IP> ROLE=decode  MODE=pull ./serve_pd.sh
```

Which expands to, on the prefill side:

```
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-32B --served-model-name Qwen --dtype bfloat16 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 32768 --max-num-seqs 8 --port 8100 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"NixlConnector","kv_buffer_device":"cuda",
    "kv_role":"kv_producer","engine_id":"prefill-engine-001","kv_rank":0,
    "kv_parallel_size":2,"kv_connector_extra_config":{"backends":["LIBFABRIC"]}}'
```

The decode server adds `--no-enable-prefix-caching`, which forces every request to fetch full KV from prefill — exactly what we are measuring. With caching on, overlapping prompts could hit the decode node's local cache and skip the P->D transfer, giving misleading numbers. Wait for both `/health` endpoints to return 200 before benchmarking.

### 5. Run the sweep

The benchmark script lives in [#57567](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/57567); it picks the proxy that matches the mode (`disagg_proxy_demo.py` for pull, `disagg_proxy_pushconnector_demo.py` for push) and drives it with `vllm bench serve`.

```
git clone https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git ~/vllm && cd ~/vllm
git fetch origin pull/57567/head:pd-bench && git checkout pd-bench
export VLLM_SRC=~/vllm
 
VLLM_SRC=~/vllm PREFILL_IP=<PREFILL_IP> DECODE_IP=<DECODE_IP> \
  MODE=pull ./run_sweep.sh
```

Then stop both servers, relaunch step 4 with `MODE=push` on each node, and rerun the sweep with `MODE=push`. Push mode additionally needs the prefill instance's NIXL coordinates (`PREFILL_ENGINE_ID`, `PREFILL_KV_HOST`, `PREFILL_SIDE_CHANNEL_PORT`, `PREFILL_TP_SIZE`, `PREFILL_PP_SIZE`) so the proxy can tell the decode node where to register; `run_sweep.sh` fills these in from the defaults used above. Keep `QPS_LIST`, `INPUT_LENS`, and `OUTPUT_LENS` identical across the two runs, and make sure `PREFILL_TP_SIZE` matches the prefill server's actual tensor-parallel size.

`results/` holds `<mode>_qps<q>_in<in>_out<out>_iter<i>.json` (plus `.log`) with per-run TTFT, ITL, throughput, and end-to-end latency. To redraw the figures:

```
python plot_push_vs_pull.py --results-dir ./results --metric ttft
python plot_push_vs_pull.py --results-dir ./results --metric tpot
```

### Troubleshooting

*   **Server crashes right after the first request** — the mode doesn't match the connector. Pull needs `NixlConnector`; push needs `NixlPushConnector`, on both P and D.
*   **`Backend 404: model ... does not exist`** — `SERVED_MODEL_NAME` doesn't match the servers' `--served-model-name` (`Qwen`).
*   **Proxy readiness times out** — confirm the proxy for the chosen mode exists under `$VLLM_SRC/examples/disaggregated/disaggregated_serving/`, and that both P and D `/health` return 200.
*   **NIXL handshake or transfer errors** — verify EFA (`fi_info -p efa`), that the side-channel port (`5600`) is open between P and D, and that `PREFILL_TP_SIZE` matches the prefill server's tensor-parallel size.

### Cleanup

```
./cleanup.sh proxy      # on the proxy / benchmark driver node
./cleanup.sh server     # on each GPU node
```

Then follow the AWS EC2 user guide to terminate the instances.

kept.heading: LING-3.1-FLASH (HUGGING FACE REPO)
kept.blurb: Ling-3.1-flash is a native hybrid reasoning model designed for complex, real-world tasks with 560 billion total parameters, 25 billion active parameters per token, and a one-million-token context window.
kept.article_text:
Title: inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash · Hugging Face

URL Source: https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash

Published Time: Wed, 10 Sep 2025 21:05:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
![Image 1](https://mdn.alipayobjects.com/huamei_qa8qxu/afts/img/A*4QxcQrBlTiAAAAAAQXAAAAgAemJ7AQ/original)

🤗 [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI) | 🤖 [ModelScope](https://modelscope.cn/organization/inclusionAI) | 🐙 [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash)

## [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#introduction) Introduction

We're introducing **Ling-3.1-flash**, an upgraded native hybrid reasoning model designed for complex, real-world tasks. With **560B** total parameters, **25B** active parameters per token, and a **1M-token context window**, Ling-3.1-flash builds upon Ling-3.0-flash with improvements in architecture and performance on real-world tasks.

With stronger real-world capabilities, Ling-3.1-flash shows improvements across a range of real-world tasks, including general-purpose agents, search, office productivity, and software engineering. It demonstrates strong performance on benchmarks such as **GDPVal-AA V2.1, HealthBench Professional, FrontierSWE, and Terminal-Bench 4.0**, covering office tasks, healthcare, software engineering, and terminal-based tool use. The model also shows improvements in specialized domains such as finance and materials science.

![Image 2: Ling-3.1-flash performance overview](https://intranetproxy.alipay.com/skylark/lark/0/2026/png/23157180/1791987400376-c61f96e8-41a7-4377-80c2-173a01132dc5.png)

## [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#model-overview) Model Overview

The table and diagram below summarize the model’s specifications and architecture.

| Architecture | Hybrid-linear MoE |
| --- | --- |
| Parameter Scale | Total 560B, Activated 25B |
| Transformer Layers | 63 KDA + 9 Gated MLA (7:1) |
| Number of Dense Layers | 4 |
| Number of Routed Experts | 512 |
| Number of Shared Experts | 1 |
| Number of Activated Experts | 8 |
| Attention Heads | 64 |
| Hidden Size | 4096 |
| Expert Intermediate Size | 1280 |
| Dense Intermediate Size | 10240 |
| Vocabulary Size | 157184 |

![Image 3: Ling-3.1-flash model architecture](https://intranetproxy.alipay.com/skylark/lark/0/2026/png/23157180/1791966963600-8408d222-3dc1-43c6-87af-f4f905a681db.png)

## [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#evaluation) Evaluation

We have conducted a comprehensive evaluation of Ling-3.1-flash across multiple authoritative benchmarks. **Ling-3.1-flash** performs strongly on representative coding/agentic benchmarks including **Terminal-Bench 4.0**, **SWE-bench Pro**, **FrontierSWE**, **GDPVal-AA V2.1**, **Automationbench**, **MCP-Atlas**, and **SkillsBench**, among others. In practice, Ling-3.1-flash delivers a strong user experience across **Claude Code**, **Kilo Code**, **Qwen Code**, **Hermes Agent**, **OpenClaw**, and other frameworks. Beyond agentic tasks, Ling-3.1-flash performs strongly on real-world tasks across **STEM**, **healthcare**, and **finance**.

We also introduce **LingCode**, a harness built on the open-source coding agent Pi and enhanced to support complex, long-horizon coding tasks that run for hours, involve hundreds of rounds of tool calls, and require repeated context compaction. LingCode delivers significant performance gains on some coding agent tasks, and we are considering open-sourcing it in the future.

![Image 4: Ling-3.1-flash evaluation results](https://intranetproxy.alipay.com/skylark/lark/0/2026/png/202156655/1791988674787-5f49370c-0853-4940-96ea-9f1e4ff20d57.png)

## [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#quickstart) Quickstart

### [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#sglang-recommended) SGLang (Recommended)

The day-0 SGLang image includes Ling-3.1-flash support, MTP (NEXTN) speculative decoding, and Hopper decode optimizations:

```
docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:dev-ling-3.1-flash
```

#### [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#run-inference) Run Inference

**Server** (8 × H200, TP8 + EP8):

```
docker run --gpus all --network host --ipc=host --rm \
  lmsysorg/sglang:dev-ling-3.1-flash \
  python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
    --model-path inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash \
    --tp 8 --ep 8 \
    --speculative-algorithm NEXTN \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
```

On 4 × GB300, use `--tp 4 --ep 4` instead. Hopper decode optimizations (optional, ~10% faster batch-1 decode) can be enabled with `SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_BLOCK_GEMV=1` and `SGLANG_ENABLE_FUSED_KDA_OUTPUT_QUANT=1`.

**Client**

```
curl -s http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "Ling-3.1-flash",
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
       "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true},
       "stream": true,
       "temperature": 1.0,
       "top_k": 20,
       "top_p": 0.95}'
```

Verified recipes for H200, GB300, H800, H100, and B200, plus HiCache (Mooncake L3), reasoning on/off, tool calling, and measured accuracy/speed numbers, are in the [SGLang Ling-3.1-flash cookbook](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/InclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash).

### [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#vllm) vLLM

#### [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#environment-preparation) Environment Preparation

```
pip install uv

uv venv ~/my_ling_env

source ~/my_ling_env/bin/activate

git clone -b vllm https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm.git

cd vllm

VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install --editable . --torch-backend=auto
```

#### [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#run-inference-1) Run Inference

**Server**

```
vllm serve "$MODEL_PATH" \
    --port "$PORT" \
    --trust-remote-code \
    --served-model-name auto \
    --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
    --enable-prefix-caching \
    --enable-expert-parallel \
    --mamba-cache-mode align \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice \
    --tool-call-parser ling3 \
    --reasoning-parser ling3 \
    --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
```

**Client**  
It is recommended to use the sampling parameters (`temperature=1.0`, `top_p=0.95`, `top_k=20`) and set `enable_thinking` to `true` for better performance.

```
curl -s http://${MASTER_IP}:${PORT}/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "auto", 
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
       "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": true},
       "stream": true,
       "temperature": 1.0, 
       "top_k": 20,
       "top_p": 0.95}'
```

## [](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ling-3.1-flash#training-content-summary) Training Content Summary

The public training-content summary identifying **Ling-3.1-flash** is available below. Please refer to the document for its covered model versions, training-content scope, summary version, and update date.

*   [Training-content summary (PDF)](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/AI-Transparency/resolve/main/Ling-3.1_TDS-Summary.pdf)
*   [Training-content documentation index](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/AI-Transparency)

This summary concerns training-content disclosure; it does not replace the model’s technical documentation, usage terms, or license.

kept.heading: HIRO-ACEV2: SIMULATING EXTREME WEATHER AT 3 KM RESOLUTION FOR A FRACTION OF THE COST (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: HiRO-ACEv2 simulates extreme weather at high accuracy and generates global 3 km climate data at 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD.
kept.article_text:
Title: HiRO-ACEv2: Simulating extreme weather at 3 km resolution for a fraction of the cost  | Ai2

URL Source: https://allenai.org/blog/hiro-acev2

Markdown Content:
We introduce [**HiRO-ACEv2**](https://huggingface.co/allenai/HiRO-ACEv2), the newest update to our High Resolution Output Ai2 Climate Emulator (HiRO-ACE) system. HiROv2 can reproduce even extremely rare rain, wind, and pressure events with high accuracy, while the full system can generate global 3 km climate data at about 1/300th the cost of X-SHiELD, a high-resolution global atmospheric model that explicitly simulates storms and other small-scale weather.

HiRO-ACE, [introduced earlier in 2026](https://allenai.org/blog/hiro-ace), has two parts: ACE, an AI model that operates at a coarser 100 km resolution, and HiRO, a model that sharpens those coarse outputs into fine 3 km detail. The biggest change in HiRO-ACEv2 is the new downscaling model, HiROv2, which can now 1) predict several high-resolution fields at once instead of just rainfall, so it can capture a much wider range of extreme weather, and 2) has improved skill in predicting extreme events.

Our main focus with HiRO-ACEv2 was to simulate extreme events well. Changes to how we train HiROv2 improved its ability to reproduce the most intense rain, wind, and pressure values. When given coarsened X-SHiELD data, it matches the target simulation's high-resolution statistics to within 3%, even for events so rare they occur only once in a million data points. It also accurately estimates the total energy of tropical cyclones, including storms it never saw during training, and generates hurricanes with realistic eyes and rain bands, though winds and pressure around the eye remain somewhat more lopsided than in X-SHiELD. Additionally, HiROv2 realistically generates strong winds flowing down mountain slopes.

We also trained an updated version of ACE for this system. Over a 10-year simulation, its hurricanes, average climate patterns, and overall distributions of rain, wind, and pressure all line up well with X-SHiELD. That tells us ACE's coarse simulations are a solid foundation for producing long-term high-resolution climate data.

Putting HiROv2 and ACE together, we generated a full year of global 3 km data. Its statistics closely match X-SHiELD's, even though HiRO was working from a simulation ACE ran on its own rather than from real X-SHiELD data. Across a 10-year run, the energy of HiRO-ACEv2's hurricanes is comparable to X-SHiELD's over the same period, and snapshots from that run show a variety of other extreme events that resemble those in X-SHiELD.

Overall, HiRO-ACEv2 offers researchers a flexible and inexpensive way to generate many versions of high-resolution rain, wind, and pressure data for extreme events over 10 years or more. Producing global high-resolution data with it costs roughly 300 times less than running X-SHiELD. If only one region is needed, the savings can be more than a hundred times greater, depending on the size of the area. We're also working on a streamlined version of HiROv2 that could make it more than ten times faster still.

We still have future work ahead of us: because HiRO learned from X-SHiELD, it only works with the version of ACE tuned to match X-SHiELD. That means it can't yet produce high-resolution data for other climates, such as a warmer future or the historical record in datasets like ERA5. Next, we plan to train on new X-SHiELD datasets, including one simulating a world 4°C warmer, so the system can handle different climates. We also plan to add outputs like near-surface temperature and snow and ice, which would allow for even more uses, such as snowpack prediction.

## Visualizing and using HiRO outputs

To make it easy to see what HiRO produces without running any inference, we built a [web demo](http://ace.allen.ai/) that shows pre-generated precipitation, wind, and sea-level pressure output from HiROv1 and HiROv2 side by side with X-SHiELD, the simulation they were trained on. The demo complements the quantitative comparisons in our [tech report](http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17693): it offers a quick visual check of how the outputs look, and lets users zoom in on their own region of interest to judge performance there.

For more in-depth analysis, the models are available to [download](https://huggingface.co/allenai/HiRO-ACEv2), and our [tutorial notebooks](https://ai2cm.github.io/ace/) walk through how to run them.
